domains.name: Swift Language Core
domains.summary: Optionals, value vs reference semantics, protocols, generics, closures, and error handling — the language questions iOS loops open with.

scenarios.title: Unwrap without the bang
scenarios.situation: Whiteboard round. The interviewer points at `let name: String? = fetchName()` and asks you to print it uppercased, but says force-unwrapping is an instant fail.
scenarios.prompt: Which is the safest idiomatic way to use this optional?
choices: Use `guard let name = fetchName() else { return }`, then use `name` non-optionally in the rest of the scope.
Write `print(fetchName()!.uppercased())` — it is concise and the value is probably there.
Write `if fetchName() != nil { print(fetchName()!.uppercased()) }` — the nil check makes the force unwrap safe.
Declare it as `String!` instead so the compiler stops complaining about optionals.
scenarios.why: guard let binds the wrapped value once and exits early on nil, so everything after it works with a non-optional. Force unwrap crashes on nil; checking != nil then force-unwrapping re-fetches and still risks races. Implicitly unwrapped optionals just hide the same crash.
scenarios.hint: What construct gives you a non-optional name for the rest of the function while handling nil in one place?
objectives: Bind optionals safely with if let / guard let

scenarios.title: Struct or class for a model?
scenarios.situation: System-design discussion. You are modeling a `Playlist` with a name and a list of songs that gets passed between view controllers.
scenarios.prompt: The interviewer asks: struct or class, and why?
choices: Start with a struct: value semantics give each owner an independent copy, so mutations in one screen cannot surprise another; reach for a class only when you need shared identity or inheritance.
Always use a class: structs copy on every assignment, which is too slow for models with arrays.
Always use a struct: classes are legacy Objective-C and banned in modern Swift.
It does not matter: Swift optimizes both to identical machine code, so pick by naming style.
scenarios.why: Swift convention is value types first. A struct copy is independent, which kills whole categories of aliasing bugs. Copy-on-write means Array/Dictionary/String copies are cheap until mutated. Classes are for shared mutable identity (a player, a session), reference semantics, and deinit.
scenarios.hint: Think about what breaks if two screens hold the same playlist and one edits it — do you want that edit shared or independent?
objectives: Choose value vs reference semantics deliberately

scenarios.title: The closure that never dies
scenarios.situation: Debugging round. A `ProfileViewController` never deallocates after dismissal. Its `viewDidLoad` contains: `api.fetchProfile { user in self.nameLabel.text = user.name }`.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause and the fix?
choices: A retain cycle: the closure captures `self` strongly, and the API client (owned by the VC, directly or not) holds the closure — use `[weak self]` in the capture list and `guard let self` inside.
The label holds a strong reference to the view controller; set `nameLabel = nil` in `viewDidDisappear`.
URLSession caches the closure forever; call `URLSession.shared.invalidateAndCancel()` on dismiss.
viewDidLoad runs twice in iOS 17; move the fetch to `viewDidAppear` to avoid double registration.
scenarios.why: Closures capture referenced objects strongly by default. If the closure's lifetime is tied (even transitively) to the object it captures, neither deallocates. The capture list `[weak self]` breaks the cycle; `guard let self = self else { return }` then gives a strong temporary for the body. Delegates avoid this by being declared `weak`.
scenarios.hint: Draw the ownership arrows: VC -> api client -> stored closure -> VC. Which arrow do you cut, and how?
objectives: Break retain cycles with capture lists

scenarios.title: Protocol with associated type
scenarios.situation: Architecture round. You propose `protocol DataSource { associatedtype Item; func item(at: Int) -> Item }` and then try to write `var source: DataSource` as a property.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the compiler reject the property, and what are your options?
choices: A protocol with an associated type (or Self requirement) cannot be used as an existential type directly — `any DataSource` still erases the associated type, so the property cannot be typed that way; use generics (`class Store<S: DataSource>`), type erasure, or redesign around a concrete requirement.
The compiler rejects it because protocols cannot have associated types at all; associatedtype is only for classes.
It compiles fine; `var source: DataSource` works in Swift 5 exactly like an interface in Java.
Add `@objc` to the protocol and the property will compile, since Objective-C protocols have no associated types.
scenarios.why: Associated types make the protocol generic over conforming types, so there is no single runtime layout for 'a DataSource'. Options: make the holder generic over `S: DataSource`, build a type-erased wrapper (AnyDataSource), or — often best in interviews — simplify the protocol so it needs no associated type.
scenarios.hint: If the protocol is generic over its conformers, what single concrete type could the property hold?

scenarios.title: Escaping closure across threads
scenarios.situation: Concurrency round. `func load(_ completion: @escaping (Result<Data, Error>) -> Void)` runs work on a background queue and calls completion there. The interviewer asks what can go wrong for the caller.
scenarios.prompt: What is the complete, correct answer?
choices: Three things: the closure is escaping so the caller must consider its lifetime (capture lists for self); it fires on a background queue so UI updates inside it must hop to the main queue; and Result must be handled for both cases — plus the API should document its callback queue.
Nothing — @escaping closures are always called on the main queue by the system.
Only that Result is awkward; the modern fix is to return an optional and document nil as failure.
The caller must wrap the call in a Task, because escaping closures cannot be called from non-async contexts.
scenarios.why: Escaping means the closure outlives the call: lifetime discipline (weak/strong dance) matters. Queue discipline matters equally: URLSession and GCD callbacks arrive off-main, so touching UI there is a bug that often manifests as flaky layout, not a crash. Senior answers also mention documenting the callback queue as API contract.
scenarios.hint: Trace the closure's two journeys: how long does it live, and which thread is it standing on when it runs?
objectives: Reason about escaping closures: lifetime + queue

scenarios.title: Design a generic cache
scenarios.situation: Whiteboard system design. 'Design an in-memory cache usable for any value type, keyed by String, with a max entry count.' You have 15 minutes.
scenarios.prompt: Which design earns full marks?
choices: A generic `final class Cache<Value>` with a dictionary plus an access-ordered doubly linked list (or ordered keys) for LRU eviction, `NSLock`/actor for thread safety, a `Value` unconstrained or constrained as needed, and a clear eviction policy stated up front — with the tradeoff discussion (simplicity vs O(1) ops).
A `[String: Any]` dictionary with a Timer that calls `removeAll()` every minute — simple and generic enough.
Subclass NSCache and override `object(forKey:)` with generics — NSCache is generic-ready and thread-safe.
Use UserDefaults with one key per entry — it persists for free and handles eviction via the OS.
scenarios.why: Interviewers grade the tradeoff narration, not just the code: why a class (shared identity) vs struct, why a lock or actor around the dictionary (dictionaries are not thread-safe), how eviction stays O(1), and what happens under memory pressure (hook `didReceiveMemoryWarning` / NSCache's auto-eviction as the discussed alternative).
scenarios.hint: Start by stating eviction policy and thread-safety plan before writing a line — the narration is half the grade.
objectives: Design generic components with stated tradeoffs

scenarios.title: The view controller that never deallocated
scenarios.situation: Memory grows with every push/pop of a detail screen. Instruments shows the view controllers never deallocate — each holds a closure property that captures self, and the closure is stored on an object the controller owns.
evidence: Observed: Memory grows with every push/pop of a detail screen. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain ARC and retain cycles (2) Fix cycles with capture lists Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct fix?
choices: A. Set the view controller to nil manually when popping; ARC needs help.

B. Break the retain cycle with a capture list: the closure captures self weakly ([weak self]) or unowned where the lifetime is provable — the cycle (controller -> closure -> controller) is the leak, and the capture list is the structural fix.
C. Retain cycles are unavoidable in UIKit; restart the app periodically.
D. Use assign instead of closures everywhere; closures are the problem.
scenarios.hint: Hint: who retains whom? Draw the arrows — the cycle is the leak.
scenarios.why: ARC deallocates when the reference count hits zero; a retain cycle (A retains B, B retains A) keeps both alive forever — the classic being a controller that owns an object holding a closure capturing the controller. The capture list ([weak self] / [unowned self]) breaks the cycle at the closure: the closure no longer strongly retains the controller, so popping the controller drops the last strong reference and both deallocate. weak (optional, nils out) is the safe default; unowned (non-optional, crashes if accessed after dealloc) only where the closure provably cannot outlive self. Manual nil-ing (choice A) fights the framework; the cycle is structural, fix it structurally.

scenarios.title: The shared model that mutated from two screens
scenarios.situation: A User object is passed to two screens; editing the name on one screen changes it on the other — sometimes desired, sometimes a bug. The team cannot predict which mutations are shared.
evidence: Observed: A User object is passed to two screens; editing the name on one screen changes it on the other — sometimes desired, sometimes a bug. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Choose value vs reference semantics (2) Apply copy-on-write reasoning Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct semantic choice?
choices: A. Always use classes; shared mutation is a feature.

B. Default to value types (structs) for models: copies are independent, mutation is local and predictable; use classes (reference semantics) only where shared identity is the requirement (view models, managers, coordinators) — the semantics should be a deliberate choice, not an accident.
C. Always use structs; classes are legacy.
D. Copy manually everywhere; semantics do not matter.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the bug is unpredictability. Which semantics make mutation LOCAL by default?
scenarios.why: Value types (structs, enums) copy on assignment: each screen's mutation is local, predictable, and thread-safe by isolation — the bug class of 'who changed my model' disappears. Reference types (classes) share: mutation anywhere is visible everywhere — correct for view models (the screen's shared state) and coordinators, wrong for data models where independence is expected. Swift's guidance (and the standard library's design) is value-first: the semantics are part of the type's contract. Always-classes (choice A) makes every mutation global; always-structs (choice C) cannot express shared identity where it is genuinely needed.

scenarios.title: The data source protocol that will not compile in an array
scenarios.situation: A DataSource protocol has an associatedtype Item. Storing [any DataSource] fails: 'protocol with associated type cannot be used as a type' (pre-Swift-5.7 style thinking), and heterogeneous sources cannot mix.
evidence: Observed: A DataSource protocol has an associatedtype Item. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Use PATs and existentials (2) Choose generics vs any Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct modern approach?
choices: A. Remove the associated type; use Any everywhere.

B. Use existentials deliberately: 'any DataSource' boxes heterogeneous conformers (with primary associated types or explicit constraints where needed); for homogeneous cases use generics (func load<D: DataSource>(_: D)). Choose generics for performance-critical homogeneous code, existentials for heterogeneous collections.
C. Associated types are broken; avoid protocols entirely.
D. One protocol per concrete type; duplication is clarity.
scenarios.hint: Hint: do you need MANY different sources in one array, or ONE source used generically?
scenarios.why: Associated types make protocols generic over their related types — powerful, but the protocol itself is not a concrete type. Swift 5.7+ existentials ('any DataSource') box conformers into a uniform type: heterogeneous arrays work, with the dynamic dispatch cost made explicit by the 'any' keyword. Primary associated types (protocol DataSource<Item>) let you write any DataSource<User> — constraining the box usefully. Generics (func load<D: DataSource>) keep the concrete type static — zero-cost abstraction for homogeneous use. The choice is architectural: existentials for type-erased collections, generics for static performance.

scenarios.title: The cache that must work for any key type
scenarios.situation: A cache is needed for String keys now, Int keys later, and custom keys eventually. The team copies the cache per key type — three implementations drifting apart.
evidence: Observed: A cache is needed for String keys now, Int keys later, and custom keys eventually. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Design generic types (2) Use opaque return types Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct generics design?
choices: A. Keep copying; each cache is simple.

B. One generic Cache<Key: Hashable, Value>: the key constraint (Hashable) is the only requirement the implementation needs; opaque return types (some View / some Cache) hide concrete types while preserving static performance — write once, use for every key type.
C. Use [AnyHashable: Any]; types are overhead.
D. Generics are too complex; use NSObject.
scenarios.hint: Hint: what does the cache implementation actually NEED from the key? Only that. Constrain to that.
scenarios.why: Generics express 'works for any T satisfying the constraints': Cache<Key: Hashable, Value> implements once against the Hashable contract — dictionary storage, subscript, eviction — and instantiates for String, Int, or custom keys with full type safety. The three copies (choice A) are a maintenance liability: a bug fix in one never reaches the others. [AnyHashable: Any] (choice C) compiles and then crashes at runtime on type mismatches — the 'flexibility' is untyped chaos. Opaque types (some View) are the companion feature: the function returns a specific-but-hidden type, keeping static dispatch while hiding implementation details — SwiftUI's entire view hierarchy is built on this.

domains.name: UIKit & SwiftUI
domains.summary: View controller lifecycle, Auto Layout, SwiftUI state and layout algorithm, and UIKit-SwiftUI interop with judgment for either.

scenarios.title: viewDidLoad vs viewWillAppear
scenarios.situation: UIKit round. The interviewer asks where to start a network fetch that should refresh every time the screen appears, and where one-time view setup goes.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct split?
choices: One-time setup (add subviews, constraints, static styling) in `viewDidLoad`; repeating work (refresh fetches, re-applying dynamic state, starting animations) in `viewWillAppear` — because viewDidLoad runs once per controller lifetime while viewWillAppear runs on every appearance including back-navigation.
Do everything in `viewDidLoad` — it runs every time the view appears, so it covers refreshes too.
Do everything in `viewDidAppear` — earlier methods run before the view exists.
Put setup in `init` and fetches in `deinit` to balance the lifecycle symmetrically.
scenarios.why: The lifecycle order is loadView -> viewDidLoad -> viewWillAppear -> viewDidLayoutSubviews -> viewDidAppear, then disappear in reverse. Code placed in the wrong hook either runs too often (duplicate observers, double fetches) or too rarely (stale data after popping back). Name the order cold — interviewers check it.
scenarios.hint: Which of these methods fires once per controller, and which fires every time the user navigates back to the screen?
objectives: Place work in the correct lifecycle hook

scenarios.title: State vs Binding
scenarios.situation: SwiftUI round. A parent view owns a `Bool` for showing a sheet; the sheet's content needs to toggle it off.
scenarios.prompt: How do you wire the state correctly?
choices: Parent declares `@State private var isPresented`, passes `$isPresented` into the child, and the child declares `@Binding var isPresented` — single source of truth lives in the parent; the child only borrows write access.
Both declare `@State var isPresented` — SwiftUI syncs same-named state automatically.
@Binding in the parent and @State in the child — bindings own the storage.
Use a global `static var` — it is visible to both views with no plumbing.
scenarios.why: @State owns storage private to a view; @Binding is a reference to someone else's state. Lifting state up (parent owns, child binds) is the core SwiftUI data-flow pattern, alongside @ObservedObject/@StateObject for reference-type models and @Environment for cross-cutting values.
scenarios.hint: Who should OWN the boolean, and what does the child need — ownership or a reference to it?

scenarios.title: Ambiguous layout in the console
scenarios.situation: Auto Layout round. The console spams 'Unable to simultaneously satisfy constraints' and a label is the wrong width at runtime.
scenarios.prompt: What is your systematic debugging approach?
choices: Read the conflicting constraint list in the log, identify the two constraints fighting over the same attribute, decide which one expresses intent, then lower a priority or remove the redundant one; use `exerciseAmbiguityInLayout` / view debugger and check intrinsic content size vs explicit width plus hugging/compression priorities.
Delete all constraints and rebuild with frames — Auto Layout logs are noise and frames never conflict.
Set every constraint priority to 1000 so the engine takes them all seriously.
Add `translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false` to every view twice to be safe.
scenarios.why: Conflicts mean over-constraining: two rules demand different values for one attribute. The fix is editorial, not additive — remove or demote, never pile on. Compression resistance and content hugging priorities resolve 'label vs fixed width' fights declaratively. Interviewers want the systematic read-the-log habit, not guessing.
scenarios.hint: The log names the fighters. What does it mean when two constraints claim the same attribute, and which one represents your real intent?

scenarios.title: The SwiftUI layout algorithm
scenarios.situation: SwiftUI deep-dive. 'Explain how SwiftUI decides a view's size' — the interviewer wants the three-step negotiation.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct explanation?
choices: Parent proposes a size to the child; the child chooses its own size within the proposal; the parent places the child in its coordinate space — and a child can only choose sizes the proposal allows, which is why fixed frames beat flexible stacks in fights.
Each view measures itself first, then tells the parent how big it is, then the parent shrinks to fit — bottom-up like UIKit's sizeToFit.
SwiftUI uses Auto Layout constraints under the hood, so the Cassowary solver decides sizes identically to UIKit.
Views have no say: the parent assigns frames directly, like UIKit's layoutSubviews.
scenarios.why: This three-step dance explains otherwise-mysterious behavior: why a `Text` in an `HStack` truncates (proposal too small), why `GeometryReader` is greedy (it takes all proposed space), and why `.fixedSize()` exists (lets the child ignore the proposal and use its ideal size). Teach the algorithm, then derive the behaviors.
scenarios.hint: Who moves first in the negotiation — parent or child — and what power does each side actually have?

scenarios.title: Wrapping a UIKit map
scenarios.situation: Interop round. The app is SwiftUI but the team needs `MKMapView` with custom annotations — 'wrap it properly.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct interop design?
choices: Conform to `UIViewRepresentable`: `makeUIView` creates the map once, `updateUIView` applies state-driven changes idempotently, and a `Coordinator` (via `makeCoordinator`) acts as the map's delegate, forwarding events back through bindings/closures.
Put the MKMapView in a UIHostingController and present it — hosting controllers bridge both directions automatically.
Subclass MKMapView as an ObservableObject so SwiftUI observes it directly.
Rewrite the map in pure SwiftUI with Canvas — interop is deprecated.
scenarios.why: UIViewRepresentable is the sanctioned bridge: create once, update declaratively. The Coordinator is the key insight — UIKit's delegate/target-action world needs an object to receive callbacks, and the coordinator (owned by SwiftUI) translates them into state changes. updateUIView must be idempotent since SwiftUI calls it on every state change.
scenarios.hint: UIKit speaks delegate; SwiftUI speaks state. What object stands between them translating both directions?
objectives: Bridge UIKit into SwiftUI with Coordinator

scenarios.title: Feed screen: pick your framework
scenarios.situation: Design discussion. 'Build the main feed of a social app — infinite scroll, images, like buttons, pull-to-refresh. UIKit or SwiftUI? Defend it.'
scenarios.prompt: Which answer shows senior judgment?
choices: Either can work — argue it: SwiftUI for speed of development and declarative state (List/LazyVStack, async image phases), UIKit for battle-tested cell reuse at massive scale and fine-grained prefetch control; then name the real risks (SwiftUI List performance quirks, UIKit boilerplate) and how you would mitigate and measure with Instruments.
SwiftUI always — UIKit is legacy and no serious team starts new screens in it.
UIKit always — SwiftUI cannot handle infinite scroll or images.
Whichever the interviewer prefers — agree with them to avoid conflict.
scenarios.why: There is no mandated winner; the grade is in the tradeoff analysis. Strong answers quantify: cell reuse and prefetch APIs in UIKit, declarative diffing and less code in SwiftUI, and a measurement plan (scroll FPS, memory during fast flings, Time Profiler). Mentioning a hybrid (SwiftUI screen, UIKit cells via interop) shows real-world pragmatism.
scenarios.hint: What breaks at 10k rows and fast flings, and how would you prove your choice handles it?
objectives: Defend framework choices with tradeoffs + measurement

scenarios.title: The detail screen that lost its scroll position
scenarios.situation: Navigating away and back resets the detail screen's scroll position and collapses expanded sections. The view rebuilds from scratch every appearance — viewDidLoad (or onAppear) re-runs the full setup.
evidence: Observed: Navigating away and back resets the detail screen's scroll position and collapses expanded sections. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Separate setup from appearance (2) Persist UI state correctly Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct lifecycle handling?
choices: A. Prevent navigation; the back button is the problem.

B. Separate one-time setup from appearance: viewDidLoad/.task once (or view-model init), viewWillAppear/onAppear for refresh-only work, and persist UI state (scroll offset, expansions) in the view model or state restoration — the view is ephemeral, the state is not.
C. Reload everything on every appearance; freshness beats state.
D. Keep the view controller alive forever; never deallocate.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the view is rebuilt; the user's place should not be. Where can 'place' live that outlives the view?
scenarios.why: Views are transient; state must live longer than the view: viewDidLoad (UIKit) runs once per instance, viewWillAppear runs every appearance — expensive setup belongs in the former, lightweight refresh in the latter. In SwiftUI, .task runs with the view's lifetime (cancelled on disappear — ideal for observations), onAppear re-runs per appearance. Scroll position and expansion state belong in the view model (or UIKit state restoration): the view reads them on appearance instead of resetting to defaults. Reload-everything (choice C) destroys the user's place for no benefit; never-deallocating (choice D) is a memory leak as architecture.

scenarios.title: The constraint conflict in the console
scenarios.situation: The console spews 'Unable to simultaneously satisfy constraints' — a 50-line dump. The layout 'mostly works' but a label is crushed on small screens. The team adds constraints until the warnings stop.
evidence: Observed: The console spews 'Unable to simultaneously satisfy constraints' — a 50-line dump. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Debug constraint conflicts (2) Use priorities correctly Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct Auto Layout debugging approach?
choices: A. Add more constraints until the warnings stop; volume wins.

B. Read the conflict: the log lists the conflicting constraints with their identifiers and priorities — find the two that fight (usually a required width vs content hugging), lower one's priority or remove the redundant one, and set identifiers on constraints to make the log readable. Ambiguity, not volume, is the disease.
C. Set translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false everywhere; that fixes conflicts.
D. Delete all constraints and use frames; Auto Layout is unreliable.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the log NAMES the conflicting constraints. What does it say is fighting?
scenarios.why: Constraint conflicts are over-determination: two constraints demand incompatible things (a required 200pt width vs a superview that is 150pt wide). Adding constraints (choice A) adds more fighters to the brawl — the log quiets only when the system breaks ties arbitrarily, which is why the label crushes 'randomly.' The fix is reading the log: each constraint prints with its identifier (set them! — constraint.identifier = 'titleWidth'), priority, and the views involved; the conflict names the redundant or over-prioritized constraint. Content hugging/compression resistance priorities are the usual suspects: the label's compression resistance vs the fixed width — lower one, or make the width <= instead of ==.

scenarios.title: The settings screen that would not refresh
scenarios.situation: A settings toggle writes to a view model, but the parent screen's summary does not update. The toggle's view model is a separate @StateObject from the parent's — two sources of truth for one setting.
evidence: Observed: A settings toggle writes to a view model, but the parent screen's summary does not update. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Design SwiftUI data flow (2) Enforce single source of truth Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct data-flow design?
choices: A. Post a notification on every change; the parent observes it.

B. Single source of truth: the setting lives in ONE @StateObject at the common ancestor; children receive @Binding (for value types) or share the @ObservedObject — the toggle writes through the binding, every reader observes the same object, and SwiftUI's dependency tracking refreshes exactly the affected views.
C. Make everything @State in every view; local state is simplest.
D. Reload the parent manually after each toggle.
scenarios.hint: Hint: two objects held 'the setting.' How many should?
scenarios.why: SwiftUI's data flow is a hierarchy of ownership: @State (owned here, private), @Binding (a reference to someone else's state — two-way), @StateObject (owns the observable object, lifetime-bound), @ObservedObject (observes an object owned elsewhere), @EnvironmentObject (observes ambient shared state). The bug was two owners for one setting — the toggle's StateObject and the parent's never synchronized because they were different objects. The fix unifies ownership: the ancestor's @StateObject is the truth; the toggle gets a @Binding (or observes the same object). Writes flow down through bindings, observations flow up through publishing — one truth, many readers, automatic refresh. Notifications (choice A) reintroduce the untyped spaghetti Combine was meant to replace.

scenarios.title: The collection view with four section types
scenarios.situation: A feed has four section types (hero, grid, list, carousel), each with different layouts. reloadData() on every update causes flicker, lost scroll position, and full re-renders — and the layout code is a switch statement from 2016.
evidence: Observed: A feed has four section types (hero, grid, list, carousel), each with different layouts. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Use diffable data sources (2) Compose layouts per section Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the modern UIKit approach?
choices: A. Keep reloadData; flicker is normal for feeds.

B. Diffable data source (NSDiffableDataSourceSnapshot — declarative state, automatic animated diffs) + compositional layout (per-section NSCollectionLayoutSection definitions) — updates are snapshots (no flicker, scroll preserved), layouts are composable per section.
C. Four separate collection views; isolation is simpler.
D. reloadData on a background thread; threading fixes flicker.
scenarios.hint: Hint: reloadData says 'everything changed.' What if you could say exactly what changed?
scenarios.why: Diffable data sources replace the imperative data-source protocol (numberOfItems, cellForItem) with snapshots: you declare the current state (sections + items, all Hashable), apply it, and the system computes the diff — animated insertions/deletions/moves, no flicker, scroll position preserved. Compositional layout replaces flow-layout math with declarative sections: each section type gets its own NSCollectionLayoutSection (hero: full-width paging; grid: 2-column; carousel: horizontal orthogonal scrolling) composed into one layout. The 2016 switch statement (layout per index path) becomes data: section kinds map to layout builders. Background reloadData (choice D) is a crash — UIKit is main-thread only.

domains.name: Concurrency on iOS
domains.summary: GCD, Operation queues, async/await, actors, and main-thread discipline — from dispatch basics to cancellation design.

scenarios.title: Why the main thread?
scenarios.situation: Fundamentals round. 'Why must UI updates happen on the main thread?'
scenarios.prompt: What is the accurate explanation?
choices: UIKit is not thread-safe: its classes assume serialized access from the main thread, so mutating views from a background queue causes race conditions — corrupted layout, missed draws, intermittent crashes. The main thread also runs the run loop that processes touch events and screen refreshes.
The main thread is simply faster — background queues are throttled by the OS.
It is a convention from Objective-C with no technical basis in Swift.
Background threads cannot allocate memory, and views need allocation.
scenarios.why: UIKit (and AppKit before it) was designed single-threaded; thread-safety was traded for performance. The rule is absolute: read or write any UIView/UIViewController off-main and you have a latent bug. URLSession completions, GCD callbacks, and async continuations all arrive off-main unless you hop back.
scenarios.hint: What breaks when two threads mutate the same view tree with no locks — and why did Apple choose not to add those locks?
objectives: State the main-thread rule and its reason

scenarios.title: async vs sync dispatch
scenarios.situation: GCD round. You need to run image decoding off the main thread, then update the UI.
scenarios.prompt: Which dispatch pattern is correct?
choices: `DispatchQueue.global(qos: .userInitiated).async { let img = decode(); DispatchQueue.main.async { self.imageView.image = img } }` — work off-main, hop back for UI; never `sync` from the main thread onto a serial queue you might already be on.
`DispatchQueue.main.sync { decode image; update UI }` — sync guarantees ordering.
`DispatchQueue.global().sync { ... }` from the main thread — sync is safer than async.
Run decoding on the main queue with `.userInteractive` QoS — the highest QoS prevents jank.
scenarios.why: async returns immediately (no blocking); sync blocks the caller until the block finishes — syncing from main to main deadlocks instantly, and syncing to a serial queue from its own block does too. QoS (.userInitiated for user-waiting work, .utility/.background for prefetch) tells the system how to prioritize, not which thread.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the calling thread under sync, and what does that imply if the caller is the main thread?

scenarios.title: Three fetches, one screen
scenarios.situation: GCD round. The profile screen needs user, posts, and followers from three endpoints before rendering.
scenarios.prompt: How do you coordinate them?
choices: Enter a `DispatchGroup` before each request, `leave` in each completion, and `notify(queue: .main)` to render — or modernize with `async let` / TaskGroup; either way, handle partial failure explicitly instead of hanging on a missing leave.
Chain them: fetch user, in its completion fetch posts, in its completion fetch followers — simple and ordered.
Fire all three and update the UI in whichever completion lands first.
Use a `DispatchSemaphore` with value 0 and wait on the main thread until all three signal.
scenarios.why: DispatchGroup is the classic 'many asyncs, one continuation' primitive — but every enter needs exactly one leave or notify never fires (a hang, not a crash, which is why it is insidious). Modern Swift prefers structured concurrency (`async let`), which the compiler helps keep balanced. Never semaphore-wait on main.
scenarios.hint: What breaks if one completion path forgets its matching call — and how does the failure manifest?

scenarios.title: Shared mutable cache
scenarios.situation: Modern concurrency round. Multiple tasks read/write a `[String: Data]` cache concurrently and it occasionally corrupts.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right fix in modern Swift?
choices: Isolate the dictionary in an `actor`: all access serializes through the actor, the compiler enforces isolation (no direct access from outside), and call sites use `await` — replacing the old serial-queue/barrier pattern with a compile-time guarantee.
Mark the dictionary `nonisolated` so all tasks can reach it quickly.
Wrap every access in `Task { }` — unstructured tasks serialize automatically.
Make it a global `var` — globals are implicitly thread-safe in Swift 6.
scenarios.why: Actors turn 'remember to use the queue' (a runtime discipline) into a compile-time rule: the type system rejects unsynchronized access. Mention the old GCD answer too (serial queue or barrier on a concurrent queue) — interviewers like hearing you know both eras. Also note actors are reentrant: awaits inside can interleave.
scenarios.hint: What did the serial-dispatch-queue pattern guarantee, and what does the actor add on top of it?

scenarios.title: The deadlock on main
scenarios.situation: Debugging round. The app freezes. The main thread's stack shows `DispatchQueue.main.sync` called from a block already running on the main queue.
scenarios.prompt: Explain the deadlock and the general rule.
choices: `sync` blocks the caller until the block executes; the block is queued on main, but main is blocked waiting — circular wait, permanent freeze. Rule: never `sync` onto the current queue (especially main); use `async`, or check `Thread.isMainThread` and branch.
The main queue is concurrent, so the block should have run — this must be an OS bug; file a radar.
sync always runs the block inline on the calling thread, so this cannot deadlock; the freeze is elsewhere.
The fix is `DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter(deadline: .now())` — the delay breaks the cycle.
scenarios.why: This is the canonical GCD interview trap: sync means 'wait'. Waiting on yourself is a textbook circular wait. The asyncAfter 'fix' only masks it. Senior follow-up: the same deadlock happens syncing onto any serial queue from a block already executing on it.
scenarios.hint: If sync means 'block until done' and the work is queued behind the blocked caller, who runs it?

scenarios.title: Images in a scrolling list
scenarios.situation: Architecture round. A feed loads thumbnails per row; fast scrolling shows wrong images flashing before the right ones.
scenarios.prompt: What is the complete fix?
choices: Cancel stale work: key each load to the cell's current item (or use `async` Tasks stored per index path and cancel on reuse / `prepareForReuse`), check cancellation before applying the image, and always set the image on the main thread — stale completions must never write to a reused cell.
Cache images in a global dictionary — once loaded, flashing stops.
Disable cell reuse so each row keeps its own image view forever.
Load images synchronously in `cellForRowAt` — ordering is then guaranteed.
scenarios.why: The bug is a race between reuse and completion: row 5's image arrives after the cell now shows row 42. Cancellation (Task.cancel, Operation.cancel, or invalidating a load token in prepareForReuse) plus a 'still the right item?' check before assignment is the full answer. This is also where SwiftUI's `.task` modifier shines — it auto-cancels when the view disappears.
scenarios.hint: Whose image is the cell showing when the slow request finally completes — and how does the cell know it is stale?
objectives: Design cancellation into async UI work

scenarios.title: The actor-isolated cache
scenarios.situation: A shared image cache is accessed from multiple tasks: reads and writes interleave, and occasionally a write lands mid-read producing a corrupted image. DispatchQueue.sync patches made deadlocks.
evidence: Observed: A shared image cache is accessed from multiple tasks: reads and writes interleave, and occasionally a write lands mid-read producing a corrupted image. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Design with actors (2) Apply Sendable correctly Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct Swift-concurrency design?
choices: A. More dispatch queues; the patching just needs tuning.

B. An actor: actor ImageCache with its methods — the compiler serializes access (actor isolation), await marks the suspension points visibly, and Sendable checking prevents sharing mutable state across tasks. The data race becomes a compile-time impossibility.
C. Make everything @MainActor; the main thread serializes all.
D. Locks around every access; actors are syntactic sugar.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the corrupted image is a data race. What language feature makes data races unrepresentable?
scenarios.why: Actors are the language-level answer to shared mutable state: all access to the actor's isolated state goes through the actor, serialized — no interleaving, no corrupted reads, no manual locks. await at the call site marks every potential suspension point, making the concurrency visible in the code (unlike the invisible interleaving of queues). Sendable conformance (checked by the compiler in Swift 6 mode) prevents the other race vector: passing mutable state between tasks. @MainActor for everything (choice C) serializes the world on the UI thread — correct, and janky. Locks (choice D) work but reintroduce the deadlock class the actor eliminates.

scenarios.title: The background fetch that blocked the UI
scenarios.situation: A 'background' fetch parses 10MB of JSON on a global queue with default QoS — but the UI still stutters. Investigation: the parse dispatches UI updates per-item (thousands of main-queue hops), and a QoS inversion lets the background work preempt the UI.
evidence: Observed: A 'background' fetch parses 10MB of JSON on a global queue with default QoS — but the UI still stutters. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Separate work phases (2) Apply QoS correctly Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct GCD discipline?
choices: A. More threads; the parse needs parallelism.

B. Boundaries and QoS: parse fully on a background queue (utility QoS), batch the result, hop to main ONCE with the complete model — and set QoS deliberately (userInitiated for user-waiting work, utility for background) so the system prioritizes correctly. Thousands of main-queue hops is the stutter.
C. Parse on the main thread; 10MB is small.
D. QoS does not matter; queues are queues.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the UI stuttered during a 'background' fetch. How many times did the background touch the main thread?
scenarios.why: Two bugs compound: the per-item main-queue hops (thousands of dispatches, each with overhead, each triggering UI work) and QoS inversion (background work at default QoS competing with the UI instead of yielding). The fix separates the phases cleanly: background queue (utility QoS — 'the user waits, but the UI stays alive') does ALL the parsing, then ONE dispatch to main delivers the finished model. QoS is the system's priority signal: userInteractive (main thread work), userInitiated (user waiting), utility (progress bars), background (prefetch) — mislabeled work gets misprioritized. Main-thread parsing (choice C) janks by construction; more threads (choice A) multiplies the hop overhead.

scenarios.title: The image pipeline with dependencies
scenarios.situation: An image pipeline needs: download -> filter -> thumbnail -> upload, with cancellation when the user scrolls past. GCD chains this with nested asyncs and a manual cancelled flag checked 'most places.'
evidence: Observed: An image pipeline needs: download -> filter -> thumbnail -> upload, with cancellation when the user scrolls past. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Model pipelines as operation DAGs (2) Propagate cancellation Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct abstraction?
choices: A. Nested GCD asyncs; the flag works if checked everywhere.

B. OperationQueue with Operation dependencies: each stage is an Operation, dependencies (filter depends on download) express the DAG, and cancellation propagates (cancel the queue/operations — each checks isCancelled at its checkpoints). The pipeline is data, not nested closures.
C. One giant async block; stages are overengineering.
D. Timers polling for stage completion.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the pipeline is a DAG with cancellation. Which API models DAGs with cancellation natively?
scenarios.why: Operation dependencies express the pipeline as a DAG: the queue runs operations whose dependencies are satisfied, in parallel where possible, in order where required — the 'download -> filter -> thumbnail -> upload' chain is four operations with three dependency edges, readable as the pipeline itself. Cancellation is first-class: cancelling the queue (or an operation) sets isCancelled, and well-written operations check it at checkpoints — the scrolled-past cell's pipeline dies promptly instead of uploading thumbnails for invisible rows. The manual flag (choice A) fails exactly where it is not checked ('most places' is not all places); nested GCD cannot express 'run these in dependency order with cancellation' without reimplementing OperationQueue badly.

scenarios.title: The analytics counter that lost events
scenarios.situation: An analytics counter increments from multiple threads: count += 1. Under load, 1000 increments yield 973 — the read-modify-write races. @Atomic does not exist in Swift.
evidence: Observed: An analytics counter increments from multiple threads: count += 1. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Fix read-modify-write races (2) Choose actor/queue/lock per context Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What are the correct thread-safety patterns?
choices: A. count += 1 is fine; 973 vs 1000 is acceptable loss.

B. Serialize the mutation: actor, serial dispatch queue, or lock (NSLock/os_unfair_lock) around the critical section — the pattern matches the context (actor for Swift-concurrency code, queue/lock for legacy). The race is read-modify-write; the fix makes it atomic.
C. Use volatile; it makes access atomic.
D. Dispatch to main for all increments; the main thread is the lock.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the increment is three steps, not one. Which step interleaves?
scenarios.why: count += 1 is read-modify-write: load, increment, store — two threads interleave (both load 5, both store 6) and an increment vanishes. The fix serializes the critical section: an actor (Swift-concurrency code — the modern answer), a serial dispatch queue (legacy code — sync/async barrier), or a lock (NSLock, or os_unfair_lock for the performance-sensitive). Swift has no 'volatile' (choice C is a Java/C++ import — and volatile was never atomicity anyway). Main-thread serialization (choice D) works but parks analytics on the UI thread — correct, and wasteful.

domains.name: Persistence on iOS
domains.summary: UserDefaults, Codable, Core Data, SwiftData, and Keychain — climbing the persistence ladder and defending each choice.

scenarios.title: Where does the auth token go?
scenarios.situation: Security round. The app gets a JWT after login and needs it across launches.
scenarios.prompt: Where should it be stored?
choices: In the Keychain (via the Security framework / a thin wrapper): it is encrypted, access-controlled by biometry/passcode policy, and not exposed in backups the way files are — UserDefaults is a plaintext plist and the wrong home for secrets.
UserDefaults — it persists across launches and takes one line of code.
A global `static var` — simple and fast, and it survives backgrounding.
Hardcode it in the binary — attackers cannot read compiled code.
scenarios.why: UserDefaults is an unencrypted plist — fine for settings, flags, and small preferences; never for tokens, passwords, or PII. Keychain items carry access groups, accessibility levels (e.g. unlocked-only), and survive app reinstall semantics differently. Say the tradeoff out loud: Keychain API is clunkier, so teams wrap it once.
scenarios.hint: What does the storage look like to someone who copies the app's sandbox off a jailbroken device?
objectives: Store secrets in Keychain, settings in UserDefaults

scenarios.title: Decode this JSON
scenarios.situation: Codable round. An endpoint returns snake_case keys and ISO8601 dates; your model uses camelCase and `Date`.
scenarios.prompt: How do you decode it cleanly?
choices: Configure `JSONDecoder` with `keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase` and `dateDecodingStrategy = .iso8601`, and only write custom `CodingKeys`/`init(from:)` for the odd keys the strategy cannot handle.
Name every property snake_case to match the JSON exactly — the server owns your model.
Decode into `[String: Any]` and cast each field manually — full control, no magic.
Write a regex that rewrites the JSON string to camelCase before decoding.
scenarios.why: Decoder strategies handle the 90% case declaratively; CodingKeys handle renames; a custom init(from:) is the escape hatch for truly irregular payloads. Mention the failure mode too: decoding errors name the key path, which makes them debuggable — unlike manual casting chains.
scenarios.hint: Which layer should own the snake_case knowledge — your model types, or the decoder configuration?

scenarios.title: Core Data background import
scenarios.situation: Core Data round. A sync imports 50k records; doing it on the view context freezes the UI.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct Core Data concurrency design?
choices: Do the import on a private-queue background context (`newBackgroundContext` or `performBackgroundTask`), save there, and let the view context merge via `automaticallyMergesChangesFromParent` — never touch a context or its managed objects off its own queue.
Do the import on the view context but wrap it in `DispatchQueue.global().async` — the queue hop is what matters.
Pass NSManagedObjects from the background context directly to the view controller — objects are thread-safe.
Disable the persistent store coordinator during import to avoid locking.
scenarios.why: Core Data's concurrency rule is queue confinement: each context belongs to its queue, and objects belong to their context — pass `objectID`s across queues, never objects. `perform`/`performAndWait` is the API. Merge policies (`NSMergeByPropertyObjectTrumpMergePolicy`) decide conflict winners. This is a favorite senior filter.
scenarios.hint: What may cross a queue boundary — the managed object, or something else?

scenarios.title: Offline article cache
scenarios.situation: Design round. A news app must show cached articles offline, refresh in background, and stay under 50MB.
scenarios.prompt: Which persistence stack do you choose and why?
choices: Core Data (or SwiftData on iOS 17+): a real object graph with fetch requests, predicates, batch deletes for the 50MB cap, and background contexts for sync — UserDefaults/FileManager JSON blobs cannot query or evict efficiently at that scale.
One big JSON file in Documents, rewritten on every sync — simplest possible persistence.
UserDefaults with one key per article — key-value is all you need.
Keep everything in memory and refetch on launch — offline mode is an edge case.
scenarios.why: The ladder: UserDefaults (settings) < Codable files (small documents) < SQLite/Core Data/SwiftData (queryable, relational-ish, large) < Keychain (secrets). Justify each rung by query needs, size, and relationships. The 50MB cap is the tell: you need eviction, which needs queries (LRU by date), which JSON blobs cannot do cheaply.
scenarios.hint: What operation does the 50MB cap force you to do regularly, and which store makes that operation cheap?

scenarios.title: Core Data model migration
scenarios.situation: Senior round. V2 of the app renames an entity attribute and makes it non-optional. Users have V1 data.
scenarios.prompt: How do you ship the migration?
choices: Ship a mapping model with a custom `NSEntityMigrationPolicy` if needed; lightweight migration handles the rename via the renaming identifier, but the new non-optional attribute needs a default value or custom policy — and you test the migration against real V1 stores, with a fallback (rebuild from server) if it fails.
Delete the old store on launch and re-download everything — migrations are not worth the code.
Just change the model; Core Data infers all migrations automatically including renames.
Version the app so V1 users cannot update — no migration needed.
scenarios.why: Lightweight migration covers additive changes; renames need renaming identifiers; anything structural (splits, non-optional without default) needs a mapping model, possibly custom policy code. The senior points: test with production-shaped V1 databases, migrate on a background queue with progress UI, and never ship a migration you cannot roll back from (keep the old store until success).
scenarios.hint: Which of your two changes is 'lightweight' and which one forces custom migration work?
objectives: Plan Core Data migrations with fallbacks

scenarios.title: Token refresh design
scenarios.situation: Security design round. 'Design token storage and refresh for our banking app.'
scenarios.prompt: What does a strong answer cover?
choices: Keychain with `kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly`, short-lived access tokens + rotating refresh tokens, refresh serialized through a single actor/queue to avoid stampedes, biometric-gated access for sensitive actions, certificate pinning discussion, and a logout path that wipes Keychain items and in-memory copies.
Store the token in UserDefaults and append it to every request header — refresh yearly.
One permanent token in the Keychain, never refreshed — rotation is server paranoia.
Keep the token only in memory — if the app restarts the user logs in again; simplest secure design.
scenarios.why: Interviewers score the threat model: where secrets rest, how they move, what happens on device loss (ThisDeviceOnly vs synced), and the refresh race (ten 401s triggering ten refreshes). Pinning and jailbreak detection are bonus discussion, framed as tradeoffs (pinning breaks corporate proxies; detection is advisory, not security).
scenarios.hint: What happens when ten requests get 401 at the same moment — and who coordinates the single refresh?
objectives: Design token lifecycle, not just token storage

scenarios.title: The token that survived reinstall
scenarios.situation: Auth tokens are stored in UserDefaults. A backup-restore moves them to a new device, and a jailbroken device reads them in plaintext. Worse: the token survived app reinstall, confusing the logout logic.
evidence: Observed: Auth tokens are stored in UserDefaults. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Store secrets in the keychain (2) Choose accessibility levels Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct secure-storage design?
choices: A. UserDefaults is fine; the backup behavior is a feature.

B. Keychain for secrets (tokens, credentials): hardware-backed encryption, access control (biometry/device-passcode policies), and explicit accessibility (when the item is readable) — plus deliberate handling of the reinstall case (kSecAttrAccessible choices, or explicit wipe on first launch). UserDefaults is for preferences, never secrets.
C. Encrypt tokens manually and keep them in UserDefaults; keychain is overkill.
D. Store tokens on the server only; the app fetches per request.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the token needs hardware encryption, access policy, and backup semantics. Which API was built for exactly that?
scenarios.why: UserDefaults is a plist: readable on jailbroken devices, included in backups, and synced — it is preferences storage wearing no security. The Keychain encrypts items with device keys (Secure Enclave on modern hardware), enforces access policies (require biometry, require device unlock), and offers accessibility levels controlling WHEN the item is readable (after first unlock, when unlocked, etc.). The reinstall survival is keychain behavior worth designing for: kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock items persist across reinstalls (same device, same backup) — handle it explicitly (wipe sensitive items on fresh install detection) instead of being surprised. Manual encryption in UserDefaults (choice C) reimplements the keychain badly — where do you store THAT key?

scenarios.title: The background import that crashed the UI
scenarios.situation: A background import writes 50k records on a background context while the UI reads on the main context. Crash: 'NSManagedObjectContext concurrency violation' — objects passed across threads.
evidence: Observed: A background import writes 50k records on a background context while the UI reads on the main context. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Apply Core Data thread confinement (2) Merge background changes Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct Core Data concurrency model?
choices: A. Do everything on the main context; background Core Data is too dangerous.

B. One context per queue: main (viewContext, mainQueueConcurrencyType) for UI, background (newBackgroundContext(), privateQueueConcurrencyType) for imports — pass OBJECT IDS (not objects) across threads, perform work in perform/performAndWait blocks, and merge via automaticallyMergesChangesFromParent.
C. Share one context across threads with a lock; locks fix everything.
D. Disable the concurrency debug flag; the crashes go away.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the crash names the rule: contexts are queue-confined. What crossed the boundary — and what is allowed to cross?
scenarios.why: NSManagedObjectContext is thread-confined: each context belongs to one queue, and touching its objects from another queue is the violation — the crash is the (correct) enforcement. The model: viewContext on main for UI reads, background contexts (private queue) for imports/writes, work wrapped in context.perform { } (which runs on the context's queue), and cross-thread references via NSManagedObjectID (thread-safe tokens, resolved per-context with object(with:)). automaticallyMergesChangesFromParent keeps the UI fresh as background saves land. Locking one shared context (choice C) serializes Core Data onto your lock and still violates the confinement contract; disabling the debug flag (choice D) hides the crash, not the corruption.

scenarios.title: The API that returns three date formats
scenarios.situation: The API returns dates as ISO8601 strings, unix timestamps, and occasionally null — in the SAME field across endpoints. The default JSONDecoder fails on two of the three, and nulls crash non-optional properties.
objectives: Contain API mess in the decoding layer
evidence: Observed: The API returns dates as ISO8601 strings, unix timestamps, and occasionally null — in the SAME field across endpoints. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Write custom decoding strategies (2) Contain API mess in the decoding layer Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct Codable strategy?
choices: A. Parse dates as Strings and convert manually everywhere.

B. Custom decoding: a dateDecodingStrategy closure (or custom Decodable init) that tries ISO8601, then timestamp, then nil — the messiness is contained in ONE decoding layer, and the model sees only Date?. Manual string juggling in view code is the alternative, and it is worse.
C. Ask the backend team to fix it; client workarounds are wrong.
D. Make every property a String; types are the problem.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the mess exists in one field. How many places should know about it?
scenarios.why: Real APIs are messy; the decoding layer is where mess goes to die: a custom dateDecodingStrategy (or init(from:) with a multi-format attempt sequence) centralizes the three-format handling in one place, so the other 200 call sites see clean Date? values. The strategy tries formats in order (ISO8601 -> timestamp -> nil for null), making the leniency explicit and reviewable. Manual string conversion (choice A) scatters the mess across the codebase — every view controller becomes a date parser. Backend fixes (choice C) are correct long-term and unavailable this sprint; the client must be robust to the API it has.

scenarios.title: The notes app that conflicts on two devices
scenarios.situation: A notes app syncs via 'last write wins' on whole documents. Editing the title on iPhone and the body on iPad loses one edit — the later sync overwrites the earlier, silently.
evidence: Observed: A notes app syncs via 'last write wins' on whole documents. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Design field-level sync (2) Resolve true conflicts honestly Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct sync design?
choices: A. Last-write-wins is fine; conflicts are rare.

B. Field-level granularity with version vectors or timestamps per field (or CRDTs for the ambitious): edits to different fields merge cleanly; true conflicts (same field, both changed) surface to the user with both versions. Offline-first means the local store is the truth and sync is reconciliation.
C. Prevent offline editing; require connectivity.
D. Lock the document during editing; no concurrent edits.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the two edits touched DIFFERENT fields. What sync granularity would have preserved both?
scenarios.why: Whole-document last-write-wins destroys the non-overlapping edit: the iPad's body edit overwrites the iPhone's title edit because the sync unit is the document. Field-level sync (each field carries its own version/timestamp) merges the title and body edits independently — the common case (different fields) resolves automatically. True conflicts (same field changed on both) cannot be auto-resolved honestly: surface both versions and let the user choose — silent data loss is never the right resolution. Offline-first inverts the architecture: the local database is the source of truth, the server is a sync peer; the app works fully offline and reconciles when connected.

domains.name: App Architecture & Testing
domains.summary: MVC/MVVM, coordinators, dependency injection, and making view models unit-testable.

scenarios.title: Massive view controller
scenarios.situation: Architecture round. A `CheckoutViewController` is 2,400 lines: networking, validation, analytics, navigation.
scenarios.prompt: What is your refactoring plan?
choices: Extract along responsibility lines: a view model (or presenter) owns state/validation, a service layer owns networking, a coordinator owns navigation, analytics moves to a thin wrapper — the VC keeps only view binding; each extraction gets a protocol seam so it is testable.
Split the file into four files of 600 lines each with the same code — smaller files are cleaner.
Rewrite it in SwiftUI — declarative UI has no massive view controllers.
Add `// MARK:` sections — organization is a navigation problem, not an architecture problem.
scenarios.why: MVC on iOS decays into 'Massive View Controller' because the controller absorbs model, networking, and flow logic. MVVM moves state/logic to a testable view model; coordinators remove navigation; DI removes singletons. The interview grade is the extraction order: start with the most testable seam (validation logic), not a big-bang rewrite.
scenarios.hint: Which responsibility in that file can you test today without launching the app — and what is blocking the rest?
objectives: Decompose massive view controllers by responsibility

scenarios.title: What is dependency injection?
scenarios.situation: Fundamentals round. 'Explain dependency injection and why iOS teams care.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the crisp answer?
choices: DI means a type receives its collaborators (usually via initializer) instead of constructing them: it makes dependencies explicit, lets tests substitute fakes/mocks, and removes hidden singletons — on iOS it is how view models become unit-testable without networking or databases.
DI is Apple's framework for injecting views into view controllers — like @IBOutlet.
DI means using singletons everywhere so dependencies are always available.
DI is a design pattern only relevant to server-side Java.
scenarios.why: Initializer injection is the default; property injection and containers (Swinject-style or hand-rolled factories) scale it. The testability argument is the one that lands: a view model taking `protocol APIClient` can be tested with a stub in milliseconds, while one that constructs `URLSession.shared` internally cannot.
scenarios.hint: Take one concrete class in the app — where are its dependencies born, and who could swap them in a test?

scenarios.title: MVVM without Combine
scenarios.situation: Architecture round. The team bans Combine/Rx — 'show me MVVM binding without reactive frameworks.'
scenarios.prompt: What is a credible binding mechanism?
choices: A tiny `Observable<T>` box class (value + listener closure, firing on set) that the view model exposes and the VC observes with `[weak self]` — or delegate callbacks / closures per event; the point is the mechanism is 20 lines, explicit, and has no framework magic to debug.
Poll the view model on a Timer every 100ms and re-render — simple and framework-free.
Use NotificationCenter for every property change — it is built in.
MVVM requires a reactive framework; without one you must use MVC.
scenarios.why: The binding mechanism is an implementation detail; MVVM is the separation (view: dumb rendering, view model: state + logic, model: data). A hand-rolled observable demonstrates you understand what the frameworks do for you (subscription management, thread hopping) — which is exactly what the 'no frameworks' constraint is testing.
scenarios.hint: Strip Combine away: what three jobs was it doing for your binding, and what is the simplest code that does each?
objectives: Build minimal bindings when frameworks are banned

scenarios.title: Coordinators
scenarios.situation: Navigation round. Deep links, A/B-tested onboarding, and modal chains have navigation logic scattered across VCs.
scenarios.prompt: Why do coordinators help, and what do they own?
choices: A coordinator owns a flow: it creates VCs, pushes/presents them, handles deep-link routing into the middle of flows, and is the single place where 'what screen comes next' lives — VCs stop knowing about each other and become reusable; child coordinators compose for sub-flows with clean teardown.
Coordinators are Apple's replacement for segues in storyboards.
They own the network layer so VCs stay thin.
They are just a naming convention for view controllers with many segues.
scenarios.why: The tell is reusability: a `ProductViewController` that pushes `CheckoutViewController` itself cannot be reused in search results. With coordinators, VCs emit events ('user tapped buy') and the coordinator decides the flow. Memory discipline matters: coordinators must release child coordinators or flows leak.
scenarios.hint: Which object in your current design knows that 'buy' leads to checkout — and could that screen be reused somewhere else today?

scenarios.title: Test the view model
scenarios.situation: Testing round. `LoginViewModel` calls a real API inside `URLSession.shared.dataTask`. 'Make it unit-testable.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the full recipe?
choices: Inject the networking behind a protocol (`APIClient`), give the test a stub implementation returning canned JSON/errors, assert state transitions (loading -> success/error) — and for URLSession specifics, stub at `URLProtocol` level so no real network runs; tests stay deterministic and fast.
Run the tests against the staging server — real responses are the only honest test.
Mark the test `async` and hope the network is fast in CI.
Testing view models is not practical; test only pure functions.
scenarios.why: The seam is the point: protocol-inject the client, and URLProtocol subclassing intercepts at the foundation level for integration-ish tests without sockets. Also assert the unhappy paths (401, malformed JSON, timeout) — interviewers check that your 'testable' claim covers failure, not just the golden path.
scenarios.hint: Where exactly does the real network enter this object, and what is the narrowest seam you can cut there?

scenarios.title: Offline-first notes app
scenarios.situation: System design. 'Design an offline-first notes app with sync.' 20 minutes.
scenarios.prompt: What architecture do you present?
choices: Local-first: SwiftData/Core Data as source of truth, repository mediating local vs remote, a sync engine with operation queue (create/update/delete tombstones), conflict resolution strategy stated (last-write-wins with vector clocks discussed, or server-wins for simplicity), background URLSession sync, and UI reflecting sync state per note.
Just call the API and cache responses in memory — offline is a nice-to-have.
Store notes as files and rsync them on launch — files are the simplest sync.
Use iCloud only — Apple handles all sync, no architecture needed.
scenarios.why: The graded pieces: single source of truth (UI never reads the network directly), the outbox pattern for offline writes, conflict strategy with a named tradeoff, and idempotency. Draw the layers: UI -> ViewModel -> Repository -> (Local store + Sync engine -> API). Mention what you would NOT build first (real-time collaboration).
scenarios.hint: A user edits the same note offline on two devices. Walk me through exactly what happens at sync time in your design.

scenarios.title: The view model with UIKit imports
scenarios.situation: A 'view model' imports UIKit, formats dates for labels, and holds IBOutlets via a delegate. It is a view controller renamed — untestable without the UI, and the Massive View Controller just moved.
evidence: Observed: A 'view model' imports UIKit, formats dates for labels, and holds IBOutlets via a delegate. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Define the view-model contract (2) Keep view models testable Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What makes a view model a view model?
choices: A. The name; MVVM is about naming conventions.

B. Platform-independent, UI-framework-free state + logic: the view model exposes @Published state and intents (methods), owns no UIKit/SwiftUI types, formats nothing for display (the view formats), and is fully testable with injected dependencies — the view is a thin rendering of the view model's state.
C. View models should own the navigation; coordinators are overkill.
D. Put all logic in the view model, including networking singletons.
scenarios.hint: Hint: can you instantiate it in a test without importing UIKit? That is the whole test.
scenarios.why: MVVM's contract: the view model is the view's testable model — it holds state (@Published), exposes intents (load(), toggle()), and knows NOTHING about UI frameworks (no UIKit import, no UIFont, no 'label text' formatting — the view formats values for display). The scenario's 'view model' violates all of it: UIKit imports, display formatting, outlet management — a view controller with a new name, carrying the same untestability. The real split: view model = what to show + what the user can do (testable, platform-free); view = how it looks (thin, declarative). Navigation belongs to coordinators (choice C confuses the patterns); networking goes behind injected protocols (choice D's singletons are the testability killer from the testing domain).

scenarios.title: The deep link into a tab the user never opened
scenarios.situation: A push notification should open an order three tabs deep. Navigation logic is scattered: view controllers push each other, the tab bar is manipulated from four places, and the deep link is unimplementable.
evidence: Observed: A push notification should open an order three tabs deep. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Centralize navigation in coordinators (2) Implement deep links Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What does the coordinator fix?
choices: A. Nothing; view controllers pushing each other is the iOS way.

B. Centralize flow in coordinators: a coordinator owns a navigation stack/tab, exposes start() and deep-link handlers (showOrder(id)), and view controllers emit events (didTapOrder) instead of navigating — the flow is one object's explicit state machine, drivable from a notification.
C. More segues; storyboard segues centralize flow.
D. A global NavigationManager singleton with 40 methods.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the deep link needs the ENTIRE flow built at once. Which object knows the entire flow?
scenarios.why: Scattered navigation is implicit flow: no object knows the whole journey, so deep links (which need the whole journey constructed at once) are impossible. The coordinator makes flow explicit: AppCoordinator owns children (one per tab), each child coordinator owns its navigation controller and the sequence of screens within it. View controllers report events up (delegate/closure: 'user tapped order 7'); the coordinator decides what happens (push detail, switch tab, present modal). The deep link becomes: appCoordinator.handle(.order(7)) -> select tab -> child.showOrder(7) — constructible because the flow lives in one place. The singleton manager (choice D) centralizes without structure — 40 methods of the same spaghetti.

scenarios.title: The singleton network client in every test
scenarios.situation: NetworkManager.shared is referenced in 60 files. Tests hit the real API (flaky, slow), and swapping the base URL for staging requires a code change. The singleton is load-bearing.
evidence: Observed: NetworkManager.shared is referenced in 60 files. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Apply constructor injection (2) Build a composition root Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct DI approach on iOS?
choices: A. Keep the singleton; it works in production.

B. Constructor injection via protocols: types take their collaborators as init parameters (typed as protocols); a composition root (app delegate/coordinator/factory) wires production implementations; tests inject fakes. The singleton becomes one injectable implementation, not a global.
C. More singletons, one per environment; switch at launch.
D. Global variables instead of singletons; simpler syntax.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the test needs a fake client. What in the design decides whether 'shared' can become 'fake'?
scenarios.why: The singleton's costs are the test's symptoms: global mutable state (tests interfere), hardcoded collaborators (no fakes), and environment baked in (staging needs a code change). Constructor injection inverts it: init(client: NetworkClient) — the type declares its needs, the composition root (where the app is assembled: scene delegate, coordinator, factory) provides the production client, tests provide fakes. The protocol is the seam: NetworkClient with URLSessionClient and FakeClient conformers. Environments become configuration: the composition root reads the scheme/build config and injects the right base URL — no code changes, no singletons. Property injection and service locators are halfway houses; constructor injection is the explicit, compiler-checked form.

scenarios.title: The 40-minute clean build
scenarios.situation: The app is one 800k-line target: clean builds take 40 minutes, every PR rebuilds the world, and two teams constantly conflict on the same target's files. Incremental builds help until they do not.
objectives: Enforce architecture via the package graph
evidence: Observed: The app is one 800k-line target: clean builds take 40 minutes, every PR rebuilds the world, and two teams constantly conflict on the same target's files. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Modularize by feature/layer (2) Enforce architecture via the package graph Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct modularization strategy?
choices: A. Faster Macs; 40 minutes is a hardware problem.

B. Extract Swift packages by feature/layer (Networking, DesignSystem, FeedFeature...): explicit dependency graphs, independent compilation (unchanged modules skip rebuilding), clear ownership per module, and enforced boundaries (the UI cannot import the database directly). Build time and team conflicts both collapse.
C. Split into 50 tiny modules immediately; more is better.
D. One module per file; ultimate granularity.
scenarios.hint: Hint: what rebuilds when one file changes — and what SHOULD rebuild?
scenarios.why: Monolith build time is superlinear: one target means one compilation unit graph — any change potentially rebuilds everything, and clean builds pay the full 40 minutes. Feature/layer modules (Swift packages) make the dependency graph explicit: changing FeedFeature rebuilds FeedFeature and its dependents only; DesignSystem (a leaf) almost never rebuilds. The boundaries are architectural, not just build performance: the package graph ENFORCES layering (FeedFeature cannot import DatabaseImpl if the graph forbids it) — the compiler becomes the architecture reviewer.
