Team conflicts drop because teams own modules, not files in a shared target. 50 tiny modules (choice C) drown in overhead; the granularity is features/layers, not files.

domains.name: Guided App Build
domains.summary: Scope a take-home, structure the project, build the networking layer, and self-review like the grader.

scenarios.title: Scoping the take-home
scenarios.situation: Take-home round. You get a 4-hour take-home: 'Build a GitHub repo browser.'
scenarios.prompt: How do you scope it to win?
choices: Read the rubric first: ship a small vertical slice done well — list, detail, search, loading/error/empty states, one clean architecture layer, tests on the view model — and write a README covering decisions and what you would add with more time; polish beats feature count.
Implement every GitHub feature you can think of — breadth impresses reviewers.
Spend 3 hours on custom animations and 1 hour on everything else — delight wins.
Skip the README and tests — reviewers only run the app.
scenarios.why: Reviewers grade decision quality under constraint: a tight slice with error states and a README that names tradeoffs beats a sprawling half-working app. Timebox explicitly (e.g., 1h architecture, 2h features, 1h polish/tests) and say what you cut and why.
scenarios.hint: If you only get credit for what is finished and documented, what do you deliberately leave out?
objectives: Scope take-homes to a polished vertical slice

scenarios.title: Project structure
scenarios.situation: Build round. Greenfield app, two engineers, expected to grow for years.
scenarios.prompt: How do you structure the project?
choices: Feature-based groups (Features/Search, Features/Detail) with shared Core (Networking, Persistence, UI components), protocols at module boundaries, and a flat dependency direction (features depend on Core, never each other) — navigable on day one, splittable into modules later.
One group per layer: all view controllers together, all models together — layers are the natural split.
A single group with everything — Xcode search is fast enough.
Mirror the storyboard scenes as groups — the UI is the architecture.
scenarios.why: Feature grouping scales because a new hire opens one folder and sees a whole vertical slice; layer grouping scatters one feature across five folders. Keep dependency arrows pointing one way so extracting a Swift package later is mechanical. Name the rule: 'a feature folder should build in your head without opening another.'
scenarios.hint: A new hire joins to fix a bug in search. How many folders must they open to understand the whole flow?
objectives: Structure by feature, depend one way

scenarios.title: Networking layer
scenarios.situation: Build round. Design the app's networking layer before writing screens.
scenarios.prompt: What does a strong networking layer look like?
choices: A protocol-based client (`APIClient` with `func request<T: Decodable>(_ route: Route) async throws -> T`), routes as an enum building URLRequests, one place for auth headers/retry/token refresh, errors as a typed enum (not NSError passthrough), and injectable session for tests.
Call `URLSession.shared.dataTask` directly in each view model — fewer abstractions, fewer bugs.
A singleton `NetworkManager` with a method per endpoint — discoverable and simple.
Embed URLs as string literals at each call site — the endpoint list lives in the API docs anyway.
scenarios.why: The enum-of-routes pattern centralizes URL construction (one place to change the host), the generic request method centralizes decoding and error mapping, and protocol injection makes every view model testable. Token refresh belongs here too — serialized, so concurrent 401s trigger one refresh.
scenarios.hint: When the API host changes or auth headers rotate, how many files do you touch?

scenarios.title: Error states are UI
scenarios.situation: Build round. Your list screen handles loading and content. The reviewer asks about the rest.
scenarios.prompt: What completes the state matrix?
choices: Every async screen models loading / content / empty / error / offline explicitly — each with its own view state, copy, and retry action — because users spend most of their time in edge states on real networks, and reviewers check them first.
A single alert on failure — errors are exceptional, one handler covers all.
Crash-free is enough: if the request fails, show the last good data silently.
Log errors to the console — users do not read error screens anyway.
scenarios.why: The state matrix is a senior shibboleth: juniors demo the happy path, seniors demo airplane mode. Design it as a single enum (`ViewState`) driving the UI so no state is unreachable, and give error states a retry that actually re-fires the request.
scenarios.hint: Turn on airplane mode and open your screen. What exactly does the user see — and can they recover without restarting?
objectives: Design every async screen's full state matrix

scenarios.title: The Instruments pass
scenarios.situation: Build round. The feed scrolls but stutters on old devices. You have one hour.
scenarios.prompt: What is your systematic performance pass?
choices: Profile first with Time Profiler (find the hot function — often image decoding or date formatting on main), fix the measured bottleneck (decode off-main, cache formatters, flatten view hierarchy), re-measure, then check Allocations/Leaks for growth during scrolling — never optimize without a before/after trace.
Rewrite the feed in UIKit — SwiftUI is the obvious cause.
Lower image quality globally — fewer pixels, less work.
Add `DispatchQueue.global().async` around the whole cell configuration — background everything.
scenarios.why: Performance work is measurement work: Time Profiler finds CPU, Allocations finds growth, Leaks finds cycles. Classic iOS wins: move decoding/formatting off main, reuse formatters (they are expensive to create), prefetch, and keep `body`/cell configuration cheap. Quote numbers in the interview — 'dropped p95 frame time from 28ms to 11ms' beats 'it feels faster.'
scenarios.hint: Before changing code, what single artifact tells you where the time actually goes?

scenarios.title: Self code review
scenarios.situation: Build round. The app works. You have 30 minutes before submitting the take-home.
scenarios.prompt: What is your self-review checklist?
choices: Read the diff like a reviewer: remove dead code and print statements, check every force unwrap/try!, verify error and empty states, run on a small device + airplane mode, confirm the README explains setup/decisions/cut scope — then submit.
Add three more features — a bigger diff looks more impressive.
Reformat everything with a new style — fresh formatting signals care.
Submit immediately — reviewing your own code adds no value.
scenarios.why: Reviewers form opinions in the first five minutes: a clean diff, no force unwraps, handled edge states, and a README that preempts their questions ('why MVVM?', 'what would you add?'). The last 30 minutes buys more signal than the previous two hours of feature work.
scenarios.hint: What will the reviewer see in the first five minutes, and what in your diff right now would make them frown?
objectives: Review your own diff like the grader

scenarios.title: The API client with auth refresh
scenarios.situation: Every API call site handles 401s independently: 12 copies of 'refresh token and retry' scattered across view models, each slightly different, two with bugs. A token-format change means 12 edits.
evidence: Observed: Every API call site handles 401s independently: 12 copies of 'refresh token and retry' scattered across view models, each slightly different, two with bugs. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Centralize networking mechanics (2) Declare endpoints as data Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct networking layer design?
choices: A. A shared helper function for refresh; copy-paste with a helper is fine.

B. Centralized client: ONE network layer (protocol + implementation) owns auth (token storage, 401 -> refresh -> retry transparently), request building, decoding, and error mapping — call sites declare endpoints; the client handles the mechanics. 12 copies become 0.
C. Each screen owns its networking; independence is good.
D. Put the refresh logic in the AppDelegate; central is central.
scenarios.hint: Hint: 12 copies of 'refresh and retry.' How many should there be?
scenarios.why: Cross-cutting mechanics (auth refresh, retry, decoding, error mapping) belong in ONE layer: the client intercepts 401s, refreshes the token, and retries transparently — call sites never see auth at all. Endpoints are declarative (enum cases: .feed(page), .order(id)) mapping to paths/methods/parameters; the client executes them. A token-format change touches one file. The 12 buggy copies (choice A's helper still leaves the retry orchestration scattered) collapse into tested-once logic. The layer is also the test seam: the protocol fakes for view-model tests, and the client's auth flow gets its own integration tests.

scenarios.title: The offline banner that never appeared
scenarios.situation: The app fails silently offline: spinners spin forever, buttons do nothing, and the error is logged where no user will ever see it. Users think the app is broken — because for them, it is.
evidence: Observed: The app fails silently offline: spinners spin forever, buttons do nothing, and the error is logged where no user will ever see it. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Design error states (2) Map typed errors to UX Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct error-handling design?
choices: A. Log errors; developers read logs.

B. Errors are UI: a typed AppError (network, auth, validation, server) maps to user-facing states — offline banner with retry, auth errors route to login, validation highlights fields, and every loading state has an error state designed. The error path is a designed screen, not an afterthought.
C. Show alert dialogs for every error; visibility is everything.
D. Retry silently forever; the user should not know.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the spinner has no error state. What SHOULD the user see when the request fails?
scenarios.why: Every async operation has three states (loading, success, error) — the app designed two. The fix is treating error as a first-class UI state: a typed error enum lets the view switch on the KIND (offline -> banner + retry button; 401 -> login flow; validation -> inline field errors; server 500 -> 'try again later' with report). The offline banner is the canonical example: persistent, non-blocking, with a retry action — the user understands and recovers. Alert-per-error (choice C) trains dismissal; silent retry (choice D) spins forever; logs (choice A) are for developers, and the user is not a developer.

scenarios.title: The feed that grew memory forever
scenarios.situation: Scrolling the feed grows memory without bound — 500MB after 5 minutes, then jetsam kills the app. The team guesses ('maybe images') and adds NSCache with a guess-sized limit. Memory still grows.
evidence: Observed: Scrolling the feed grows memory without bound — 500MB after 5 minutes, then jetsam kills the app. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Profile with generations (2) Verify fixes by re-measurement Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct Instruments workflow?
choices: A. Guess and patch; profiling takes too long.

B. Measure first: Allocations instrument with generations (mark before/after scrolling — the growth between marks IS the leak), Leaks for cycles, Time Profiler for the CPU side — the generation diff names the exact surviving objects; fix what it proves, not what you guess.
C. NSCache everywhere; caching fixes memory.
D. Lower the image quality; smaller images, smaller problem.
scenarios.hint: Hint: memory grew, but WHAT grew? The guess said images. What does the generation diff say?
scenarios.why: Unbounded growth has a specific cause, and guessing ('maybe images') treats the symptom class, not the instance: the NSCache guess did not help because the leak was abandoned view controllers (a retain cycle), not images. The Allocations generation workflow is the diagnosis: mark generation A, scroll, mark B — the diff lists exactly what survived and should not have (the view controllers, the closures, the image pipeline's unreleased buffers). Leaks finds the cycles; the memory graph shows the retaining path. Fix the proven cause (break the cycle / bound the cache with eviction), re-run generations, and watch the growth flatten — the measurement IS the verification.

scenarios.title: The design that broke at large text sizes
scenarios.situation: The design looks perfect at default text size. At Accessibility XXXL, labels truncate, buttons overlap, and the layout breaks — discovered by a user with low vision, not by testing. The app is effectively unusable for them.
evidence: Observed: The design looks perfect at default text size. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Design for Dynamic Type (2) Verify with VoiceOver Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct accessibility practice?
choices: A. Lock the text size; the design is the design.

B. Design for the range: Dynamic Type throughout (preferred fonts, no fixed heights on text containers), layouts that grow (stacks over fixed frames), full VoiceOver labels/hints on interactive elements, and TEST at XXXL + VoiceOver — accessibility is a design constraint from the start, not a retrofit.
C. Accessibility is a nice-to-have for version 2.
D. Larger default font for everyone; one size fits all.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the user changed ONE system setting and the app broke. What design assumption did that setting violate?
scenarios.why: Fixed-size design is exclusionary by construction: iOS users who need larger text (low vision, aging) get a broken app — and it is a large population, not an edge case. The practice: Dynamic Type (UIFont.preferredFont / .font(.body) with scaling) so text follows the user's setting; layouts that accommodate growth (stacks, wrapping, scrollable containers — never fixed-height labels); meaningful accessibility labels/hints (the 'x' button says 'Close', not 'x'); and verification at the extremes (XXXL + VoiceOver on every screen). Locking text size (choice A) is both hostile and App-Store-risky; 'version 2' (choice C) ships exclusion as a feature.

domains.name: Mock Interview Circuit
domains.summary: Full-loop rehearsal: rapid-fire fundamentals, whiteboard coding, debugging under time, and behavioral STAR.

scenarios.title: Explain ARC in 60 seconds
scenarios.situation: Phone screen. 'Explain Automatic Reference Counting like I'm a smart backend engineer.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the 60-second version that passes?
choices: Swift tracks how many strong owners each class instance has; when the count hits zero it deallocates immediately and deterministically — no garbage collector pauses. The interview-relevant part: strong/weak/unowned annotations control the count, and cycles (A owns B owns A, or a closure capturing self) leak because the count never reaches zero.
ARC is Swift's garbage collector — it pauses your app periodically to free memory.
ARC means you never think about memory — the compiler handles everything including cycles.
ARC only applies to structs; classes use manual retain/release.
scenarios.why: The backend-engineer framing wants the contrast: deterministic refcounting vs tracing GC (no pause-the-world, but cycles leak instead of being collected). Then land the iOS specifics: weak for delegates, capture lists for closures, unowned only when lifetime is provably longer.
scenarios.hint: If there is no garbage collector, what frees the object — and what single pattern defeats that mechanism?
objectives: Explain ARC crisply with the cycle caveat

scenarios.title: Whiteboard: debounce
scenarios.situation: Coding round. 'Implement debounce for a search field: wait 300ms after the last keystroke before firing.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the clean approach?
choices: Keep a `Timer`/`Task` handle; on each keystroke invalidate/cancel the previous one and schedule a new one for +300ms; fire the search in the handler — and in modern Swift, a cancellable `Task` with `try? await Task.sleep` checked for cancellation is the idiomatic version.
Sleep 300ms on the main thread after each keystroke, then fire — the delay accumulates naturally.
Fire the search on every keystroke and let the server deduplicate.
Use a while loop checking the clock — precise and dependency-free.
scenarios.why: Debounce = cancel previous, schedule new. The interview checks two things: cancellation discipline (invalidating the timer/task) and thread awareness (UI work back on main). Mention throttle vs debounce unprompted — it signals you know the family, not just the one function.
scenarios.hint: What must happen to the previous scheduled firing when a new keystroke arrives?

scenarios.title: Crash under time pressure
scenarios.situation: Onsite debugging. The app crashes on launch for one tester: `EXC_BAD_ACCESS` in a view controller's `viewDidLoad`. You have 10 minutes and the device.
scenarios.prompt: What is your triage order?
choices: Reproduce, then read the crashed thread's stack: EXC_BAD_ACCESS in viewDidLoad usually means messaging a deallocated object (zombie) or a force unwrap — enable Zombie Objects / check the line, verify outlets are connected, look for use of an object before its owner exists; narrate each hypothesis as you rule it out.
Delete derived data and clean the build folder — most launch crashes are stale caches.
Comment out viewDidLoad entirely — if it stops crashing, the bug is in there somewhere.
Ship a try/catch around viewDidLoad — crashes in production are worse than silent failures.
scenarios.why: Interviewers watch the method, not just the fix: reproduce first, read the stack before guessing, form hypotheses from the crash type (EXC_BAD_ACCESS = bad memory access; SIGABRT = assertion/exception), and verify the fix by re-running the repro. Narrating hypotheses out loud is half the score.
scenarios.hint: What does the crash type itself tell you before you read a single line of code?
objectives: Triage crashes by type, then stack, then hypothesis

scenarios.title: Your hardest bug
scenarios.situation: Behavioral. 'Tell me about the hardest bug you ever fixed.'
scenarios.prompt: What structure makes this answer land?
choices: STAR compressed: the symptom and why it was hard (intermittent, production-only), your systematic narrowing (what you ruled out and how), the root cause, the fix plus the guard you added (test, assertion, monitoring) — ending with what you changed in your process afterward.
Describe the bug in deep technical detail for five minutes — depth proves skill.
Pick a trivial bug so you look fast and competent.
Say you have never had a truly hard bug — honesty is refreshing.
scenarios.why: Behavioral answers are graded on structure and self-awareness, not bug impressiveness. The process-change ending ('now I always add a regression test for race conditions') turns a war story into evidence of growth. Quantify where you can: 'crashed for 2% of sessions, took three days, fixed with a 5-line change.'
scenarios.hint: What did this bug change about how you work — that is the real question being asked.

scenarios.title: Design a chat app
scenarios.situation: System design onsite. 'Design the iOS client for a 1:1 chat app.' 30 minutes, whiteboard.
scenarios.prompt: What do you draw first, and what do you cover?
choices: Data flow first: message list driven by a local store (Core Data) as source of truth, a sync/socket layer appending inbound messages, an outbox for unsent messages with retry, UI as a function of store state — then cover pagination, optimistic send, push notification handling, media upload progress, and what you would defer (E2E encryption protocol details).
Start with the color scheme and bubble shapes — chat is a UI problem.
Draw the server architecture — the interviewer said iOS client but servers matter more.
List every feature (reactions, threads, search) — completeness first, depth later.
scenarios.why: Client system design is scored on: source of truth, data flow direction, offline/optimistic behavior, and scope control ('I am deferring X'). scenarios.prompt: What is the correct whiteboard approach?

B. Narrate the design first (cancel previous work when new input arrives, wait for a quiet period, then fire), then implement simply (Combine: .debounce(for:scheduler:); manual: DispatchWorkItem cancellation or async Task with sleep + cancellation check) — the interview scores the reasoning trace, so think aloud the whole time.
C. Write code silently; the code speaks for itself.
D. Debounce is impossible without Combine; say so.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the interviewer cannot score thinking they cannot hear. What should they hear?

scenarios.title: Design typing indicators
scenarios.situation: The system-design round: 'Design a chat app.' The candidate jumps to 'we will use WebSockets' and stalls. The interviewer redirects: 'Start with typing indicators — design just that feature end to end.'

scenarios.prompt: What is the correct system-design approach?
choices: A. Name technologies first; the stack is the design.

B. Requirements -> scale -> data flow -> components: clarify (1:1 or group? ephemeral indicators?), estimate (messages/sec, fan-out), design the flow (client sends 'typing' events throttled, server fans out to conversation members, clients render with timeout), then discuss tradeoffs (WebSocket vs push, ordering, presence) — structured, from requirements outward.
C. Draw boxes immediately; diagrams impress.
D. 'It depends' for 45 minutes; never commit.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the interviewer narrowed it to typing indicators. What is the SMALLEST complete design for that feature?
scenarios.why: System design interviews score structured thinking: clarifying requirements first ('typing indicators for 1:1 and group? how long until it clears?') prevents designing the wrong thing; back-of-envelope scale (10k concurrent typists x fan-out) sizes the solution; the data flow (client event -> server -> members -> UI timeout) is the design; technologies (WebSocket, APNs) are implementation details chosen LAST against the flow's needs. Tech-first (choice A) inverts this — WebSocket for what requirement? Boxes-first (choice C) draws the unconsidered. 'It depends' without ever deciding (choice D) is evasion; the format wants requirements -> decision -> tradeoffs, with the tradeoffs named explicitly.

domains.name: Advanced SwiftUI
domains.description: View identity, custom layouts, navigation, performance, and the layout system — SwiftUI beyond the basics.

scenarios.title: The text field that forgets what you typed
scenarios.situation: A list of editable rows: scrolling causes text fields to show other rows' text. The rows are built with ForEach over indices, and each row holds @State.
evidence: Observed: A list of editable rows: scrolling causes text fields to show other rows' text. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain view identity (2) Fix state-migration bugs in lists Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause and the fix?
choices: A. SwiftUI lists are buggy with text fields; use UIKit instead.

B. View identity: ForEach over indices gives rows unstable identity, so SwiftUI recycles the wrong @State. Identify rows by a stable ID (ForEach(items, id: \.id)) so each row's state attaches to the right model element.
C. Move the @State to the parent; shared state fixes recycling.
D. Add .id(UUID()) to each row so identity is always fresh.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the state didn't disappear — it attached to the wrong row. What decides 'which row is which'?
scenarios.why: SwiftUI diffs views by identity: for dynamic content, identity comes from the ForEach id. Over indices, inserting/deleting/reordering rows shifts which model element sits at index 2 — but the @State stays glued to the row's structural position, so state appears to 'move' between rows. Stable IDs (the model's own id) bind each row's state to the element, not the position: reorder all you want, state follows the data. .id(UUID()) (choice D) is worse — a fresh UUID every render means identity never stabilizes and state resets constantly.

scenarios.title: The view that takes all the space (or none)
scenarios.situation: An HStack contains a Text and a custom chart view. The chart either crushes the text to zero or explodes past the screen edge, depending on modifiers. The developer is stacking .frame() modifiers randomly.
evidence: Observed: An HStack contains a Text and a custom chart view. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain the layout negotiation (2) Size views with intent Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct mental model?
choices: A. SwiftUI layout is unpredictable; use fixed frames everywhere.

B. The three-step negotiation: parent proposes a size, child chooses its size, parent positions it. Views report their ideal size; stacks divide space by priority (.layoutPriority) and flexibility; .frame() constrains the proposal, not the content — understanding the negotiation replaces modifier roulette.
C. Modifiers apply bottom-up; the last frame always wins.
D. Custom views cannot participate in layout; wrap everything in GeometryReader.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the parent OFFERS a size; the child CHOOSES. Which side is your chart failing on?
scenarios.why: SwiftUI layout is a negotiation, not a command: the parent proposes a size (often 'take what you need, up to X'), the child returns its chosen size (its ideal, fitted into the proposal), and the parent places it. HStack divides available space among children by their flexibility: fixed-size views (Text with content) take their ideal; flexible views (Spacer, .frame(maxWidth: .infinity)) absorb the rest; .layoutPriority breaks ties. The chart misbehaves because its ideal size is ambiguous — the fix is giving it layout meaning (a sensible ideal via .frame with min/ideal/max, or a custom Layout), not more random frames. GeometryReader (choice D) breaks the negotiation (it takes all offered space) — a last resort, not a layout strategy.

scenarios.title: The tag cloud that HStack cannot build
scenarios.situation: The design calls for a flowing tag cloud: tags wrap to multiple rows, left-aligned, with even spacing. HStack truncates, VStack stacks wrong, and LazyVGrid needs fixed columns.
evidence: Observed: The design calls for a flowing tag cloud: tags wrap to multiple rows, left-aligned, with even spacing. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Implement the Layout protocol (2) Build wrapping layouts Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct SwiftUI approach?
choices: A. Compute frames manually with GeometryReader and absolute positioning.

B. Implement the Layout protocol: measure subviews (sizeThatFits), place them row by row with place(at:), cache the computation — a FlowLayout of ~40 lines that the system treats as a first-class layout (animatable, composable).
C. It cannot be done in SwiftUI; drop to UIKit.
D. Use a ScrollView of HStacks and hardcode the row breaks.
scenarios.hint: Hint: HStack/VStack/LazyVGrid are just Layout implementations. What stops you from writing your own?
scenarios.why: The Layout protocol is SwiftUI's escape hatch for custom arrangements: sizeThatFits proposes sizes to subviews and returns the container's size; placeSubviews positions each subview. A flow layout measures each tag, accumulates x until the row is full, wraps, and reports the total height — the parent then negotiates with a real size instead of a guess. Because it is a protocol (not a hack), the layout animates, composes with stacks, and respects the environment. Hardcoded row breaks (choice D) shatter on Dynamic Type and localization; GeometryReader manual layout (choice A) fights the system instead of extending it.

scenarios.title: The deep link that cannot navigate
scenarios.situation: Marketing wants a push notification to open the app directly on an order's detail screen, three levels deep. The app uses NavigationLinks scattered through views — there is no programmatic way to drive the stack.
evidence: Observed: Marketing wants a push notification to open the app directly on an order's detail screen, three levels deep. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Drive navigation with data (2) Implement deep links Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct navigation architecture?
choices: A. It cannot be done; SwiftUI navigation is view-driven only.

B. NavigationStack with a path: a @State NavigationPath (or [Route] array) bound to the stack; pushing is appending to the path — deep links construct the path programmatically ([.orders, .order(id), .tracking]), and navigationDestination maps routes to views. Navigation becomes data.
C. Present everything modally; modals can be chained programmatically.
D. Keep NavigationLinks but trigger them with hidden isActive bindings everywhere.
scenarios.hint: Hint: if navigation were DATA instead of scattered view triggers, how would you build a three-level stack from a notification?
scenarios.why: NavigationStack(path:) externalizes the navigation state into data: the path array IS the stack, so pushing = appending, popping = removing, and deep-linking = constructing the array from the notification payload. navigationDestination(for:destination:) maps each route type to its view — one registration per route, not scattered links. The old isActive-binding web (choice D) is unmaintainable precisely because navigation state lives in a dozen booleans; the path unifies it. This is also what makes state restoration trivial: persist the path, restore the stack.

scenarios.title: The scroll that drops frames
scenarios.situation: A feed scrolls at 20fps. Instruments shows body re-evaluating for every row on each keystroke in the search field — the search @State lives at the top, and every row depends on the top-level view.
evidence: Observed: A feed scrolls at 20fps. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Diagnose SwiftUI invalidation (2) Colocate state and use Equatable Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct performance fix?
choices: A. Wrap everything in DispatchQueue.main.async; threading fixes UI.

B. Isolate state: move the search field's @State (or the filter) into a dedicated subview so keystrokes invalidate only the search bar; make rows depend on stable identities and Equatable to skip redundant diffs — SwiftUI is fast when invalidation is local.
C. Set .drawingGroup() on the list; flattening fixes frame rate.
D. Reduce the number of rows; SwiftUI cannot scroll long lists.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the search text changed. Why did ROW bodies re-run?
scenarios.why: SwiftUI re-evaluates body for views whose dependencies change — @State at the top invalidates the entire subtree, so every keystroke rebuilds every row's body (even though the diff then discards most of it; body evaluation itself is the cost). The fix is dependency hygiene: state lives as low as possible (the search bar owns its text), rows take only what they need (the item, not the world), and EquatableView conformance lets SwiftUI skip views whose inputs did not change. LazyVStack/LazyVGrid ensure offscreen rows are not built at all. .drawingGroup() (choice C) flattens rendering but does not reduce body evaluation — it treats the symptom downstream of the actual cost.

scenarios.title: The card that jumps instead of morphing
scenarios.situation: Tapping a feed card should morph it into the detail screen (image flies, title slides). Instead the detail appears with a fade — the two screens are separate view hierarchies and SwiftUI sees no relationship.
evidence: Observed: Tapping a feed card should morph it into the detail screen (image flies, title slides). Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Build morphing transitions Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What connects the two hierarchies for a morphing transition?
choices: A. matchedGeometryEffect with a shared namespace
B. Hero transitions via UIViewControllerAnimatedTransitioning only
C. .transition(.slide) on the detail view
D. Animating opacity is the only cross-hierarchy option
scenarios.hint: Hint: the two images are the 'same' artwork in the user's mind. How do you tell SwiftUI they are the same element?
scenarios.why: matchedGeometryEffect is SwiftUI's answer to hero transitions: views in different hierarchies (or different positions) that share an id within a @Namespace are treated as the same visual element — SwiftUI computes both frames and animates between them during the transition. The namespace scopes the ids (so two feeds do not collide); isSource controls which instance defines the geometry. Without it, the hierarchies are unrelated and you get fades; with it, the artwork flies and the title slides — the morph is declarative, a few modifiers instead of a custom animator.

domains.name: Combine Framework
domains.description: Publishers, operators, subjects, schedulers, and error handling — reactive programming on iOS, and when to choose it over async/await.

scenarios.title: The notification center spaghetti
scenarios.situation: A settings screen updates via NotificationCenter: observers registered in three places, userInfo dictionaries cast unsafely, and a missed removal crashes the app. The team wants a typed reactive replacement.
evidence: Observed: A settings screen updates via NotificationCenter: observers registered in three places, userInfo dictionaries cast unsafely, and a missed removal crashes the app. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Build publisher/subscriber chains (2) Manage subscription lifetime Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What does Combine change?
choices: A. Nothing; NotificationCenter with careful removal is equivalent.

B. Combine replaces stringly-typed broadcasts with typed publisher/subscriber chains: a @Published property or PassthroughSubject emits values, operators transform them, and the subscription is a cancellable token with deterministic lifetime — the data flow is declared, typed, and cancellable in one place.
C. Combine is only for networking; UI updates stay on NotificationCenter.
D. Replace notifications with delegates; Combine adds nothing.
scenarios.hint: Hint: what broke — the notification, or the stringly-typed, manually-managed plumbing around it?
scenarios.why: NotificationCenter's failures are structural: string names (typos compile), untyped userInfo (casts crash), and manual observer removal (miss one, crash). Combine's publisher/subscriber model fixes each: publishers declare their Output and Failure types (the compiler checks the chain), operators (map, filter, combineLatest) transform declaratively, and subscribing returns an AnyCancellable — storing it in a Set<AnyCancellable> ties the subscription's lifetime to the owner's, with cancellation automatic on deinit. The data flow becomes a readable pipeline instead of scattered post/observe pairs.

scenarios.title: The nested callback pyramid of doom
scenarios.situation: Fetching a user, then their orders, then each order's shipping status produces nested closures four levels deep. Error handling is duplicated at every level, and cancellation is impossible.
evidence: Observed: Fetching a user, then their orders, then each order's shipping status produces nested closures four levels deep. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Sequence with flatMap (2) Centralize error handling Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: Which Combine operators flatten this?
choices: A. Nested sinks; Combine does not flatten, it just renames callbacks.

B. flatMap chains the dependent fetches (each publisher's output feeds the next), catch/mapError centralizes error handling, and the single AnyCancellable cancels the whole chain — the pyramid becomes a vertical pipeline with one error path and one cancellation token.
C. DispatchGroup; Combine is the wrong tool for sequencing.
D. More nesting but with better variable names.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the pyramid nests because each step needs the previous step's VALUE. What operator feeds one publisher's output into the next publisher?
scenarios.why: flatMap is the sequencing operator: it takes each upstream value, returns a NEW publisher, and subscribes to it — the dependent fetch becomes the next pipeline stage instead of a nested closure. Errors travel downstream as Failure values: one catch (recover with a fallback publisher) or mapError at the end handles every stage's failure uniformly. The entire chain is one subscription — cancelling the token cancels the in-flight network request too (URLSession publishers support cancellation). The pyramid's real costs were duplicated error handling and no cancellation; the pipeline fixes both structurally.

scenarios.title: The delegate that needs three listeners
scenarios.situation: A Bluetooth manager uses a delegate — but now three screens need the connection events. Delegates are one-to-one; the team is adding a multicast delegate hack with an array of weak references.
evidence: Observed: A Bluetooth manager uses a delegate — but now three screens need the connection events. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Choose Passthrough vs CurrentValue subjects (2) Bridge imperative APIs Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct Combine approach?
choices: A. The multicast delegate hack; it works.

B. Expose the events as a Subject (PassthroughSubject for events, CurrentValueSubject for state): the manager sends into the subject, any number of subscribers subscribe — multicast by design, typed, with no weak-array bookkeeping.
C. Keep the delegate and add NotificationCenter for the extra screens.
D. Singletons with callbacks; everyone polls.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the manager PRODUCES events imperatively; the screens CONSUME them reactively. What type is both?
scenarios.why: Subjects are the imperative-to-reactive bridge: a Subject is both a subscriber (you call .send() on it) and a publisher (others subscribe). PassthroughSubject forwards events to current subscribers (no replay — like a delegate call); CurrentValueSubject holds a current value and replays it to new subscribers (like @Published, but manually driven). The Bluetooth manager sends connection events into the subject; three screens subscribe independently — multicast without weak arrays, typed without userInfo, cancellable without removeObserver. The multicast-delegate hack (choice A) reimplements, badly, what subjects are.

scenarios.title: The UI update from a background thread
scenarios.situation: A Combine chain does network + JSON parsing, then updates @Published properties — and the app crashes with a purple runtime warning: UI updated from a background thread. The chain never specified a scheduler.
objectives: Keep UI work on main declaratively
evidence: Observed: A Combine chain does network + JSON parsing, then updates @Published properties — and the app crashes with a purple runtime warning: UI updated from a background thread. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Place subscribe(on:) and receive(on:) (2) Keep UI work on main declaratively Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct scheduler discipline?
choices: A. Wrap every sink in DispatchQueue.main.async; schedulers are overkill.

B. Declare schedulers in the chain: .subscribe(on:) for where UPSTREAM work runs (background queue for network/parse), .receive(on:) for where DOWNSTREAM delivery happens (RunLoop.main / DispatchQueue.main for UI) — the crash was unspecified delivery, and the fix is declarative, not scattered asyncs.
C. Do everything on the main thread; background work is premature optimization.
D. Schedulers only matter for timers; ignore them elsewhere.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the chain has two sides — where the work RUNS and where the results ARRIVE. Which side crashed?
scenarios.why: Combine operators execute wherever the upstream delivers unless told otherwise: URLSession publishers deliver on background URLSession queues, so the @Published assignment (and SwiftUI's reaction) happens off-main — the purple warning is the diagnosis. .receive(on: DispatchQueue.main) moves downstream delivery to main: everything after it (the sink, the @Published write) runs on main. .subscribe(on:) moves the upstream subscription side (where the work starts) — typically a background queue for heavy producers. Scattered DispatchQueue.main.async (choice A) works but hides the threading model; declared schedulers make it visible and reviewable. Main-threading everything (choice C) janks the UI on parse-heavy payloads.

scenarios.title: The flaky endpoint that fails the whole screen
scenarios.situation: An endpoint flakes 10% of the time. The Combine chain propagates the first failure to the sink's completion, the screen shows an error, and the user must pull-to-refresh. Product wants automatic resilience.
evidence: Observed: An endpoint flakes 10% of the time. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Build resilient pipelines (2) Choose retry/catch/timeout policies Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct Combine resilience pattern?
choices: A. catch and show cached data always; errors should never surface.

B. Layered: .retry(n) for transient failures (with backoff via delay where needed), .catch for fallback publishers (cached data), .mapError to unify failure types, and timeout to bound hangs — resilience as pipeline stages, each with a visible policy.
C. Infinite retry; the endpoint will succeed eventually.
D. Ignore errors in the sink; the UI will figure it out.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the flake is transient (10%), the hang is possible, and stale data beats no data. Which operator handles each?
scenarios.why: Resilience composes from small operators: retry(2) resubscribes on failure (transient flakes succeed on attempt 2-3); catch substitutes a fallback publisher (stale cache with a 'last updated' banner — honest degradation); timeout(5, scheduler:) converts hangs into failures so retry/catch can act; mapError unifies URLError/DecodingError into the domain's error type. Each operator is a visible policy decision, reviewable in the chain. Infinite retry (choice C) hammers a downed server and drains batteries; silent catch-all (choice A) hides real outages behind stale data with no signal.

scenarios.title: The new feature: Combine or async/await?
scenarios.situation: The team debates the new feed feature: half want Combine (existing expertise), half want async/await (modern, simpler). The decision is being made on taste.
evidence: Observed: The team debates the new feed feature: half want Combine (existing expertise), half want async/await (modern, simpler). Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Choose between Combine and async/await Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the principled way to choose?
choices: A. Always Combine; consistency beats everything.

B. Match the tool to the shape: async/await for single-shot request/response (clearer, structured, cancellable via Task); Combine for continuous event streams, multicasting, backpressure, and complex operator chains (debounce, combineLatest over time). Many apps use both, bridged where they meet.
C. Always async/await; Combine is deprecated.
D. Flip a coin; they are interchangeable.
scenarios.hint: Hint: is the feed a single answer or a stream of events over time?
scenarios.why: The tools have different centers of gravity: async/await excels at sequential asynchronous work (fetch, decode, display) with structured cancellation via Task hierarchies — the code reads like synchronous code. Combine excels at values-over-time: UI event streams (search-as-you-type with debounce), multicasting one source to many subscribers, and operator-heavy transformations (combineLatest of three inputs). Forcing request/response through Combine adds ceremony; forcing continuous streams through async/await means hand-rolling AsyncStreams and operators. The mature codebase uses both: async/await at the network boundary, Combine (or AsyncSequence) for the reactive UI layer, bridged with .values or AsyncStream.

domains.name: Testing with XCTest
domains.description: Unit tests, UI tests, mocks, async testing, and snapshot tests — the testing discipline iOS interviews probe.

scenarios.title: The view model that cannot be tested
scenarios.situation: A view model creates its own URLSession, reads UserDefaults directly, and posts to NotificationCenter. Tests would need the network, real defaults, and observer cleanup — so there are no tests.
evidence: Observed: A view model creates its own URLSession, reads UserDefaults directly, and posts to NotificationCenter. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Design testable view models (2) Inject fakes via protocols Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What makes a view model testable?
choices: A. Test with the real network; integration tests are the only honest tests.

B. Dependency injection: the view model takes its dependencies (network client protocol, storage, clock) as init parameters — tests inject fakes/mocks, production injects the real ones. Testable is a design property, not a testing-library feature.
C. Subclass the view model in tests and override the network methods.
D. Make everything static so tests can stub it globally.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the test needs a FAKE network. What in the design decides whether a fake can be substituted?
scenarios.why: Untestable code is code with hardcoded collaborators: the view model that news up its own URLSession cannot run without the network, by construction. Injection inverts this: init(network: NetworkClient, store: Store) — production passes the live implementations, tests pass fakes (a stub client returning canned JSON, an in-memory store). Protocols define the seams (NetworkClient as a protocol, URLSession conforming via extension); the view model never knows it is being tested. Subclass-and-override (choice C) tests a different class than production runs; statics (choice D) create global test pollution.

scenarios.title: The test that passes before the code runs
scenarios.situation: An async test calls viewModel.load() (which is async) without awaiting, then asserts immediately — passing vacuously because the assertion runs before the load completes. Or worse: it sleeps 2 seconds and hopes.
evidence: Observed: An async test calls viewModel.load() (which is async) without awaiting, then asserts immediately — passing vacuously because the assertion runs before the load completes. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Write async XCTest methods (2) Test Combine with expectations Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct async testing discipline?
choices: A. Sleep with a generous margin; 5 seconds is always enough.

B. Make the test itself async and await the unit directly (func testLoad() async throws): the test suspends until load() completes — no sleeps, no races, no vacuous passes. For Combine publishers, use XCTestExpectation with fulfill on emission (or await the .values sequence).
C. Test async code synchronously by calling the underlying sync methods.
D. Async code cannot be tested; test around it.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the test must run its assertions AFTER the async work. What synchronizes 'after' — a clock, or the work itself?
scenarios.why: XCTest supports async test methods natively: func testLoad() async throws — the test suspends at await viewModel.load() and resumes when it completes, so assertions run after the work, deterministically. Sleeps (choice A) are races with a timeout: too short flakes, too long slows the suite, and neither proves ordering. The vacuous pass (asserting before completion) is the worst outcome — a green suite that tests nothing. For Combine: expectations (expectation(description:), waitForExpectations) or the modern await publisher.values.first() — both synchronize on the emission, not the clock.

scenarios.title: The mock that tests the mock
scenarios.situation: A test uses a hand-rolled mock with 12 verification flags; the test asserts the flags, not the behavior. Refactoring the view model (same behavior, different call order) breaks 40 tests.
evidence: Observed: A test uses a hand-rolled mock with 12 verification flags; the test asserts the flags, not the behavior. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Choose fakes vs mocks (2) Write refactor-proof tests Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct test-double discipline?
choices: A. More detailed mocks; verification is the point of testing.

B. Prefer state-based fakes over interaction mocks: assert on OUTCOMES (the view model's published state) with simple stubs/fakes, and reserve interaction verification for true commands (did it SAVE?). Overspecified interaction tests break on harmless refactors.
C. Never use doubles; test with real dependencies.
D. One mega-mock for all dependencies; reuse everywhere.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the refactor changed no behavior but broke 40 tests. What were those tests actually asserting?
scenarios.why: Tests should assert outcomes, not choreography: after load(), assert vm.items == expected (state) — not 'service.fetch was called exactly once before cache.write' (interactions). Interaction-heavy tests couple to implementation: reordering two internal calls (behavior-identical) breaks 40 tests, and the team learns to fear refactoring — the opposite of what tests are for. Fakes (in-memory store, stub service) give state-based assertions naturally; mocks (verify) are reserved for commands with side effects (save, send, track) where the interaction IS the outcome. The mega-mock (choice D) couples every test to every dependency.

scenarios.title: The UI test suite that takes 3 hours
scenarios.situation: The team UI-tests everything: every validation message, every edge case, 400 XCUITest cases launching the app fresh each time. The suite takes 3 hours, flakes on animations, and developers ignore it.
evidence: Observed: The team UI-tests everything: every validation message, every edge case, 400 XCUITest cases launching the app fresh each time. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Scope UI tests to journeys (2) Stabilize XCUITest Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What belongs in UI tests?
choices: A. Everything; UI tests are the most realistic.

B. UI tests for critical user journeys only (login, purchase, core flow) — the paths where integration across the real stack matters. Validation logic and edge cases belong in unit tests (fast, deterministic). Launch arguments stub the backend so UI tests do not depend on the network.
C. Delete all UI tests; they are inherently flaky.
D. Screenshot every screen on every commit; pixels are the contract.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the suite tests validation messages by launching the app 400 times. Where could those assertions live instead?
scenarios.why: UI tests are the most expensive tests per assertion: full app launch, real UI stack, timing-sensitive — minutes each, flaky by nature (animations, system dialogs). Their value is integration across the REAL stack: the critical journeys where view + view model + navigation + persistence must work together. Everything else (validation rules, edge cases, formatting) is cheaper and more deterministic as unit tests — the pyramid again. Launch arguments/environments (e.g. -ui-testing with stubbed services) remove the network flakiness; accessibility identifiers (not label text) make the tests robust to copy changes.

scenarios.title: The redesign that broke 40 screens
scenarios.situation: A design-system color change ships, and 40 screens render wrong — discovered by users, not tests. Unit tests passed (logic unchanged); UI tests passed (journeys still work). Nobody tested LOOKS.
evidence: Observed: A design-system color change ships, and 40 screens render wrong — discovered by users, not tests. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Write snapshot tests (2) Review visual diffs Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What catches visual regressions?
choices: A. Manual QA on every screen for every change; humans see visuals.

B. Snapshot tests: render views/screens to reference images, diff on each run — the color change fails 40 snapshots instantly, showing exactly which screens changed. Run on a fixed simulator/device config; review diffs as the change's blast radius.
C. UI tests already cover this; the suite was just incomplete.
D. Visuals cannot be tested; accept the risk.
scenarios.hint: Hint: unit tests check logic, UI tests check journeys. What checks that the screen LOOKS right?
scenarios.why: Logic tests and journey tests are blind to rendering: the color change altered no behavior and broke no flow, so both suites stayed green while 40 screens looked wrong. Snapshot tests fill the gap: they render the view hierarchy to an image and pixel-diff against a recorded reference — any visual change fails loudly, with the diff image showing exactly what moved. The workflow: record references on a fixed configuration (device, OS, Dynamic Type size), run on changes, and REVIEW the diffs — the 40 failures ARE the blast-radius report for the design change. Flakiness comes from nondeterminism (dates, random data, animations) — the test data must be fixed.

scenarios.title: The tests that pass locally and fail in CI
scenarios.situation: Tests are green on laptops, red in CI. Causes: tests depend on execution order, share simulator state, and assume network. CI runs them in parallel on fresh simulators — exposing every hidden dependency.
evidence: Observed: Tests are green on laptops, red in CI. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Make tests hermetic (2) Split suites with test plans Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What makes tests CI-reliable?
choices: A. Run CI sequentially on one machine; parallelism is the problem.

B. Hermetic tests: isolated state per test (setUp/tearDown, fresh fakes), no order dependence (randomize execution to prove it), no network (stubbed), and test plans separating fast unit runs (every PR) from slow UI runs (nightly) — CI exposes the coupling; fix the tests, not the runner.
C. Retry failed tests until green; CI flakiness is normal.
D. Fewer tests; the suite was too ambitious.
scenarios.hint: Hint: CI changed the environment, not the code. What did the new environment reveal about the tests?
scenarios.why: CI is the honesty machine: fresh simulators, parallel execution, and no developer state expose every hidden coupling — order dependence, shared UserDefaults, network assumptions. The fix is hermetic tests: each test sets up its own world (fresh fakes, isolated storage) and tears it down; randomized order execution (Xcode supports it) PROVES independence instead of assuming it. Test plans split the suite: the PR gate runs the fast unit slice (minutes), the nightly runs UI/snapshot slices — developers get fast feedback without waiting for the 3-hour suite. Retries (choice C) normalize flakiness; sequential CI (choice A) hides the coupling until it bites elsewhere.

domains.name: App Store Deployment
domains.description: Provisioning, TestFlight, App Store Connect, CI/CD, and review — shipping iOS apps to real users.

scenarios.title: The build that signs on one Mac only
scenarios.situation: The app archives on the lead's Mac but fails to sign on CI and on teammates' machines: 'No signing certificate found.' The certificate lives in one login keychain, unexported.
evidence: Observed: The app archives on the lead's Mac but fails to sign on CI and on teammates' machines: 'No signing certificate found.' The certificate lives in one login keychain, unexported. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain the signing chain (2) Centralize signing assets Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct code-signing setup?
choices: A. Export the .p12 from the keychain and email it to everyone; sharing is caring.

B. Centralized signing: certificates and profiles in a private encrypted repo (match-style) or Xcode Cloud/CI-managed signing, with App Store Connect API keys for CI — every machine derives signing from the shared source; no keychain archaeology, no emailed .p12s.
C. Disable code signing; it is optional for TestFlight.
D. Everyone creates their own certificate; more certificates, more resilience.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the private key exists in exactly one keychain. How many places need to sign?
scenarios.why: Apple's signing chain (certificate + private key + provisioning profile + App Store Connect) breaks when the private key lives in one keychain: CI cannot sign, teammates cannot archive, and the bus factor is 1. The fix is a single source of truth: an encrypted repo holding the certs/profiles (fastlane match model) that every machine syncs, or fully CI-managed signing — plus App Store Connect API keys (revocable, scoped) instead of Apple IDs with 2FA in CI scripts. Emailed .p12s (choice A) spray the private key across inboxes; per-person certs (choice D) multiply the maintenance and hit Apple's certificate limits.

scenarios.title: The beta nobody tested
scenarios.situation: The build goes to TestFlight, the team announces 'please test,' and release day arrives with zero feedback — then users find the crash in the first hour. The beta existed; the testing did not.
evidence: Observed: The build goes to TestFlight, the team announces 'please test,' and release day arrives with zero feedback — then users find the crash in the first hour. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Run a structured beta (2) Stage the release Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What makes TestFlight actually find bugs?
choices: A. More testers; invite the whole company.

B. Structured beta: internal group (dogfood daily builds), external group with a test plan (what to try, what changed, known issues), crash/feedback triage with SLAs, and staged rollout (1% -> 10% -> 100% phased release) — the beta is a program with assignments and a clock, not an invitation.
C. Skip beta; TestFlight delays releases.
D. TestFlight is only for crash collection; manual testing is separate.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the beta had testers and builds. What converts builds + testers into FOUND bugs?
scenarios.why: 'Please test' is not a program: without assignments nobody tests, without a test plan testers wander, and without triage the feedback evaporates. The structure: internal testers on every build (the team dogfoods — they find the crash in week 2, not release day), external testers with a focused plan per build ('test the new checkout flow on iPad; known issue: dark mode glitch on settings'), and feedback triage (crashes auto-symbolicated, feedback reviewed on a cadence). Phased release (1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%) bounds the blast radius of what the beta missed. More testers (choice A) without structure just scales the silence.

scenarios.title: The rejection on launch week
scenarios.situation: Launch week: App Store review rejects the app — 'Guideline 5.1.1: privacy policy link missing; permission prompts lack purpose strings.' The team scrambles; launch slips two weeks.
evidence: Observed: Launch week: App Store review rejects the app — 'Guideline 5.1.1: privacy policy link missing; permission prompts lack purpose strings.' The team scrambles; launch slips two weeks. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Pass App Store review (2) Respond to rejections Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What prevents review rejections?
choices: A. Nothing; review is random and unavoidable.

B. Pre-submission review checklist against the guidelines: privacy policy URL (in app + listing), purpose strings for every permission (NSCameraUsageDescription etc. — specific, honest), no placeholder content, test accounts for reviewers, and a rejection-response plan (fix fast, appeal with specifics). Most rejections are checklist items, not judgment calls.
C. Submit at the last minute; reviewers are lenient under time pressure.
D. Remove all permissions; no permissions, no rejections.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the rejection named two specific, checkable items. When could they have been checked?
scenarios.why: Most rejections are mechanical, not mysterious: missing privacy policy, generic purpose strings ('needs camera access' — for WHAT?), placeholder text, crashes on the reviewer's device, or login walls with no demo account. The checklist catches them before submission: every permission has a specific, honest purpose string; the privacy policy is linked and accurate; the app is tested on the reviewer's likely configuration; a demo account is provided with the notes. Rejections still happen — the plan covers that too: read the resolution center message precisely, fix exactly what it names, respond point-by-point, appeal with specifics when the reviewer erred. Last-minute submission (choice C) just compresses the fix window.

scenarios.title: The release that only one person can cut
scenarios.situation: Releases happen when the lead has a free afternoon: archive on their Mac, upload, write release notes from memory, notify QA by chat. The lead is on vacation; the hotfix waits.
evidence: Observed: Releases happen when the lead has a free afternoon: archive on their Mac, upload, write release notes from memory, notify QA by chat. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Automate the release chain (2) Remove release bus factors Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What does iOS CI/CD automate?
choices: A. Nothing; iOS releases need the human touch.

B. The pipeline: commit -> CI builds + runs the fast test slice -> tags cut release branches -> archive + sign (centralized signing) -> upload to TestFlight with generated notes -> notify. The hotfix becomes: merge, tag, pipeline runs — no heroics, no vacation-blocking.
C. Automate the upload only; building is fine manually.
D. CI for iOS is too slow; skip it.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the hotfix waited for a PERSON. What should it have waited for instead?
scenarios.why: The bus factor of 1 is the risk: release knowledge lives in one person's afternoon ritual. CI/CD externalizes it: every commit builds and tests (fast slice on PR, full suite nightly), release tags trigger the archive-sign-upload chain with the centralized signing assets, release notes generate from commit messages/PR titles, and notifications go to the right channels automatically. The hotfix path becomes boring — merge to the hotfix branch, tag, watch the pipeline — which is exactly what you want at 2 AM. Upload-only automation (choice C) leaves the fragile manual archive; the pipeline must own the whole chain to be trustworthy.

scenarios.title: The 100% rollout with a crash
scenarios.situation: The release goes to 100% on day one. A crash affecting 5% of users (an old iOS version) spikes within hours — 50,000 users crash-looping before the team can react. The fix takes a day; the damage is done.
evidence: Observed: The release goes to 100% on day one. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Run phased releases (2) Define halt triggers Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What release discipline bounds this?
choices: A. Test more; the crash should have been caught.

B. Phased release with monitoring gates: 1% (day 1) -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%, with crash-rate and key-metric alarms at each gate and a defined halt/rollback trigger — the 5% crash is caught at 1% (500 users, not 50,000), the rollout halts, and the fix ships before most users ever see the build.
C. Release on Fridays; the weekend gives time to fix.
D. Pull the app from the store; removal is the rollback.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the crash was inevitable; the 50,000 victims were not. What bounds the victim count?
scenarios.why: No testing catches everything — the old-iOS-version crash is exactly the class that escapes labs. Phased release accepts this: the rollout itself is the final test, conducted on 1% of users with alarms on crash rate, launch success, and key business metrics. The gate criteria are pre-defined (halt if crash rate exceeds X% for Y minutes); halting is a trigger pull, not a meeting. The fix then ships through the same phases. Friday releases (choice C) maximize the time the crash burns unattended; store removal (choice D) is the nuclear option for when phased halt is insufficient.

scenarios.title: The privacy label that lies
scenarios.situation: The App Store privacy label says 'Data Not Collected' — but the app includes an analytics SDK that collects device identifiers. A user files a complaint; Apple pulls the app pending review.
evidence: Observed: The App Store privacy label says 'Data Not Collected' — but the app includes an analytics SDK that collects device identifiers. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Maintain accurate privacy labels (2) Audit SDK data collection Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct privacy posture?
choices: A. Labels are marketing; minimal accuracy is fine.

B. Accurate privacy nutrition labels (audit every SDK's data collection — the SDKs collect under YOUR label), App Tracking Transparency prompts where tracking applies (with a clear value explanation), and data minimization (do not collect what you do not need) — the label is a legal attestation, and SDKs are your responsibility.
C. Remove the label; unlisted collection is safer.
D. Blame the SDK vendor; their collection is their problem.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the SDK collected the data, but whose NAME is on the App Store page?
scenarios.why: The privacy label is YOUR attestation covering YOUR app including its SDKs: the analytics SDK's identifier collection is your collection in Apple's (and regulators') eyes. The discipline: audit every SDK (what does it collect? can it be configured down? is there a privacy-preserving alternative?), declare accurately, request tracking permission (ATT) only where the value exchange is clear to the user, and minimize collection to begin with — the data you never collect cannot leak, breach, or be mislabeled. Vendor-blame (choice D) fails with Apple and with regulators; the label is yours.

scenarios.prompt: What is the most effective way to prepare?

B. Diagnostic first: run scenario drills across all domains to find weak areas, study those lessons with hands-on try-it exercises, drill again, then run mock interviews (timed, aloud) — loop until weak areas clear. Interview skill is performed, not read.

scenarios.situation: Interview day: four rounds (coding, concepts, system design, behavioral). The candidate prepared the material but never rehearsed the formats — and underperforms everywhere.
evidence: Work the bootcamp in this order: iOS Engineering Interview Prep. Each section assumes the previous one — jumping ahead is the fastest way to build shallow, fragile knowledge.

For every domain: read the lesson (learn the concept), clear the scenario drills (apply it under no time pressure), complete the labs (do it hands-on), then prove it in the mock (timed, weakest-areas-first). Learners who skip the loop retain facts; learners who run it retain skill.
scenarios.prompt: What is the interview-day game plan?
choices: A. Answer each question as it comes; preparation is enough.

B. Format-matched execution: coding -> think aloud continuously, clarify before coding; concepts -> 60-second structured answers (core/example/fix/verify); system design -> requirements/scale/flow/tradeoffs; behavioral -> STAR with the debugging process as the product. Rehearsed formats, executed calmly.
C. Rush through to show speed; speed impresses.
D. Give the longest answers possible; detail proves depth.
scenarios.hint: Hint: you rehearsed four formats for weeks. What does interview day change?
scenarios.why: Each round scores a different skill with a different format: coding scores the reasoning trace (silence scores zero — narrate); concepts score structured communication (the 60-second template); system design scores structured thinking (requirements outward); behavioral scores process and growth (STAR with the debugging narrative). Unrehearsed candidates underperform because the formats are unfamiliar, not because the knowledge is missing — the mock circuit exists to make the formats routine. Rushing (choice C) sacrifices the trace; rambling (choice D) buries the signal.
