scenarios.title: Designing the capstone app
scenarios.situation: You will build a habit-tracking app: habits list, streaks, reminders, statistics, and iCloud sync. It must work offline, sync across devices, support Dynamic Type and VoiceOver, and ship to TestFlight.
evidence: Deliverable bar: Design a modular app architecture; Apply offline-first sync. A reviewer with no prior context should be able to reproduce your result from your writeup and repo alone.

Working demo (not screenshots of a plan), an architecture diagram showing how the pieces connect, a README with setup steps, and a 2-minute narrated walkthrough. If any one of these is missing, the project isn't done.
scenarios.prompt: What architecture satisfies these constraints?
choices: A. One view with all the logic; it is a small app.

B. Modular Swift packages (HabitsCore: models+logic, SyncEngine: CloudKit sync, DesignSystem: components), MVVM per feature with coordinators for flow, actor-isolated stores, repository pattern over Core Data/CloudKit, and the offline-first sync design — each requirement lands in an explicit architectural decision.
C. Everything in the app target; modules are overhead for small apps.
D. Skip sync; offline-only is simpler.
scenarios.hint: Hint: 'work offline, sync across devices' — which two architectural decisions answer those?
scenarios.why: Each requirement maps to a decision: offline-first + sync -> repository pattern with field-level sync over CloudKit (the sync lesson); cross-device -> versioned models; Dynamic Type/VoiceOver -> DesignSystem components built accessible-first; TestFlight -> the deployment pipeline from the appstore domain. MVVM + coordinators keep features testable and flows deep-linkable; actor-isolated stores make the concurrent sync safe; packages enforce the layering (UI cannot touch CloudKit directly). The monolith (choice C) works until the sync logic tangles with the UI — the architecture pays for itself at the first merge conflict. Skipping sync (choice D) deletes a stated requirement.

scenarios.title: Building it in the right order
scenarios.situation: The architecture is set. The build must proceed in verifiable slices — no big-bang integration, and TestFlight gets builds early, not at the end.
evidence: Deliverable bar: Build in vertical slices; Ship to TestFlight early. A reviewer with no prior context should be able to reproduce your result from your writeup and repo alone.

Working demo (not screenshots of a plan), an architecture diagram showing how the pieces connect, a README with setup steps, and a 2-minute narrated walkthrough. If any one of these is missing, the project isn't done.
scenarios.prompt: What build sequence keeps every step demonstrable?
choices: A. Build everything, then TestFlight at the end.

B. Vertical slices with early TestFlight: (1) HabitsCore + list UI (TestFlight #1: the list works), (2) streaks + stats (unit-tested pure logic), (3) reminders + notifications, (4) sync engine (two-device test), (5) accessibility pass (XXXL + VoiceOver audit), (6) CI/CD + phased TestFlight — each slice shippable, each TestFlight build a demo.
C. UI first, logic later; screens impress stakeholders.
D. Sync first; it is the hardest part.
scenarios.hint: Hint: at the week-2 check-in, what do you DEMO?
scenarios.why: Vertical slices deliver a working app at every step: slice 1 is a usable habits list on TestFlight in week 1 — stakeholders see progress, and the deployment pipeline is proven immediately (not discovered broken at the end). Pure logic (streaks) gets unit tests; sync gets the two-device test; accessibility gets its audit pass; the pipeline automates it all. Hardest-first (choice D) delays the visible win and the pipeline proof; UI-first (choice C) builds screens on logic that does not exist. Early TestFlight is the forcing function: signing, provisioning, and distribution work from week 1.

scenarios.title: Interviewing with the capstone
scenarios.situation: The app ships to TestFlight. Now it must serve the job hunt: a demo that lands in interviews, and a writeup covering the decisions interviewers will probe.
evidence: Deliverable bar: Demo the capstone effectively; Write architecture decision logs. A reviewer with no prior context should be able to reproduce your result from your writeup and repo alone.

Working demo (not screenshots of a plan), an architecture diagram showing how the pieces connect, a README with setup steps, and a 2-minute narrated walkthrough. If any one of these is missing, the project isn't done.
scenarios.prompt: What makes the capstone interview-effective?
choices: A. 'I built an app' plus a link; the work speaks for itself.

B. The 5-minute demo script (offline mode -> two-device sync -> accessibility tour), the architecture writeup (decisions + tradeoffs + what you would change at 10x), and the TestFlight link — interviewers probe decisions, and the writeup answers before they ask. The demo is rehearsed, timed, and resilient to questions.
C. A long feature list; more features impress more.
D. Keep it private; interviews are about whiteboards.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the interviewer will ask 'why did you choose X?' — where is that answer already written?
scenarios.why: Interviewers hire judgment: the writeup's decision log (why MVVM+coordinators, why field-level sync, why packages — with the rejected alternatives) is what the system-design and architecture rounds probe, and writing it is preparing the answers. The demo script turns the app into theater: airplane mode (offline-first proven live), two-device edit (sync proven live), XXXL toggle (accessibility proven live) — each requirement demonstrated, not claimed. A feature list (choice C) invites 'why' questions you have not prepared; the writeup prepares them. 'The work speaks for itself' (choice A) leaves the interviewer to discover your decisions unguided.

lessons.title: iOS Engineering Interview Prep — Core concepts
concepts: Interview loops test four things: Swift language precision (optionals, value/reference, closures), framework depth (lifecycle, layout, state), concurrency discipline (queues, actors, main thread), and judgment (tradeoffs, scoping, debugging method). Every answer should touch the 'why', not just the 'what'.

Optionals are the language's null-safety contract: bind with guard/if let, chain with ?., default with ??, and treat every force unwrap as a crash you scheduled. Implicitly unwrapped optionals are for outlets and migration, not convenience.

Memory is deterministic: ARC frees at zero strong references, so your job is managing the graph — weak delegates, capture lists in escaping closures, and the discipline to draw ownership arrows when something leaks.

Concurrency has two eras and you must speak both: GCD (queues, QoS, groups, barriers) and structured Swift concurrency (async/await, Task, actors, MainActor). The invariant across both: UI on main, shared mutable state isolated, cancellation designed in.

Persistence is a ladder, not a favorite: UserDefaults for settings, Codable files for documents, Core Data/SwiftData for queryable graphs, Keychain for secrets. Choose by query needs and threat model, and say so out loud.
The meta-skill is narration: state assumptions, name tradeoffs, timebox, and verify. Interviewers hire the engineer who reasons visibly — the code is evidence, the thinking is the product.

example.walkthrough: One snippet, four interview themes: cancellation before new work (no stale writes to reused rows), debounce via cancellable sleep, weak self in the escaping task, and the MainActor hop for UI. If you can narrate each line's 'why', you are ready for the concurrency round.

pitfalls: Common trap: force-unwrapping 'because it is never nil' — interviewers treat every ! as a scheduled crash.
Common trap: touching UIKit from a URLSession completion handler without hopping to main — flaky layout, not a clean crash.
Common trap: answering 'which is better, UIKit or SwiftUI?' with a winner instead of tradeoffs plus a measurement plan.
Common trap: storing tokens in UserDefaults because the Keychain API is verbose — say the threat model out loud.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Ios Interview move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: View Identity: Why Your List Rows Lose State
concepts: View identity is how SwiftUI matches views across renders: explicit (.id), structural (position in the hierarchy), or ForEach-provided.
ForEach over a Range gives positional identity — insertions/deletions shift identity and orphan @State; ForEach over Identifiable models gives stable identity.
@State lifetime is tied to view identity: unstable identity means state resets or migrates to the wrong row — the classic scrolling-text-field bug.
Value-type models with stable ids (UUID, database keys) are the fix at the data layer; the view layer just needs id: \.id to use them.

example.walkthrough: Item is Identifiable, so ForEach(items) uses item.id as identity. Each Row's @State now belongs to that specific item: scrolling, inserting, or deleting rows keeps every text field glued to its model element. The buggy version (ForEach(items.indices)) keyed identity by position — row 3's state stayed at position 3 while the data moved. This is the single most-tested SwiftUI concept in interviews because it bites every real app.

pitfalls: ForEach over indices for mutable lists — positional identity + @State = state migration bugs; use Identifiable models.
.id(UUID()) or .id(randomValue) — identity churn destroys state on every render; ids must be stable across renders.
Sharing one @State across rows in the parent — 'fixes' migration by making every row edit the same value; the state model is wrong, not just the identity.
Assuming List handles identity automatically — List still needs the ForEach id; the container does not invent stable identity for you.
lessons.try_it: Build a list of 20 editable rows with ForEach over indices, scroll and observe the bug, then switch to Identifiable models and verify the fix.

lessons.title: The SwiftUI Layout Algorithm
concepts: Three steps: parent proposes -> child chooses -> parent positions. Every layout question is answered by walking these steps.
Ideal size: Text knows its ideal (content size); shapes/views without intrinsic content need explicit sizing or they collapse/expand unexpectedly.
Stacks distribute by flexibility: fixed children take ideals, flexible ones (Spacer, maxWidth: .infinity) share the remainder; .layoutPriority() biases the split.
.frame() modifies the PROPOSAL to the child (and alignment of the result) — frame(width: 100) proposes 100pt; the child's ideal may still differ, and alignment decides placement.

example.walkthrough: Text takes its content size (fixed); ChartView is offered the remainder with a sensible ideal of 200pt — it can shrink to 100 or grow to fill, and layoutPriority(1) ensures the text never gets crushed when space is tight. No modifier roulette: each modifier expresses one layout intention (priority, flexibility bounds), and the three-step negotiation produces a predictable result on every screen size.

pitfalls: Random .frame() stacking — each frame re-proposes; without the negotiation model the result is voodoo, not layout.
GeometryReader as a first resort — it greedily takes all proposed space and breaks lazy containers; prefer the Layout protocol or alignment guides.
Forgetting .layoutPriority in tight stacks — the wrong child gets crushed; priority is the tiebreaker, use it deliberately.
Assuming .frame(width:) sets content size — it sets the proposed size; a Text in a 100pt frame still sizes its text to content and aligns within.
lessons.try_it: Build the HStack, remove all frames, predict the layout from the three steps, then add back one modifier at a time verifying each prediction.

lessons.title: Custom Layouts with the Layout Protocol
concepts: The Layout protocol: sizeThatFits(proposal:subviews:cache:) measures, placeSubviews(bounds:proposal:subviews:cache:) positions — two methods, full layout power.
Subviews are measured with proposals and placed explicitly — you control wrapping, alignment, and spacing per row, not per container.
Cache expensive computation (makeCache) — layout runs frequently (rotations, Dynamic Type); the cache keeps custom layouts cheap.
Custom layouts compose: they work inside ScrollViews, animate with .animation, and respect layoutPriority — first-class citizens, not workarounds.

example.walkthrough: sizeThatFits walks the tags with a running x-offset, wrapping when the next tag exceeds the proposed width, accumulating row heights — returning the true container size so parents negotiate correctly. placeSubviews repeats the walk, calling subview.place(at: CGPoint, proposal:) for each tag. The result behaves like a built-in: it wraps on narrow screens, expands on wide ones, and animates tag insertions — ~40 lines replacing an impossible HStack puzzle.

pitfalls: GeometryReader manual positioning — absolute frames that break on rotation, Dynamic Type, and localization; the Layout protocol exists to avoid this.
Hardcoded row breaks — shatter the moment text sizes change; measure, do not assume.
Skipping the cache — layout recomputes on every invalidation; cache row metrics in makeCache.
Forgetting proposals in placeSubviews — placing subviews with .unspecified proposals ignores their flexibility; propose sensibly.
lessons.try_it: Implement FlowLayout for a tag cloud; test with 5 tags and 50, with large Dynamic Type, and in landscape — verify wrapping in all cases.

lessons.title: Navigation in SwiftUI: Stacks, Paths, and Deep Links
concepts: NavigationStack(path:) + navigationDestination: the path array is the single source of truth for the stack — navigation as data.
Routes as enums with associated values (case order(id:)) — type-safe destinations; the path is [Route], deep links construct it directly.
Programmatic control: append to push, removeLast to pop, removeAll to pop to root — plus path persistence for state restoration.
One destination registration per route type — no scattered NavigationLinks; the mapping lives with the stack, testable in isolation.

example.walkthrough: The path drives everything: user taps append routes, the back button removes them, and the push notification assigns the three-element array — the app opens exactly on the tracking screen with a working back stack. Routes as an enum keep destinations type-safe and exhaustive; adding a route is a new case plus one switch branch. State restoration falls out for free: encode the path, decode on launch.

pitfalls: Scattered NavigationLink(isActive:) webs — navigation state in a dozen booleans; deep links and restoration become impossible.
Stringly-typed destinations — the enum with associated values gives the compiler the route map; strings give you runtime crashes.
Ignoring the path for state restoration — the path IS restorable state; persisting it is a few lines for a first-class feature.
Deeply nesting NavigationStacks — one stack per tab/window; nested stacks fight over the path and confuse the back gesture.
lessons.try_it: Convert one NavigationLink chain to a path-driven stack; then simulate the deep link by assigning a 3-element path and verify the back stack.

lessons.title: SwiftUI Performance: When the View Body Runs Too Often
concepts: Invalidation is dependency-driven: a view's body re-runs when its @State/@ObservedObject/inputs change — hoisted state invalidates whole subtrees.
State colocation: keep @State as low as the feature allows; the search field's text belongs to the search bar, not the screen.
EquatableView: views whose inputs are Equatable skip body re-evaluation when inputs are unchanged — the opt-out of redundant work.
Lazy containers (LazyVStack, List) build only visible rows; combined with stable identities, scrolling stays at 60fps with 10k items.

example.walkthrough: SearchBar owns the text field: keystrokes invalidate only the bar. Rows are Equatable on their item — when the filter changes the list, only rows with changed items re-evaluate. The top-level view still holds the query string for filtering, but the TEXT FIELD's rapid state churn no longer reaches the rows. Profile before/after in Instruments' SwiftUI template: body evaluation counts collapse, frame rate recovers.

pitfalls: Hoisting all @State to the top 'for simplicity' — simplicity that invalidates 500 rows per keystroke; colocate state with its feature.
.drawingGroup() as a performance fix — it changes RENDERING, not body evaluation; the rows still rebuilt, just flattened.
Equatable on views with unstable inputs — if the input identity churns (UUID per render), Equatable never matches; fix identity first.
Premature optimization without Instruments — the SwiftUI instrument shows body counts; optimize what it proves, not what you guess.
lessons.try_it: Build the laggy feed, profile body evaluation counts in Instruments, apply state colocation + Equatable, and compare the counts.

lessons.title: Publishers, Subscribers, and the Data Flow
concepts: Publisher declares Output and Failure types: the chain is type-checked end to end — a map from Int to String cannot silently become a cast crash.
@Published turns a property into a publisher; PassthroughSubject/CurrentValueSubject are manual publishers for imperative events and state.
Subscribing returns AnyCancellable: store in a Set<AnyCancellable>; cancellation is deterministic (deinit or explicit cancel), never a forgotten removeObserver.
Operators (map, filter, removeDuplicates, debounce) compose the transformation as data, not as scattered callbacks — the pipeline reads top to bottom.

example.walkthrough: $username is the publisher of the @Published property; map transforms each emission to a Bool; assign writes it to isValid; store keeps the subscription alive with the view model. No notification names, no userInfo casts, no manual removal — when the view model deinits, the bag deinits and the subscription cancels. The validation logic is a declared pipeline: future developers read the data flow instead of hunting observers.

pitfalls: Stringly-typed NotificationCenter for new code — the typo'd name and the missed removal are structural, not carelessness.
Forgetting .store(in: &bag) — the subscription cancels immediately (the cancellable deinits); the pipeline silently never fires.
Retain cycles via assign(to:on:) capturing self strongly — in long-lived chains prefer sink with [weak self] or assign(to:) on @Published (iOS 14+).
Subscribing on every body evaluation — SwiftUI views are structs; subscriptions belong in the view MODEL's init, not the view's body.
lessons.try_it: Convert one NotificationCenter flow to a @Published + operator chain; verify the observer-removal crash class is gone by construction.

lessons.title: Operators: The Vocabulary of Transformation
concepts: flatMap: upstream value -> new publisher; flattens dependent async sequences into a linear chain — the pyramid killer.
combineLatest/zip: parallel publishers merged (latest values vs paired values) — for independent fetches that join at the end.
catch: replaces a failure with a fallback publisher — error recovery as a pipeline stage, not a duplicated closure.
One subscription, one cancellation: the chain's AnyCancellable cancels upstream work (including URLSession tasks) — structured concurrency for the reactive world.

example.code:
fetchUser(id)                          // Publisher<User, Error>
    .flatMap { user in fetchOrders(user) }      // Publisher<[Order], Error>
    .flatMap { orders in fetchStatuses(orders) }// Publisher<Status, Error>
    .catch { _ in Just(Status.unknown) }        // fallback, stays typed
    .sink(receiveValue: { render($0) })
    .store(in: &bag)
example.walkthrough: Three dependent fetches read top-to-bottom: each flatMap receives the previous value and returns the next publisher. Any stage's failure flows to the single catch, which substitutes a fallback — one error path for the whole chain. The sink renders; the stored cancellable owns the lifetime. Compare the nested version: same work, four indentation levels, three error handlers, zero cancellation.

pitfalls: Nested sinks inside sinks — the pyramid in Combine clothing; flatMap exists to prevent exactly this.
Ignoring the Failure type — mismatched failures (URLError vs DecodingError) need mapError to unify before catch; the compiler enforces it, read the error.
flatMap with unbounded concurrency on lists — flatMap(maxPublishers:) bounds it; unbounded flatMap over 1000 items fires 1000 requests.
Forgetting cancellation propagation — the chain cancels cleanly ONLY if each publisher supports it; custom publishers must honor cancel.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite a 3-level nested network callback as a flatMap chain with one catch; verify cancellation actually cancels the in-flight request.

lessons.title: Subjects: The Imperative Bridge
concepts: PassthroughSubject: send events to current subscribers, no replay — the delegate replacement for event streams.
CurrentValueSubject: holds .value, replays latest to new subscribers — the state-holder for 'current connection status' style data.
Subjects multicast natively: N subscribers, one send — no weak-reference arrays, no manual fan-out.
Prefer @Published over CurrentValueSubject in view models (@Published IS a subject-backed publisher with cleaner syntax); reach for subjects at the boundary layers.

example.walkthrough: connectionEvents multicasts the momentary event (three screens each get it); state replays .connected to a screen that subscribes later (it missed the event but gets the current truth). The distinction matters: events (it happened) vs state (it is so) — PassthroughSubject for the former, CurrentValueSubject for the latter. Both are typed (ConnectionEvent/ConnState, Never fails) — the compiler, not a cast, guarantees the payload.

pitfalls: PassthroughSubject for state — late subscribers miss the current value; state needs CurrentValueSubject (or @Published).
CurrentValueSubject for one-shot events — new subscribers get a stale 'event' replayed as if it just happened; events need PassthroughSubject.
Exposing subjects as Subjects (mutable) — expose as AnyPublisher via .eraseToAnyPublisher(); the send() capability stays private.
The multicast delegate hack — weak arrays, manual iteration, untyped; subjects obsolete it.
lessons.try_it: Convert a one-to-many delegate (or notification) into a subject pair (events + state); subscribe two consumers and verify both receive.

lessons.title: Schedulers: Where Work Happens
concepts: .subscribe(on:): the scheduler where upstream work executes — background queues for network, parsing, disk.
.receive(on:): the scheduler where downstream values are delivered — main for anything touching UI/@Published bound to views.
The purple warning ('publishing changes from background threads') is the scheduler bug's signature — it names the exact @Published assignment.
Operators between receive(on:) calls run on the most recent scheduler — place receive(on:) right before the UI boundary, not at the chain's start.

example.code:
URLSession.shared.dataTaskPublisher(for: url)
    .subscribe(on: DispatchQueue.global(qos: .userInitiated))
    .map { try JSONDecoder().decode(Feed.self, from: $0.data) }
    .receive(on: DispatchQueue.main)   // UI boundary: everything after is main
    .sink(receiveValue: { self.items = $0.items })
example.walkthrough: Network and decoding run on a background queue (subscribe(on:)); the decoded items cross to main at receive(on:); the @Published assignment and SwiftUI's update happen on main — no purple warning. The scheduler declarations ARE the threading documentation: a reviewer sees exactly where the background/main boundary is. Move receive(on:) above the map and decoding blocks the main thread — placement is the semantics.

pitfalls: No schedulers specified — upstream defaults rule; URLSession delivers off-main and the UI write crashes.
receive(on:) placed too early — everything after it (including heavy parsing) runs on main; put it at the UI boundary.
DispatchQueue.main.async scattered in sinks — works, but the threading model is invisible; prefer declared schedulers.
Assuming @Published is thread-safe — it is not; the main-thread requirement is real, and the purple warning is the proof.
lessons.try_it: Build the chain without schedulers, trigger the purple warning, then add subscribe/receive and verify it disappears.

lessons.title: Error Handling and Retry in Pipelines
concepts: retry(n): resubscribe on failure — for TRANSIENT faults; pair with delay/backoff so retries do not hammer a struggling server.
catch: failure -> fallback publisher — degraded-but-honest UI (cached data + staleness banner), not a spinner of doom.
timeout: hangs become failures — bounds the worst case so retry/catch policies actually engage.
mapError: unify failure types into the domain error — the chain's Failure type is a contract; keep it intentional.

example.code:
fetchFeed()
    .timeout(8, scheduler: DispatchQueue.global())
    .retry(2)                                   // transient flakes
    .catch { _ in cachedFeed() }                // honest fallback
    .mapError { AppError.network($0) }          // unified type
    .receive(on: DispatchQueue.main)
    .sink(...)
example.walkthrough: The pipeline reads as the resilience policy: 8-second bound, two retries for flakes, cached fallback with the error mapped to the app's type, delivered on main. A reviewer sees every decision — retry count, timeout, fallback — instead of discovering them in a bug report. Tune the numbers from production data: retry counts and timeouts are operational parameters, not constants.

pitfalls: Infinite retry — a downed endpoint becomes a battery-draining hammer; bound every retry.
catch that swallows everything silently — stale data with no staleness signal is misinformation; banner the fallback.
retry without timeout — hangs never fail, so retry never engages; bound first, then retry.
No mapError — the chain's Failure type accretes (URLError today, DecodingError tomorrow); unify deliberately.
lessons.try_it: Point the chain at a flaky test endpoint; verify retry recovers, timeout bounds the hang, and catch serves the fallback — each independently.

lessons.title: Unit Testing View Models
concepts: Dependency injection is the testability mechanism: collaborators enter through init (or properties), so tests substitute fakes without changing the unit.
Protocol seams: depend on protocols (NetworkClient), not concretes (URLSession) — fakes conform to the same protocol production types do.
Fakes over mocks for state: a fake (in-memory store, stub client) behaves like the real thing deterministically; mocks verify interactions — use each for its job.
No statics/singletons in the unit's dependencies: global state leaks between tests (order-dependence); injected instances are isolated per test.

example.walkthrough: The view model knows only the protocol; the test injects a stub returning canned items instantly — no network, no waiting, deterministic. The load() test asserts items/error state transitions; a second stub throws, asserting the error path. Production injects the URLSession-backed service. Same class, both worlds — because the dependency was a parameter, not a hardcoded construction.

pitfalls: Hardcoded URLSession/UserDefaults/singletons — untestable by construction; every 'new' inside the unit is a testing dead end.
Subclass-and-override in tests — tests a subclass, not the shipped class; behavior can diverge silently.
Static/global test doubles — leak state across tests; order-dependent suites rot.
Testing through the real network — slow, flaky, and unusable offline; the network gets integration tests, the view model gets fakes.
lessons.try_it: Take one untestable class, extract its collaborators into init-injected protocols, and write the first test with a stub — feel the design change.

lessons.title: Async Testing: Awaiting the Real Thing
concepts: Async test methods (async throws) await the unit directly — assertions run after completion by construction, not by timing luck.
Never sleep-and-hope: sleeps are races (flake when slow, waste when fast); synchronize on the work (await, expectations, sequences).
XCTestExpectation for callback/Combine code: fulfill() on the event, waitForExpectations(timeout:) bounds the wait — the timeout is a failure signal, not a scheduling tool.
await publisher.values: AsyncSequence bridging turns emissions into awaitable values — the modern, sleep-free way to test Combine chains.

example.walkthrough: The test reads sequentially because await makes it so: load() completes (or throws), then assertions run — deterministic on every machine, fast (the stub returns instantly), and honest (a broken load() fails the test). Compare the sleep version: same assertions, but their meaning depends on machine speed. The async test's meaning depends on nothing but the code.

pitfalls: Sleep-based synchronization — flaky when slow, wasteful when fast; the suite rots either way.
Asserting without awaiting — the vacuous green test; worse than no test because it claims coverage.
Timeouts as scheduling (waitForExpectations with huge timeouts and no fulfill path) — the test always 'passes' by timing out slowly.
Testing async code via sync internals — tests the plumbing, not the behavior; await the public async API.
lessons.try_it: Find a sleep-based async test (or write the vacuous version deliberately), convert it to async/await, and run it 50 times — count the flakes before and after.

lessons.title: Mocks, Stubs, and Fakes: Choosing Doubles
concepts: State over interaction: assert the resulting state (items, error, loading flags) — behavior-preserving refactors keep passing.
Fakes (working in-memory implementations) for queries; mocks (verify calls) for commands — the double matches the dependency's role.
Stubs answer canned responses (fetch returns [.sample]); mocks verify interactions (verify save called once) — different tools, different jobs.
Overspecified tests are a tax on refactoring: every verified interaction is a promise the implementation must keep — verify only what matters.

example.walkthrough: The fake implements the protocol with a real (in-memory) behavior — no verification flags, no call-order assertions. The test drives the view model and asserts the resulting state in the fake: behavior, not choreography. Refactor the view model's internals freely — as long as the state is right, the test passes. The mock-based suite would have 40 failures for the same refactor.

pitfalls: Verifying every interaction — couples tests to call order/count; harmless refactors break the suite and teach fear of change.
Hand-rolled mocks with flag forests — the test asserts the mock's bookkeeping, not the unit's behavior.
One shared mega-mock — every test depends on every dependency's mock surface; changes ripple everywhere.
Mocking value types and pure functions — nothing to verify; use real values.
lessons.try_it: Take one interaction-heavy test, rewrite it state-based with a fake, then refactor the unit's internals and watch the new test survive.

lessons.title: UI Tests: What to Automate (and What Not To)
concepts: UI tests = critical journeys: the 5-10 flows that must work end-to-end (login, checkout, core loop) — integration value justifies the cost.
Unit tests = logic and edge cases: validation, formatting, state transitions — fast, deterministic, cheap.
Stability practices: accessibility identifiers (not text), launch args to stub backends, disable animations in test scheme — flakiness is engineered out.
Screenshot tests for visual regression (snapshot libraries): targeted at design-critical screens, not every screen — pixels change, journeys matter.

example.walkthrough: The launch arguments put the app in test mode (stubbed backend, reset data) — the test is deterministic and network-free. Accessibility identifiers decouple the test from visible copy: marketing rewrites the label, the test still finds the field. This is the maintainable UI test: hermetic, identifier-driven, and reserved for journeys worth the minutes they cost.

pitfalls: UI-testing everything — 3-hour suites that everyone ignores; the pyramid exists because UI tests are the expensive tip.
Text-based element queries — copy changes break tests; accessibility identifiers are the stable contract.
Real network in UI tests — backend flakes become test flakes; stub via launch args.
Animations on in tests — timing flakes; the test scheme should reduce motion/animations.
lessons.try_it: Pick the 5 most critical user journeys in a sample app; write ONE UI test for the top journey with launch args and identifiers.

lessons.title: Snapshot Testing: Catching Visual Regressions
concepts: Snapshot tests pixel-diff rendered views against references — the only automated check for 'looks right.'
Fixed test configuration: same simulator, OS, Dynamic Type size, and deterministic data — nondeterminism (dates, randomness) is the flakiness source.
Review diffs as blast radius: 40 failures on a color change is INFORMATION — it shows the change's true reach for sign-off.
Scope to design-critical surfaces: components, key screens — not every transient state; snapshots are for the visual contract.

example.walkthrough: The test renders the button to an image and compares against the recorded reference: a color, font, or padding change fails with a diff image highlighting the pixels. First run records the reference (review it — the reference IS the spec); subsequent runs guard it. Applied to the design-system components, the color change fails the component snapshots first — caught at the source, not on 40 screens by users.

pitfalls: Nondeterministic snapshot data — dates, UUIDs, random content make every run fail; fix the data, not the test.
Unreviewed reference recording — the first run's image becomes the spec; a wrong initial render gets enshrined as correct.
Snapshot-everything — transient states and full-screen flows churn; snapshot components and key screens.
Ignoring diffs ('just re-record') — re-recording without reviewing the diff approves unknown visual changes; the diff review is the test.
lessons.try_it: Add one snapshot test for a design-system component with fixed data; change a color and observe the diff-driven blast-radius report.

lessons.title: Provisioning: Certificates, Identifiers, and Profiles
concepts: Signing needs four aligned pieces: development/distribution certificate (+ private key), App ID, provisioning profile, and App Store Connect record — one mismatch breaks the build.
Single source of truth for signing assets: encrypted repo (match) or CI-managed — every machine syncs instead of hand-managing keychains.
App Store Connect API keys for automation: scoped, revocable, no 2FA prompts — Apple IDs in CI scripts are a reliability and security hole.
Separate identities per purpose: development (run on device), ad-hoc (TestFlight internal), App Store (release) — the profile must match the intent.

example.code:
# The match model (conceptual):
# 1. Certs + profiles live in an encrypted git repo (one source of truth)
# 2. Each machine/CI job: match appstore --readonly  (syncs, never mutates)
# 3. CI uses an App Store Connect API key, not an Apple ID
# Result: signing works identically on every machine, first try.
example.walkthrough: The readonly sync is the key discipline: machines consume signing assets but never create them ad hoc, so the repo stays the single truth and certificate sprawl never starts. CI with an API key removes the human (and their 2FA) from the automation path. New teammate onboarding becomes 'run the sync command' instead of a half-day keychain ritual.

pitfalls: Emailed .p12 files — private keys in inboxes, unrevocable sprawl, and no one knows who has what.
Ad-hoc certificate creation per machine — hits Apple's limits and fragments the truth; sync, do not create.
Apple ID + password in CI — 2FA breaks automation and the credential is over-scoped; API keys exist for this.
One distribution cert for everything forever — when it expires or leaks, every app breaks at once; plan rotation.
lessons.try_it: Document your (real or hypothetical) app's signing chain: which cert, which profile, where the private key lives, and how CI signs.

lessons.title: TestFlight: Beta Testing That Finds Bugs
concepts: Two-tier beta: internal (every build, the team — dogfooding catches the obvious), external (planned builds, real users — catches the real-world).
Test plan per build: what changed, what to exercise, known issues — testers need direction, not just access.
Feedback triage: crashes symbolicated and assigned, feedback reviewed on cadence — the beta's output is findings with owners.
Phased release: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with monitoring gates — the final safety net for what the beta missed.

example.code:
# Beta program checklist (per release):
# [ ] Internal build N dogfooded 5+ days, crash-free
# [ ] External group invited with test plan (changes + focus areas)
# [ ] Feedback triage: 2x/week, findings -> tickets with owners
# [ ] Phased release scheduled: 1%/day1 -> 10%/day3 -> 100%/day7
# [ ] Rollback criteria defined (crash rate > X% -> halt rollout)
example.walkthrough: Each checkbox is a gate: the internal soak proves stability, the test plan directs external effort, triage converts feedback to fixes, phased release bounds residual risk, and rollback criteria make 'halt' a planned decision. The crash in the scenario gets caught at the internal soak or the 1% phase — never by the full user base on day one.

pitfalls: 'Please test' betas — builds without plans produce silence; structure (plan, triage, cadence) produces bugs found.
External-only beta — strangers find edge cases; the team must dogfood first to catch the obvious.
100% day-one release — the beta's misses hit everyone at once; phase the rollout.
No rollback criteria — when the crash spikes, 'should we halt?' becomes a debate instead of a trigger.
lessons.try_it: Write the beta test plan for a hypothetical release (focus areas, known issues, triage cadence, phased schedule) in one page.

lessons.title: App Store Review: Getting Approved the First Time
concepts: The common rejection checklist: privacy policy link, specific purpose strings per permission, no placeholders/crashes, demo account + reviewer notes.
Purpose strings must be specific and honest: 'We use the camera to scan barcodes for price lookup' — not 'Needs camera access.'
Reviewer notes are your advocate: demo credentials, feature walkthrough, explanations of non-obvious flows — help the reviewer succeed.
Rejection response: fix exactly what is named, reply point-by-point in Resolution Center, appeal with evidence if wrong — fast, precise, professional.

example.walkthrough: Each purpose string tells the user (and reviewer) exactly why the permission is needed — specific, honest, tied to a feature. The demo account removes the login wall for the reviewer; the privacy URL is reachable from both the app and the listing. This is the 30-minute checklist that saves the two-week launch slip.

pitfalls: Generic purpose strings — the #1 mechanical rejection; write them like user-facing copy, because they are.
No demo account — the reviewer hits a login wall and rejects; provide credentials and a walkthrough.
Placeholder content in the submission — 'lorem ipsum' anywhere is an instant rejection; the binary must be launch-clean.
Arguing with reviewers emotionally — Resolution Center is a support ticket; precise, polite, evidence-based responses win appeals.
lessons.try_it: Run the checklist against a real or hypothetical app: list every permission, write its purpose string, verify the privacy link and demo account.

lessons.title: CI/CD for iOS: From Commit to TestFlight
concepts: Pipeline stages: build + fast tests on every PR (minutes, the gate), archive/sign/upload on release tags, notes + notifications automated.
Signing in CI via the centralized source (match/CI-managed) + API keys — the pipeline signs exactly like every developer machine.
Release branches + tags as the trigger: the tag IS the release decision; the pipeline executes it identically every time.
Artifacts and dSYMs archived per build: crash symbolication for every TestFlight build, retained — the debugging paper trail.

example.code:
# Release flow (the pipeline's contract):
# 1. git tag v2.4.1 && git push --tags
# 2. CI: build + unit tests (PR gate already green)
# 3. CI: archive (Release config), sign via match readonly
# 4. CI: upload to TestFlight + generate notes from PR titles
# 5. CI: notify #releases; dSYMs archived
# Hotfix: same flow from the hotfix branch. No humans archiving.
example.walkthrough: The tag is the only human action — everything after is deterministic automation using the same signing truth every machine uses. Notes from PR titles keep them accurate (written when the work was fresh, not from vacation-memory). Archived dSYMs mean the inevitable crash report symbolicates against the exact build. Boring, repeatable, vacation-proof.

pitfalls: Manual archiving rituals — bus factor 1, vacation-blocked hotfixes; the pipeline exists to end this.
CI without centralized signing — the pipeline fails where the lead's Mac succeeded; signing truth must be shared.
Notes from memory — inaccurate and late; generate from PR titles/commit messages.
No dSYM archiving — the crash report arrives and cannot be symbolicated; the debugging trail starts at the pipeline.
lessons.try_it: Diagram the pipeline for a hypothetical app (triggers, stages, signing, notifications); identify the current bus-factor-1 step.

lessons.title: Phased Release and Rollback
concepts: Phased rollout: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% over days — each phase is a production experiment with a small blast radius.
Monitoring gates per phase: crash rate, launch failures, key metrics vs baseline — automated alarms, not vibes.
Halt triggers pre-defined: 'crash rate > 2% for 30 min -> halt rollout' — the decision is made calmly in advance, executed fast.
Rollback readiness: previous version's phased status, expedited review path for the fix — the recovery is also planned, not improvised.

example.code:
# Phased release plan:
# Day 1: 1%  — alarms: crash rate, launch success, purchase conversion
# Day 3: 10% — same gates; compare metrics vs previous version
# Day 5: 50% — gates + support ticket volume watch
# Day 7: 100%
# HALT TRIGGERS: crash rate >2% 30min | conversion drop >10% | new crash cluster
# On halt: pause rollout, fix, re-phase from 1%.
example.walkthrough: The plan makes the rollout a controlled experiment: each phase has explicit gates, the halt triggers are numeric (no debate at 2 AM), and the recovery path (fix, re-phase) is defined before it is needed. The scenario's crash trips the day-1 halt at 500 affected users — two orders of magnitude fewer victims, and the fix ships before phase 2.

pitfalls: 100% day-one releases — maximum blast radius for the inevitable escaped bug; the phase IS the safety net.
Gates without numbers — 'watch the metrics' is not a trigger; define the thresholds in advance.
No halt authority — if halting needs a meeting, the crash burns during the meeting; pre-authorize the trigger.
Friday releases — the crash burns all weekend; release early in the week when the team is present.
lessons.try_it: Write the phased plan + halt triggers for a hypothetical release; define who can pull the halt trigger and how.

lessons.title: ARC and Retain Cycles
concepts: ARC: automatic reference counting — objects deallocate when strong references hit zero; Swift manages it, but cycles defeat it.
Retain cycle anatomy: controller -> closure (property) -> controller (captured self) — the two strong arrows that never release.
Capture lists: [weak self] (self becomes optional, safe) vs [unowned self] (non-optional, provably-alive only) — weak is the default, unowned the optimization.
The debug flow: memory graph debugger in Xcode shows the cycle visually — purple warnings name the exact retaining pair.

example.walkthrough: The commented line is the leak: the closure (stored on self) captures self strongly — self retains the closure, the closure retains self, neither deinits. The fix's [weak self] makes the capture weak: self can deallocate (popping the controller), the closure's self becomes nil, and the optional chaining safely no-ops. Verify in the memory graph debugger: push/pop the controller, confirm no purple cycle warning and the deinit prints.

pitfalls: Strong self in stored closures — the #1 iOS memory leak; every stored/escaping closure capturing self needs a capture-list decision.
[unowned self] by default — crashes when the closure outlives self (async completions!); weak is the safe default, unowned only for provable lifetimes.
Forgetting delegate patterns need weak — delegates must be weak var; a strong delegate is the same cycle wearing different clothes.
Assuming ARC handles cycles — it does not; cycles are the developer's responsibility, and the memory graph debugger is the proof tool.
lessons.try_it: Build the leaking controller, confirm with the memory graph debugger, fix with [weak self], and verify deinit fires.

lessons.title: Value vs Reference Semantics
concepts: Value semantics (struct/enum): assignment copies — independent mutation, predictable, isolation-friendly for concurrency.
Reference semantics (class): assignment shares — one instance, visible-everywhere mutation; correct for identity (this SPECIFIC view model).
Copy-on-write: Swift's collections look like value types but share storage until mutation — value semantics with reference-type performance.
Choose deliberately: models/data -> struct; shared state/identity/lifetime -> class; the type declares the mutation contract.

example.code:
struct User { var name: String }        // value: copies are independent
class SessionManager { /* ... */ }            // reference: shared identity
var a = User(name: "Ann")
var b = a; b.name = "Bo"                    // a.name still "Ann" — local, predictable
example.walkthrough: The struct copy isolates the screens: editing b never touches a — the 'sometimes a bug' class vanishes because sharing requires opting into classes. SessionManager as a class is the deliberate exception: there is ONE session, and every consumer must see the same one — shared identity is the requirement, so reference semantics are correct. The rule: default struct, justify class.

pitfalls: Class models by habit — every data model becomes shared mutable state; the 'who mutated this' bug class follows.
Struct for shared identity — copying the view model per screen desynchronizes the UI; identity needs the class.
Mutating a struct through a shared reference (inout/class wrapper confusion) — know which semantics you have before reasoning about mutation.
Large structs copied in hot loops — copy-on-write covers collections, but huge custom structs have real copy costs; measure before 'fixing' with classes.
lessons.try_it: Take one model used on two screens; convert class->struct (or vice versa) and observe which bugs appear or disappear.

lessons.title: Protocols with Associated Types and Type Erasure
concepts: Associated types relate a protocol's types (Item, Section); the protocol with PATs is a constraint, not a concrete type.
'any' existentials (Swift 5.7+): boxes any conformer — heterogeneous collections work, dynamic dispatch cost explicit.
Primary associated types (protocol P<T>): any P<User> — existentials with constraints, the pragmatic middle ground.
Generics over the protocol (func f<D: DataSource>) preserve static typing and performance — use when the concrete type is known at the call site.

example.walkthrough: The existential array mixes RemoteSource and CacheSource (both DataSource<String>) — impossible with bare generics, trivial with 'any'. The generic function keeps the concrete type for the hot path: the compiler specializes it, no boxing. Primary associated type <Item> constrains the existential usefully (only String sources) — the pre-5.7 'cannot use PAT protocol as type' error is now a choice, not a wall.

pitfalls: 'any' everywhere — boxing has costs (allocation, dynamic dispatch); use generics where the type is statically known.
Type-erasing by hand (AnyDataSource wrappers) out of habit — Swift 5.7 existentials obsolete most manual type erasers; check before writing one.
Forgetting primary associated types — any DataSource without constraints is often too loose; constrain the box.
Using existentials in performance-critical loops — measure; the abstraction has a price, pay it where heterogeneity is worth it.
lessons.try_it: Build a DataSource protocol with associatedtype; store heterogeneous conformers in [any DataSource<Item>] and write one generic algorithm over it.

lessons.title: Generics and Opaque Types
concepts: Generics: write once against constraints (Key: Hashable), instantiate for any conforming type — type-safe reuse, zero duplication.
Constraints are the contract: the implementation may only use what the constraint guarantees — the compiler enforces the minimal interface.
Opaque types (some P): 'a specific type conforming to P, but I am not telling you which' — static performance, hidden implementation (some View).
Type erasure is the fallback: when generics cannot express it (heterogeneous storage), 'any' boxes — generics first, erasure when needed.

example.walkthrough: The struct is written once against the Hashable constraint — subscript, eviction, and statistics all live in one place. Instantiations are fully typed: Cache<String, User> cannot accept an Int key — the compiler, not a runtime cast, enforces it. Adding a custom key type means conforming it to Hashable (often automatic) — no cache changes. The three drifting copies collapse into one tested implementation.

pitfalls: Copy-paste per type — the drifting implementations; generics exist to end this.
[AnyHashable: Any] 'flexibility' — runtime casts instead of compile-time types; the crash moves to production.
Over-constraining (Key: Hashable & Codable & Sendable when only Hashable is needed) — constraints should be minimal; each one excludes valid uses.
Opaque type misuse (returning different concrete types per branch) — 'some' requires ONE underlying type; branches must agree.
lessons.try_it: Convert two copy-pasted type-specific implementations into one generic; instantiate for both types and delete the copies.

lessons.title: View Lifecycle and State Restoration
concepts: UIKit: viewDidLoad (once) vs viewWillAppear/viewDidAppear (every appearance) — setup vs refresh, never confused.
SwiftUI: .task (lifetime-bound, auto-cancelled) vs onAppear (per appearance) — observations in .task, refresh triggers in onAppear.
UI state (scroll offsets, expansions, selections) belongs in the view model or restoration archive — the view renders state, it does not own it.
UIKit State Restoration / SwiftUI SceneStorage: system support for persisting UI state across launches — the process-death case, not just navigation.

example.walkthrough: The view model (StateObject — lifetime of the view hierarchy) owns the expansion state and the items: navigating away and back reuses the same view model, so expansions persist. .task loads once per view lifetime and cancels on disappear — no duplicate loads, no leaked observations. The view is a pure function of vm's state: rebuilds are harmless because the state was never in the view to begin with.

pitfalls: Setup in viewWillAppear/onAppear — re-runs per appearance: duplicate network calls, reset scroll, re-registered observers (leaked).
UI state in the view (@State for scroll position across navigation) — @State dies with the view hierarchy; view-model or restoration storage survives.
.task for per-appearance work — .task cancels on disappear; per-appearance refresh belongs in onAppear, not .task.
Ignoring state restoration — process death wipes navigation; SceneStorage/restoration APIs exist for exactly this.
lessons.try_it: Build a detail screen with expansions; navigate away and back, kill the process, and verify state survives each — fixing where it does not.

lessons.title: Auto Layout Under the Hood
concepts: Conflicts = over-determined layout: two+ constraints demand incompatible geometry — read the log, find the fighters, remove or deprioritize one.
Constraint identifiers (constraint.identifier = '...') turn the 50-line dump into a readable named conflict — set them on every programmatic constraint.
Content hugging (resist growing) vs compression resistance (resist shrinking) priorities — the intrinsic-size negotiation; most 'crushed label' bugs live here.
Inequality constraints (<=, >=) express flexibility: width <= 200 bends where width == 200 breaks — prefer relations that degrade gracefully.

example.walkthrough: The log showed the 200pt required width fighting the 150pt reality. Lowering to 999 (or <=) makes the width yield: on wide screens it is 200, on narrow it compresses — the label survives instead of the system breaking a constraint at random. Identifiers made the log readable: without them, the dump is memory addresses. This is the entire Auto Layout debugging method: identify, read, deprioritize-or-remove.

pitfalls: Constraint volume as a fix — more constraints, more conflicts; the log quiets by arbitrary tie-breaking, and layout becomes random.
No identifiers on programmatic constraints — the conflict log is unreadable memory addresses; always set identifiers.
Required (1000) on everything — nothing can yield; use 999/high for 'prefer' and 1000 only for 'must.'
translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints left true — the autoresizing constraints fight yours; the classic duplicate-constraint crash (choice C's cargo cult).
lessons.try_it: Create a conflicting layout deliberately, read the log with identifiers set, and fix it by priority adjustment — twice, with different conflicts.

lessons.title: SwiftUI Data Flow: State, Binding, ObservedObject, Environment
concepts: Single source of truth: each piece of state has exactly one owner (@State/@StateObject); everyone else binds or observes.
@Binding = two-way reference to another view's state — the child writes, the owner (and all readers) update.
@StateObject (owner, lifetime-bound) vs @ObservedObject (borrower) — the distinction prevents the double-ownership bug in the scenario.
@EnvironmentObject for cross-cutting state (theme, session) — ambient, but explicit at the injection site; overuse hides dependencies.

example.walkthrough: settings is created once by the parent's @StateObject; the toggle writes through $settings.darkMode (a Binding — the write lands in the one object); the summary observes the same object via environment. One toggle flip publishes once, and SwiftUI refreshes exactly the views that read darkMode. No notifications, no manual reloads, no second source of truth — the data flow IS the architecture.

pitfalls: Two @StateObjects for one setting — the scenario's bug; ownership must be singular.
@ObservedObject where @StateObject belongs — the object gets recreated (state resets) because nobody owned its lifetime.
@EnvironmentObject without injection — runtime crash ('no ObservableObject of type'); the environment must be populated at the root.
Notifications/KVO for view data flow — untyped, unscoped; the property wrappers exist to replace exactly this.
lessons.try_it: Build the two-owner bug deliberately, observe the desync, then unify to one @StateObject + bindings and verify all readers update.

lessons.title: Diffable Data Sources and Compositional Layout
concepts: Snapshots are declarative state: NSDiffableDataSourceSnapshot<section, item> — apply the new state, the system animates the diff.
Items must be Hashable with STABLE ids — the diff matches by identity; unstable ids (index-based) produce the flicker snapshots were meant to fix.
Compositional layout: NSCollectionLayoutSection per section kind, composed in one UICollectionViewCompositionalLayout — layouts as data, not switch statements.
Orthogonal scrolling sections (carousel inside vertical feed) are declarative — the nested scroll behavior that took custom layouts in 2016.

example.walkthrough: The snapshot declares the feed's full state; apply() diffs against the current UI — only changed items animate, scroll position holds, no flicker. Each section's items go to their section; the compositional layout renders hero/grid/list/carousel per its section definition. Updating one item is: mutate the model, rebuild the snapshot, apply — the UI equivalent of SwiftUI's declarative update, in UIKit.

pitfalls: reloadData for every update — flicker, lost scroll, full re-render; the snapshot exists to replace this.
Unstable item identifiers — index-based ids make the diff see 'everything changed'; stable model ids or it did not happen.
Monolithic flow layout with index-path switches — the 2016 pattern; compositional sections replace it declaratively.
Applying snapshots off-main — UIKit main-thread rule applies; diffing is cheap, but the apply is main-only.
lessons.try_it: Convert one reloadData-based collection view to diffable + compositional; update a single item and verify no flicker and preserved scroll.

lessons.title: Swift Concurrency: async/await and Actors
concepts: Actors serialize access to their isolated state — the compiler, not discipline, prevents the interleaving.
await marks suspension points: every actor call shows where the task may suspend — concurrency made visible.
Sendable: the compiler-checked contract for cross-task values — value types and actors are Sendable; shared mutable classes are not.
Actors are reentrant: an await inside an actor method can interleave with other calls — design for it (check state after awaits).

example.walkthrough: Reads and writes serialize through the actor: the corrupted-mid-read interleaving is structurally impossible — the storage dictionary is never touched concurrently. The call site's await documents the suspension; the actor's reentrancy means a second caller can interleave AT the await points (not mid-dictionary-access), which is the correct granularity. No locks, no queues, no deadlocks — the compiler holds the invariant.

pitfalls: DispatchQueue.sync patches — the deadlock in the scenario; sync from the queue's own thread is the classic self-deadlock.
@MainActor for non-UI state — serializes background work onto the UI thread; actors belong on their own executor.
Ignoring actor reentrancy — state checked before an await may change by resumption; re-check after awaits.
Non-Sendable types crossing tasks — the compiler warning (error in Swift 6) is the race detector; do not silence it with @unchecked without proof.
lessons.try_it: Convert a queue-protected cache to an actor; write a concurrent stress test and verify no corruption and no deadlock.

lessons.title: Dispatch Queues and QoS
concepts: Phase separation: background does the work COMPLETELY, main receives the FINISHED result — one hop, not thousands.
QoS is priority: userInitiated (user waiting now) > utility (user waiting with progress) > background (invisible) — label work honestly or the scheduler cannot help.
QoS inversion: high-priority work waiting on low-priority work — the system boosts, but deliberate QoS avoids the pathology.
Serial vs concurrent queues: serial for resource protection (the cache's queue), concurrent for parallelizable work — the queue type is a correctness tool, not just throughput.

example.walkthrough: The parse runs entirely on the utility queue — the main thread never sees the 10MB. One hop delivers the complete model; the UI updates once. The QoS labels tell the system the truth: this work matters to the waiting user (utility) but must never preempt the interface. Profile in Instruments: main-thread CPU during the fetch drops to near zero.

pitfalls: Per-item main-queue hops — thousands of dispatches; batch the work, hop once.
Default QoS on user-waiting work — the scheduler deprioritizes it behind the UI; label userInitiated/utility deliberately.
Main-thread parsing 'because it is simpler' — 10MB of JSON on main is dropped frames by construction.
Sync dispatches to unknown queues — sync from main to a queue that might be main (or blocked) deadlocks; prefer async with completion.
lessons.try_it: Instrument the per-item-hop version vs the batched version; measure main-thread CPU and frame drops during the fetch.

lessons.title: Operation Queues and Dependencies
concepts: Operation dependencies model DAGs: addDependency expresses ordering; the queue parallelizes everything the DAG allows.
Cancellation propagates: cancel on the queue/operation sets isCancelled — operations check at checkpoints and exit early; scrolled-past work dies.
maxConcurrentOperationCount tunes parallelism (the pipeline's throughput knob); qualityOfService labels the work for the system.
Async Operations (isAsynchronous) wrap callback-based work — the operation completes when the callback fires, keeping the DAG honest for network stages.

example.walkthrough: The four operations and three edges ARE the pipeline — readable, and the queue executes the DAG with maximal parallelism. Cell reuse cancels the queue: in-flight download aborts, downstream operations never start (dependencies unmet on cancelled ops), no orphaned uploads for invisible cells. Each operation checks isCancelled at its checkpoints — the discipline that makes cancellation real rather than nominal.

pitfalls: Manual cancelled flags — 'checked most places' is the bug; Operation's isCancelled is the checked-everywhere mechanism.
Nested GCD for DAGs — reimplements OperationQueue poorly; dependencies, cancellation, and parallelism are native to operations.
Forgetting isCancelled checkpoints — cancellation without checkpoints is a flag nobody reads; check at every stage boundary.
Unbounded concurrent operations — 100 cells x 4 ops = 400 concurrent; maxConcurrentOperationCount bounds the stampede.
lessons.try_it: Build the 4-stage pipeline with operations; scroll fast and verify cancelled pipelines do not upload.

lessons.title: Thread Safety Patterns
concepts: Read-modify-write is the race shape: load/increment/store must be atomic — serialization (actor/queue/lock) is the fix.
Actors: the Swift-concurrency answer — isolated state, await at call sites, compiler-checked.
Serial queues: the GCD answer — sync for return values, async for fire-and-forget; barriers for reader/writer patterns.
Locks (NSLock/os_unfair_lock): the lowest-level answer — fastest, manual, deadlock-capable; prefer actors/queues unless measured otherwise.

example.walkthrough: The actor makes track(_:) atomic: concurrent tasks serialize through the actor, each read-modify-write completing before the next begins — 1000 increments yield exactly 1000. The call site awaits (suspension visible); the implementation has no locks, no queues, no manual discipline — the language holds the invariant. For legacy GCD code, the equivalent is a serial queue with sync/async around the same dictionary.

pitfalls: Assuming += is atomic — it is three operations; the 973/1000 result is the proof.
'volatile' in Swift — does not exist; and where it exists (other languages) it never provided atomicity.
Main-thread serialization for background data — correct but wasteful; the UI thread is not a general lock.
Lock without unlock paths (early returns) — use defer { lock.unlock() } or prefer actors/queues that cannot forget.
lessons.try_it: Stress-test the counter (1000 concurrent increments) with no protection, then with an actor — assert exact counts.

lessons.title: Keychain and Secure Storage
concepts: Keychain = secrets: tokens, passwords, certificates — hardware-backed, access-controlled, the only correct home for credentials.
Accessibility levels (kSecAttrAccessible...) define WHEN readable: afterFirstUnlock (background refresh) vs whenUnlocked (foreground-only, stricter).
Access control policies: require biometry or device passcode for the crown jewels (refresh tokens) — the keychain enforces, not your code.
UserDefaults = preferences (theme, flags) — never secrets; the plist is readable, backed up, and synced.

example.code:
let query: [String: Any] = [
    kSecClass as String: kSecClassGenericPassword,
    kSecAttrAccount as String: "authToken",
    kSecValueData as String: tokenData,
    kSecAttrAccessible as String: kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked
]
SecItemAdd(query as CFDictionary, nil)  // hardware-encrypted, unlock-gated
example.walkthrough: The token lands in the keychain as a generic-password item, readable only when the device is unlocked — background thieves and backup browsers get ciphertext. Wrapping this in a small KeychainService (save/load/delete with proper status checking) hides the CFDictionary ceremony. First-launch detection (a UserDefaults flag — appropriate use!) wipes stale tokens when the semantics demand it.

pitfalls: Secrets in UserDefaults — plaintext plist, backup-propagated, jailbreak-readable; the scenario's breach.
Ignoring keychain status codes — SecItemAdd returns errSecDuplicateItem etc.; unchecked, the 'save' silently failed.
Wrong accessibility level — afterFirstUnlock for a foreground-only token widens the readable window unnecessarily; match level to need.
Surprise reinstall persistence — design for it (wipe or keep, deliberately); the keychain outlives the app by default.
lessons.try_it: Store a token in the keychain with whenUnlocked accessibility; verify it is unreadable from a backup extraction mindset — then implement first-launch wipe.

lessons.title: Core Data Stack and Concurrency
concepts: Thread confinement: each context lives on one queue; perform/performAndWait run work on that queue — never touch a context's objects elsewhere.
Object IDs cross threads, objects do not: pass NSManagedObjectID, resolve with object(with:) in the target context.
Background writes: newBackgroundContext() (private queue) for imports — the UI never blocks on 50k inserts.
automaticallyMergesChangesFromParent: background saves merge into viewContext — the UI refreshes without manual merge code.

example.walkthrough: The import runs entirely on the background context's queue — the main thread never stalls on 50k inserts. Saving publishes to the parent; automaticallyMergesChangesFromParent pulls the changes into the viewContext; the fetched-results controller animates the new rows in. No object crossed a thread (the import created its own), no lock, no violation — the concurrency model IS the architecture.

pitfalls: Passing NSManagedObjects across queues — the violation; object IDs are the currency of cross-thread references.
Touching viewContext from background — even 'just a read' violates confinement; use perform or a background context.
Disabling -com.apple.CoreData.ConcurrencyDebug — the flag exists to catch violations in development; shipping with it off hides corruption.
Main-thread imports — 50k inserts on viewContext freeze the UI for seconds; background contexts exist for this.
lessons.try_it: Trigger the concurrency violation deliberately (with the debug flag on), then fix with background context + object IDs and verify it disappears.

lessons.title: Codable Custom Decoding Strategies
concepts: Custom dateDecodingStrategy: one closure handles all date shapes — the mess is contained, models stay clean.
init(from:) for structural mess: custom keys, nested containers, type coercion — the full escape hatch, used surgically.
Optionals model nullability honestly: the API sends null sometimes, so the property IS optional — non-optional + null is a crash by design.
keyDecodingStrategy (.convertFromSnakeCase) and keyed containers handle naming mismatches — decode the API's shape, expose yours.

example.walkthrough: The closure tries ISO8601 string first, then unix timestamp, then falls back — one place, explicit order, reviewable leniency. Every model using this decoder gets the tolerance for free; the alternative (per-model init(from:) date hacks) duplicates the mess. Strictness is a choice: return distantPast (lenient) or throw (strict, surfacing bad data) — decide per field, document it.

pitfalls: Stringly-typed models — parsing dates in view code; the mess metastasizes to every screen.
Non-optional properties for nullable fields — the null crash; model the API's actual nullability.
One global lenient decoder for everything — leniency should be per-field/per-decoder; global leniency hides real data errors.
Ignoring decoding errors in production — log and monitor decode failures; the API WILL change shape again.
lessons.try_it: Build the three-format decoder; feed it all three shapes plus null and verify each decodes to the expected Date?.

lessons.title: Offline-First Sync Design
concepts: Sync granularity decides conflict behavior: field-level merges non-overlapping edits; document-level destroys them.
Offline-first: local store is the truth, server is a peer — the app works in tunnels; sync reconciles, not authorizes.
Conflict resolution ladder: automatic merge (different fields) -> last-write-wins per FIELD (same field, timestamp) -> user resolution (true conflicts, both versions shown).
Idempotent, order-independent sync operations: retries and reordering must not corrupt — design the protocol for the network you have, not the one you wish for.

example.walkthrough: Each field carries its own version: the merge takes the higher version per field independently — the title edit and body edit combine without conflict. Only same-field concurrent edits need resolution, and those get the honest treatment: show both, let the human decide. This is the design behind production sync (CloudKit, Realm, CRDTs) — the granularity insight, not the specific library, is the interview answer.

pitfalls: Document-level last-write-wins — silent data loss on non-overlapping edits; the scenario's bug.
Requiring connectivity — offline is a feature (tunnels, planes, rural); offline-first is the architecture, not a fallback.
Auto-resolving true conflicts silently — same-field concurrent edits need human judgment; picking by timestamp loses someone's work quietly.
Sync as an afterthought — the local schema must carry versions/timestamps from day one; retrofitting sync onto a sync-ignorant schema is a rewrite.
lessons.try_it: Design the field-level sync for a 3-field note (title, body, tags); simulate the two-device edit and verify both survive.

lessons.title: MVVM in Practice
concepts: View model = state + intents, framework-free: @Published properties, methods for user actions, zero UIKit/SwiftUI imports.
The view formats: dates, numbers, strings for display are the VIEW's job — the view model exposes values, not label text.
Dependencies injected (protocols), never singletons: the view model is constructed with its collaborators — testable by design.
Unidirectional flow: view -> intent -> view model -> state -> view — the loop is explicit, debuggable, and testable at the view-model layer.

example.walkthrough: No UIKit import, no formatting, no outlets: state (email, isLoading, error), derived state (canSubmit), intents (submit()), injected auth. The test constructs it with a fake, drives intents, asserts published state — the entire login logic verified without a simulator. The SwiftUI view (or UIViewController) binds to the published state and formats for display — thin, replaceable, untested-by-design (the logic lives below it).

pitfalls: UIKit imports in the view model — the 'renamed view controller' smell; the import is the diagnosis.
Display formatting in the view model ('$' + amount) — the view's job; view models expose values.
Singletons in the view model — untestable by construction; inject protocols.
Navigation logic in the view model — navigation is a coordinator/flow concern; view models emit events, coordinators route.
lessons.try_it: Audit one view model: list its imports and dependencies — every UIKit import or singleton is a finding; refactor one.

lessons.title: The Coordinator Pattern
concepts: Coordinators own flow: navigation stacks, tab selection, modal presentation — the journey as an explicit object.
View controllers emit events, never navigate: didTapOrder(id) goes up; the coordinator pushes down — flow logic leaves the view layer.
Deep links become coordinator methods: handle(route) constructs any reachable state — testable without tapping.
Child coordinators per flow (one per tab/feature), parent coordinating children — the hierarchy mirrors the app's information architecture.

example.walkthrough: showOrder(id:) is the deep-link primitive: constructible from anywhere (notification, widget, shortcut), testable without UI (assert the pushed VC's view model), and reusable (the in-app tap calls the same method). The view controller never imports the next screen — it reports the tap; the coordinator routes. Flow changes (insert a screen, reorder) touch one file, not twelve view controllers.

pitfalls: View controllers pushing view controllers — implicit flow; deep links and tests become impossible.
Segue webs — storyboard flow is invisible to code; programmatic deep links cannot traverse it.
Singleton navigation manager — centralized spaghetti; coordinators distribute flow by feature with clear ownership.
Coordinators holding view state — coordinators own FLOW, view models own STATE; mixing them recreates the massive VC.
lessons.try_it: Extract one flow (two screens) into a coordinator; then implement the deep link as a coordinator method and test it without UI.

lessons.title: Dependency Injection on iOS
concepts: Constructor injection: collaborators as init params, typed as protocols — needs declared, fakes substitutable, compiler-checked.
Composition root: one place assembles the object graph (app/coordinator/factory) — environments differ HERE, not in 60 files.
Protocols as seams: depend on NetworkClient, not URLSessionClient — the fake conforms to the same protocol.
Singletons become injectables: the 'shared instance' survives as the production implementation, passed in — not accessed globally.

example.walkthrough: The environment decision lives in ONE place: Config.baseURL (per scheme) selects staging/prod, and the test target injects FakeClient. The 60 files each declare init(client: NetworkClient) — the compiler enforces the wiring, and no file knows about singletons, environments, or test doubles. Adding a new environment (QA) is a config entry, not a code change.

pitfalls: Singletons as the wiring — global state, untestable, environment-baked; the scenario's 60-file problem.
Service locator as 'DI' — the global in disguise; dependencies hidden, tests still coupled to the locator.
Environment switches scattered in code (#if STAGING in 12 files) — the composition root exists to centralize this.
Injecting concretes instead of protocols — no seam for fakes; the protocol IS the testability.
lessons.try_it: Convert one singleton user to constructor injection with a protocol; write the first test with a fake and feel the design shift.

lessons.title: Modularization with Swift Packages
concepts: Module = compilation boundary: unchanged modules skip rebuilding — clean-ish builds become incremental by construction.
Dependency graph as architecture: packages declare dependencies; the graph enforces layering (UI -/-> DB directly).
Ownership per module: teams own packages, not files — conflicts move from 'same target' to explicit API boundaries.
Extract by seam: start with leaves (DesignSystem, Networking) and stable features — the modules with the cleanest boundaries go first.

example.walkthrough: The package manifest IS the architecture document: FeedFeature's dependencies are explicit and reviewable. A change to the feed rebuilds two modules, not 800k lines — PR builds drop from 40 minutes to single digits. The forbidden import (DatabaseImpl) is the real prize: layering violations become compile errors, not code-review debates.

pitfalls: Big-bang 50-module split — months of churn; extract incrementally, leaves first.
Circular dependencies between modules — the graph must be a DAG; cycles mean the boundary was drawn wrong.
Modules as pure build optimization — the boundary enforcement (layering) is the durable win; build time is the bonus.
One module per file — dependency-graph overhead without architectural meaning; granularity is features/layers.
lessons.try_it: Identify the best leaf module in a sample app (design system? networking?); sketch its package boundary and dependents.

lessons.title: Networking Layer Design
concepts: One client owns the mechanics: auth (refresh-on-401 transparently), retry, decoding, error mapping — call sites declare WHAT, the client handles HOW.
Declarative endpoints: enum cases -> (path, method, params) — adding an endpoint is a case, not a networking implementation.
Transparent auth refresh: the 401 -> refresh -> retry loop lives inside the client; view models never see tokens.
The client is the test seam: protocol fakes for unit tests; the refresh/retry logic gets dedicated integration tests with a stub server.

example.walkthrough: The view model declares .feed(page: 1) and gets typed items — no URLs, no tokens, no 401 handling in sight. The client's request method is the single place where auth, retry, decoding, and error mapping live: tested once (stub server returning 401 then 200), correct everywhere. The token-format change is one file; the 12 scattered copies are gone because there is nothing to scatter.

pitfalls: Auth logic per call site — the 12 buggy copies; cross-cutting mechanics must be centralized.
View models building URLs — stringly-typed endpoints scattered; the enum makes endpoints declarative and reviewable.
No test seam (concrete client, no protocol) — view-model tests hit the network; the protocol is the fake point.
Silent token refresh failures — refresh failure must surface as a defined error (re-login flow), not a mysterious retry loop.
lessons.try_it: Design the Endpoint enum + client protocol for a 5-endpoint API; implement the 401-refresh-retry once and test it with a stub.

lessons.title: Error Handling as UX
