concepts: Typed errors (AppError): network/auth/validation/server — the view switches on kind, each kind gets its designed UX.
Every loading state needs its error state: the error screen is DESIGNED (copy, art, actions), not a stack trace in an alert.
Offline as a persistent state: banner + queued actions + auto-retry on reconnect — offline is normal, not exceptional.
Errors carry recovery: retry buttons, login routes, field highlights — the error tells the user what to DO, not just what broke.

example.walkthrough: The view model exposes a state enum (loading/loaded/failed) — the view renders each, and the failed case gets a designed ErrorView with error-specific copy and actions (retry for offline, login for unauthorized). No spinner can spin forever: every request resolves to loaded or failed, and failed is a screen, not a log line. This is the 'error states are UI' principle made structural.

pitfalls: Spinner-without-error-state — the infinite spinner; every async op needs its failure rendering.
Alert-per-error — dismissal training; reserve alerts for destructive confirmations, design error states inline.
Logs as the error UX — the user never sees the console; errors must surface in the interface.
Generic 'something went wrong' everywhere — the typed error exists to give SPECIFIC recovery; generic copy wastes it.
lessons.try_it: Audit one flow's three states (loading/success/error); design the missing error state with copy and recovery actions.

lessons.title: Instruments: Finding the Leak
concepts: Generations (Allocations): mark before/after an action — the diff is the leak, named object by object.
Leaks + memory graph: cycles and their retaining paths — the 'who keeps this alive' answer, visualized.
Measure, fix, re-measure: the second generation run proves the fix; profiling without the re-run is superstition.
Jetsam reports (MetricKit/Xcode organizer) show the production crashes — the field data that prioritizes which leak to fix first.

example.walkthrough: The generation diff replaced the guess ('maybe images') with the fact (200 leaked view controllers); the memory graph named the retaining path (the network task's closure); the fix was one capture list; the re-run proved it. Total time: less than the NSCache guessing took, with a verified result instead of a hoped one. This is the performance workflow generally: instrument, identify, fix, verify — never guess.

pitfalls: Guess-and-patch ('maybe images') — treats the symptom class; the generation diff names the actual objects.
NSCache as a talisman — caches bound memory only if the leak IS the cache; unbounded growth needs diagnosis first.
No re-measurement — the fix is unverified hope; generations before AND after or it did not happen.
Ignoring jetsam reports — production memory kills are the prioritization data; profile what the field proves is broken.
lessons.try_it: Run the generation workflow on any scrolling screen; find the top surviving object type and explain why it survives.

lessons.title: Accessibility and Dynamic Type
concepts: Dynamic Type everywhere: preferred fonts scale with the user's setting — fixed font sizes ignore the user's needs.
Layouts that grow: stacks, flexible containers, scroll views — fixed-height text containers truncate; design for the range, not the default.
VoiceOver labels/hints/traits: every interactive element announces its purpose and state — test with VoiceOver on, eyes closed.
Test the extremes: XXXL text + VoiceOver + increased contrast on every screen — the extremes are where the exclusions hide.

example.code:
// The checklist, as code:
Text(order.total)                  // .font(.body) scales; no fixed size
    .font(.body)                   // Dynamic Type by default
    .minimumScaleFactor(0.8)       // graceful shrink before truncate
Button("Checkout") { }
    .accessibilityLabel("Checkout, 3 items, $42.50")  // purpose + state
    .accessibilityHint("Double tap to place your order")
example.walkthrough: The Text scales with the user's setting (no fixed 17pt); minimumScaleFactor degrades gracefully instead of truncating. The button's label announces purpose AND current state (3 items, total) — a VoiceOver user gets what a sighted user sees. The hint teaches the gesture. This is the per-element discipline; the per-screen discipline is testing it all at XXXL.

pitfalls: Fixed font sizes — ignores the user's accessibility setting; the XXXL breakage.
Fixed-height labels/containers — truncation and overlap at large sizes; grow or scroll.
Missing accessibility labels — VoiceOver announces 'button' for six buttons; labels are the UI for blind users.
Testing only at default settings — the extremes are untested, so the exclusions ship; XXXL + VoiceOver is the test plan.
lessons.try_it: Turn on XXXL + VoiceOver, navigate your (or a sample) app's main flow, and list every breakage — then fix the top three.

lessons.title: The 60-Second Technical Explanation
concepts: The 60-second template: core (one sentence) -> example (the canonical case) -> fix (the action) -> verify (the proof).
One sentence first: if you cannot state the core in one sentence, you do not own the concept yet.
Canonical examples beat abstract definitions: the closure-capturing-self IS retain cycles for working purposes.
End with verification: the junior who can check (memory graph) is independent; the one who cannot is dependent.

example.walkthrough: Four beats, ~60 seconds, each answering one junior question. Notice what is absent: ARC implementation details, weak vs unowned subtleties, edge cases — the 60-second version is the ACTIONABLE version. Depth follows if asked ('when would you use unowned?') — the structure invites follow-ups instead of drowning them.

pitfalls: Rambling without structure — 3 minutes, no landing; the template exists to prevent exactly this.
Depth before action — internals before the fix; the junior needs the fix first, the theory later.
No verification step — 'fixed' without proof is hope; the memory-graph check closes the loop.
One explanation for all audiences — the 60-second junior version differs from the senior deep-dive; calibrate to the listener.
lessons.try_it: Record yourself explaining three concepts in 60 seconds each with the template; listen for the landing.

lessons.title: Whiteboard Coding: Debounce and Throttle
concepts: Narrate continuously: restate the problem, state the design, then code — the reasoning trace IS the deliverable.
Debounce = wait for quiet: cancel pending work on new input, fire after the silence period — the storm becomes one request.
Throttle = at most one per window (the sibling operator): leading/trailing edge options — know both, the interview may ask.
Combine .debounce vs manual: know the one-liner AND the manual mechanics — the whiteboard may forbid frameworks.

example.walkthrough: Both versions express the same design: new input cancels the pending fire, only the quiet period triggers the search. The Combine version is the production answer; the manual version is the whiteboard-proof answer (no framework assumed). Throttle (the follow-up question): same shape, but 'at most one per 300ms' instead of 'after 300ms quiet' — one sentence shows you know the family.

pitfalls: Silent coding — the interviewer scores thinking; silence scores zero.
Freezing on timer mechanics — narrate the DESIGN first; the mechanics follow, and partial credit accrues.
Debounce/throttle confusion — know both precisely; the follow-up WILL probe the sibling.
No cancellation in the manual version — without cancel(), it is just a delay, not a debounce.
lessons.try_it: Whiteboard (paper, no IDE) both versions from memory, narrating aloud — then compare against the reference.

lessons.title: System Design: Chat App
concepts: Clarify first: scope the feature (who sees indicators? timeout? group semantics?) — design the right thing.
Scale envelope: events/sec, fan-out factor, latency budget — numbers before components.
Data flow before boxes: client -> server -> members -> timeout-clear — the flow IS the design; components serve it.
Tradeoffs explicitly: WebSocket (real-time, battery) vs push (delayed, efficient); ordering guarantees; presence vs polling — name the costs of your choices.

example.walkthrough: The design fits in a paragraph because the scope is tight: throttled events (not per-keystroke), server fan-out without persistence (ephemeral state), client-side timeouts (resilience to missed stops). The scale note justifies the simplicity: typing traffic is orders below message traffic, so the 'boring' solution suffices — and saying so demonstrates the estimation habit. Tradeoffs named: WebSocket for real-time (battery cost) vs piggybacking on message polling (delay); timeout vs explicit stop (robustness vs precision).

pitfalls: Technology-first answers — 'WebSockets' without a requirement; the stack serves the flow, not vice versa.
Skipping clarification — designing group typing when the ask was 1:1; the first 5 minutes decide the next 40.
No numbers — 'it scales' without events/sec or fan-out math; estimation is a scored skill.
Never committing — perpetual 'it depends'; the format rewards a decided design with named tradeoffs.
lessons.try_it: Design typing indicators on paper in 20 minutes (requirements, scale, flow, tradeoffs); then expand to message delivery receipts.

lessons.title: Behavioral: Your Hardest Bug
concepts: STAR: Situation (brief) -> Task (stakes) -> Action (the debugging, in detail) -> Result (fix + prevention).
The Action is the product: hypotheses, evidence, instruments, wrong turns — narrate the THINKING, not just the timeline.
Wrong turns are assets: 'I guessed X; the data said Y' demonstrates evidence-driven debugging better than a lucky first guess.
Result = fix + prevention: the regression test, the monitoring alert, the process change — the bug paid tuition; show the learning.

example.walkthrough: Two minutes, four beats: the situation is one line, the stakes one line, the action is the meat (hypothesis -> evidence -> fix -> lesson-from-wrong-turn), and the result includes the prevention (checklist + test). The wrong turn is IN the story deliberately — it is the evidence of growth. Prepare three such stories (hardest bug, biggest disagreement, biggest failure) with this structure before the interview.

pitfalls: Unstructured 10-minute rambles — no beats, no landing; STAR exists to prevent this.
Outcome-only stories ('I fixed it') — the interviewer cannot see your thinking; narrate the process.
Hiding wrong turns — the lucky-guess story is less impressive than the evidence-driven one; show the work.
No prevention — 'fixed' without the test/monitoring/process change is an incomplete result; the tuition must show.
lessons.try_it: Write your hardest-bug story in the 4-beat script; time it at 3 minutes; deliver it aloud twice.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: Four content types: lessons (mental models), scenarios (reasoning under pressure), labs (hands-on proof), mock circuit (the performance rehearsal).
The loop: drill -> weak domains -> study + try-it -> re-drill -> mock interview aloud. Repeat until the weak list is empty.
Think aloud from day one: narrate every scenario answer and every lab — the interview scores the reasoning trace.
Track accuracy per domain over time; flat scores mean change the method, not the hours.

example.code:
Week 1: diagnostic scenario pass, all domains (honest, aloud).
Week 2-3: lessons + try-it for the two weakest domains; re-drill.
Week 4: labs for weak domains; full mock circuit (timed, recorded).
Repeat: the mock's weakest domain becomes next week's focus.
example.walkthrough: The loop turns content into a training program: diagnosis aims effort, lessons build models, labs build proof, and the mock circuit rehearses the performance. Recording the mocks feels awkward and works — you hear the silences where the interviewer starts doubting.

pitfalls: Linear reading — equal time on strong and weak; the diagnostic exists to prevent this.
Silent studying — the interview is spoken; every silent rep misses the actual skill.
Mock-as-verdict before preparation — the first mock is a diagnostic instrument.
Skipping try-it exercises — reading about actors is not writing one; fluency needs the keyboard.
lessons.try_it: Run one diagnostic scenario pass this week, aloud; write down your three weakest domains.

lessons.title: Study Strategy for iOS Interviews
concepts: Build per concept: a tiny app exercising each pattern — the failure modes you meet are the interview answers.
Explain aloud (Feynman): the sentence where you stumble names the gap; 60-second versions for every major concept.
Whiteboard weekly: debounce, layout, retain cycles — thinking aloud under time, the actual interview skill.
Both frameworks: SwiftUI AND UIKit — the market is mixed; 'legacy' knowledge is still interview knowledge.

example.code: Per lesson: read -> build the try-it in a playground/app -> explain the why aloud in 60s -> whiteboard one related problem -> drill scenarios next day (spaced).
example.walkthrough: The protocol builds all three interview muscles per lesson: construction (build), communication (explain), performance (whiteboard), with spaced drilling for retention. Slower per lesson than reading; dramatically faster per interview-ready skill.

pitfalls: API memorization — freezes on twist questions and system design; the follow-up is where interviews are won.
Passive talks at 2x — exposure without construction decays within days.
Framework tribalism — skipping UIKit (or SwiftUI) halves your interview surface.
Silent practice — the interview is spoken; unrehearsed communication fails under pressure.
lessons.try_it: Pick one lesson, run the full protocol, and record the 60-second explanation — listen for the hedge.

lessons.title: Course Map: The iOS Interview Landscape
concepts: Layer 1 — Language: swift-core. The vocabulary: what the code means.
Layer 2 — UI + Data: ui-frameworks, swiftui-advanced, persistence. What the user sees and what survives.
Layer 3 — Concurrency: concurrency, combine-framework. What happens simultaneously.
Layer 4 — Structure + Quality: architecture, testing-xctest. How it is organized and proven. Layer 5 — Shipping: appstore-deploy. How it reaches users. Mock circuit: the rehearsal, throughout.

example.code:
Sequence: swift-core -> ui-frameworks (+ swiftui-advanced) -> persistence -> concurrency (+ combine) -> architecture -> testing -> appstore-deploy.
Mock circuit: start week 3, weekly thereafter.
Capstone: last — it integrates all layers into one shipped app.
example.walkthrough: The chain is the prerequisite graph made visible; the mock circuit's early start builds the performance muscle in parallel with the knowledge. If a layer-4 lesson confuses you, the map points at the layer-1/2/3 lesson to revisit — confusion becomes a pointer.

pitfalls: Random order — the confusion in architecture is usually a missing language prerequisite; the map names it.
Mock circuit only at the end — performance needs reps; start rehearsing once basics are solid.
Skipping 'easy' layers — swift-core subtleties (existentials,Sendable) are exactly what senior interviews probe.
Capstone first — integration without the parts is overwhelm.
lessons.try_it: Draw the five layers from memory, place each domain, mark your position — then study down from any confusion.

lessons.title: Interview-Day Strategy
concepts: Coding: clarify first, narrate always, test your code aloud — the trace is the deliverable.
Concepts: 60-second template (core/example/fix/verify) — structured, landable, follow-up-inviting.
System design: requirements -> scale -> flow -> tradeoffs — decide and name the costs.
Behavioral: STAR, action-as-process, wrong-turns-included — the debugging story is the thinking sample.

example.code:
Day-before: light review, sleep, logistics (location/link, ID, charger).
Day-of: arrive early, breathe, warm up with one easy problem aloud.
Per round: listen fully, clarify, structure, execute, verify.
After: write down every question asked — the debrief improves the next loop.
example.walkthrough: The routine removes novelty: the formats are rehearsed, the logistics are handled, the warm-up gets the voice going. 'Listen fully, clarify' counters the top failure mode — answering the wrong question fast. The after-action notes turn every interview (pass or fail) into preparation for the next.

pitfalls: Silent coding — the interviewer cannot score unheard thinking.
Answering before clarifying — the wrong solution, quickly; clarify first, always.
Rambling answers — no structure, no landing; the templates exist for this.
No debrief — the questions evaporate; write them down and the next interview is easier.
lessons.try_it: Do one full mock round per format this week, recorded; review for the specific failure mode of each format.

lessons.title: Capstone Architecture: The App Design
concepts: Modular packages: HabitsCore (domain), SyncEngine (CloudKit), DesignSystem (accessible components) — boundaries enforced by the package graph.
MVVM + coordinators per feature: testable view models, deep-linkable flows — the architecture lessons applied.
Repository over persistence: the view models see a HabitRepository protocol; Core Data/CloudKit hide behind it — sync changes do not ripple to UI.
Offline-first sync: local truth, field-level merge, honest conflict UI — the sync design from the persistence domain, built in from day one.

example.code:
Module map:
HabitsCore: Habit, StreakCalculator (pure, tested), repository protocols
SyncEngine: CloudKit sync, version vectors, conflict resolution UI
DesignSystem: accessible components (Dynamic Type + VoiceOver verified)
App: coordinators, DI composition root, scenes
Acceptance: airplane-mode full function; two-device edit merges; XXXL usable.
example.walkthrough: The map makes the architecture reviewable: each package owns a bounded context, the acceptance criteria are the requirements turned executable (airplane mode, two-device merge, XXXL). StreakCalculator as a pure function is the testing lesson applied — the core logic has no dependencies at all. The conflict-resolution UI is a designed screen (the error-states lesson), not an afterthought.

pitfalls: Monolith app target — sync logic tangles with UI at the first feature; the package boundaries prevent this.
Sync as an afterthought — retrofitting versions onto a sync-ignorant schema is a rewrite; day-one design.
Inaccessible design system — retrofitting VoiceOver/Dynamic Type onto finished components; accessible-first in DesignSystem.
No acceptance criteria — 'works offline' without the airplane-mode test is a wish; criteria make it engineering.
lessons.try_it: Draw the module map and write the three acceptance tests first — they define done before code exists.

lessons.title: Capstone Build Guide: From Zero to TestFlight
concepts: Slice vertically: each slice is end-to-end (logic + UI + test) and TestFlight-shippable — progress is always demonstrable.
TestFlight from slice 1: the deployment pipeline is proven early; every later slice rides it.
Test per slice appropriately: pure-logic unit tests, view-model tests with fakes, two-device sync test, XXXL/VoiceOver audit.
Accessibility as a slice, not a phase: the audit pass has acceptance criteria (XXXL usable, VoiceOver navigable) like any feature.

example.code:
# Slice gates (each: build + test + TestFlight):
# S1: list works offline (unit: HabitsCore; UI: list journey)
# S2: streaks correct (property-based tests on StreakCalculator)
# S3: reminders fire (notification tests with fake scheduler)
# S4: two-device edit merges (sync integration test)
# S5: XXXL + VoiceOver audit passes (manual + snapshot)
# S6: CI green, phased TestFlight rollout
example.walkthrough: Each gate is the slice's definition of done: the tests prove the behavior, TestFlight proves the shipping. The two-device sync test is the requirement made executable; the XXXL audit is the accessibility requirement made executable. A slice is done when its gate is green AND it is on TestFlight — code-complete without shipping is not done.

pitfalls: Big-bang TestFlight at the end — signing/provisioning surprises on deadline week; ship from slice 1.
Testing only at the end — the pyramid per slice; untested slices accumulate risk silently.
Accessibility as 'later' — retrofitting onto finished screens; the audit slice exists to prevent this.
Skipping the two-device test — 'sync works' without the merge test is the wishful version.
lessons.try_it: Implement slice 1 (core + list) and get it on TestFlight (internal) before building slice 2.

lessons.title: Capstone Demo and Writeup
concepts: Demo script (5 min): offline proof, sync proof, accessibility proof — requirements demonstrated live, in order, timed.
Architecture writeup: decisions + rejected alternatives + tradeoffs + 10x-scale changes — the interview prep writes itself.
TestFlight link: the interviewer can touch the app — tangibility beats description.
Honest limitations section: what is unfinished and why — self-awareness scores higher than feature inflation.

example.code:
# Demo script:
# 0:00 'Habit tracker, offline-first, syncs via CloudKit'
# 0:30 Airplane mode ON: full function (the offline proof)
# 1:30 Two devices: edit title here, body there -> both merge (sync proof)
# 3:00 Settings -> XXXL text: layout holds (accessibility proof)
# 4:00 VoiceOver on: navigate the list (inclusion proof)
# 4:30 'Architecture notes in the README; TestFlight link below'
example.walkthrough: Five minutes, four proofs, each mapped to a requirement: the demo is the acceptance criteria performed live. The script is rehearsed and timed — and each proof invites the interviewer's follow-up ('how does the merge work?'), which the writeup has already prepared you to answer. This is the capstone as interview artifact, not just as app.

pitfalls: Feature-list demos — breadth without proof; the demo should prove requirements, not enumerate features.
No writeup — 'why' questions get rambling answers; the decision log makes them crisp.
Unrehearsed demos — live bugs and dead air; the script is rehearsed like the mock interviews were.
Hiding limitations — interviewers find them; owning them with reasoning ('sync is field-level; true conflicts need the resolution UI because...') shows maturity.
lessons.try_it: Write the demo script and the first three decision-log entries; rehearse the demo twice, timed.

simulations.title: The retain cycle
simulations.brief: ProfileViewController never deallocates after dismissal. The Memory Graph shows a purple cycle — explain it and break it.

steps.symptom: ProfileViewController never deallocates after dismissal; the Memory Graph shows a retain cycle.
options: Capture self weakly: { [weak self] in ... } and guard-let a strong reference inside
Set the closure to nil in viewDidLoad
steps.explain: A closure capturing self strongly while self owns the closure is a textbook cycle. [weak self] breaks it; the guard-let re-strengthens safely for the call.

steps.symptom: Cycle fixed. Now a repeating Timer keeps the settings screen alive.
evidence: timer = Timer.scheduledTimer(withTimeInterval: 1, repeats: true) { _ in self.tick() }
options: Invalidate the timer on the view's teardown path — repeating timers retain their target
Move the timer to the AppDelegate
steps.explain: A scheduled repeating timer retains its target (via the closure) until invalidated. Ownership of the timer's lifetime belongs to the screen.

steps.symptom: Both fixed. Prove it in the interview.
options: Dismiss the screen and show the Memory Graph with no purple exclamation — deinit prints confirm
steps.explain: The proof is visual and mechanical: dismiss, and the graph shows no cycle. A deinit print is the cheapest regression signal.

simulations.debrief: Retain cycles are ownership diagrams: find who holds whom, break one link with weak, and prove it in the Memory Graph.

simulations.title: The frozen UI
simulations.brief: Tapping Sync freezes the UI for 4 seconds while photos upload. The interviewer is watching the main thread.

steps.symptom: Tapping Sync freezes the UI for 4 seconds while photos upload.
evidence: Main thread blocked in uploadAll() — synchronous URLSession
options: Move the upload off the main thread (URLSession data task / async-await) and update UI on completion
Show a spinner on the main thread during the upload
Split the upload into smaller synchronous chunks
Disable the Sync button while uploading
steps.explain: UIKit demands a responsive main thread. Async work with a completion that hops back to Main is the entire pattern.

steps.symptom: Upload is async now, but the progress bar updates from the background closure and sometimes never redraws.
evidence: progressView.progress = p // called from URLSession delegate queue
options: Dispatch UI updates to the main queue: DispatchQueue.main.async { ... }
steps.explain: UIKit is not thread-safe: every UI mutation must happen on the main thread. The hop is one line and non-negotiable.

steps.symptom: Smooth now. The interviewer asks about Swift concurrency instead of GCD.
options: Mark UI-touching code @MainActor so the compiler enforces main-thread execution
steps.explain: @MainActor moves the main-thread rule from convention to compiler enforcement — the modern answer to the same discipline.

simulations.debrief: UI responsiveness is a threading contract: work off-main, UI on-main, and let @MainActor enforce it.

simulations.title: The Core Data migration crash
simulations.brief: Adding an attribute crashes existing installs on launch. Walk the interviewer through the migration taxonomy.

steps.symptom: Adding a 'nickname' attribute crashes existing installs: 'Can't find mapping model for migration'.
evidence: added optional attribute nickname to User entity
options: Enable lightweight migration (NSMigratePersistentStoresAutomaticallyOption) — adding an optional attribute is inferable
Write a manual mapping model for every change
Ship a new app instead of an update
steps.explain: Additive, inferable changes migrate automatically with the lightweight options. Manual mapping models are for renames and splits.

steps.symptom: Lightweight migration on. Now splitting 'name' into 'firstName'+'lastName' still crashes.
options: Write a custom NSEntityMigrationPolicy mapping the old name into the two new attributes
Do the split in code after launch
steps.explain: Non-inferable changes need an explicit mapping model plus policy. That is the line between lightweight and heavyweight.

steps.symptom: Migration works. How do you test it in CI?
evidence: v1 store file checked into test fixtures
options: Migrate the fixture v1 store in a test and assert user data survives
Manually upgrade once on a device
steps.explain: Migration tests replay the real upgrade: old store in, migrated store out, data asserted. Fixtures make it repeatable.

simulations.debrief: Core Data migrations split on inferability: lightweight for additive changes, mapping models for the rest, fixtures proving both.

simulations.title: The flaky XCUITest
simulations.brief: The login UI test fails on CI whenever the mock server is slow. Stabilize it live for the interviewer.

steps.symptom: Login UI test fails on CI when the mock server is slow: the test taps Sign in before the button enables.
options: Wait on the real condition with an XCTNSPredicateExpectation instead of a fixed sleep
Run UI tests only on simulators
steps.explain: Expectations wait for the actual state; sleeps guess at timing. The flake disappears when the test observes instead of assumes.

steps.symptom: Expectation added. Still flakes when animations run long on CI.
evidence: CI simulators are slow; animations take 3x longer
options: Disable animations in the test scheme (UIView.setAnimationsEnabled(false))
steps.explain: Animations are the other timing variable. Disabling them in tests removes a whole class of flakes deterministically.

evidence: UI tests gate the release branch
options: Gate on them and treat every new flake as a P1 bug
steps.explain: Flake tolerance compounds. Gating plus immediate flake triage is what keeps a UI suite trustworthy at scale.

simulations.debrief: Flaky UI tests are timing assumptions: wait on predicates, kill animations, and gate.

simulations.title: Whiteboard: offline-first sync
simulations.brief: System-design round: offline-first notes with two-device sync conflicts. 40 minutes — reason out loud.

steps.symptom: Design offline-first notes: instant render offline, sync when online, conflicts possible.
evidence: two devices, same account, spotty network
options: Local store (Core Data/SwiftData) as source of truth; a sync engine pushes/pulls deltas; the UI observes the store
The UI fetches from the server on every appear
steps.explain: Source-of-truth locally means the UI never waits on network. Sync is a background reconciliation against that store.

steps.symptom: Interviewer: both devices edit the same note offline. Resolve it.
evidence: device A: 'buy milk'; device B: 'buy oat milk'
options: Last-writer-wins with a deterministic tiebreak, surfaced in UI when data was merged — or CRDTs if ordering matters
Crash and ask the user to pick a device
steps.explain: Conflicts need a deterministic rule plus user visibility. LWW with timestamps is the pragmatic default; CRDTs when merge semantics matter.

steps.symptom: Last: the sync engine itself — how is it structured?
options: A sync coordinator owned by the repository: push local changes, pull remote deltas, write both through the store in transactions
Sync code inside every view model
Poll the server from the view
steps.explain: Sync belongs behind the repository boundary: one coordinator, transactional writes, and the UI never knows the network exists.

simulations.debrief: Offline-first is a layering decision: the store is truth, sync reconciles behind the repository, conflicts resolve deterministically.

points: How you detected the slip early.
How you renegotiated scope with data.
What you changed in estimation afterward.
pitfalls: Claiming you never miss deadlines.
Blaming others without owning your part.

behavioral.prompt: How did you learn SwiftUI (or structured concurrency) when it was new?
behavioral.framework: Learning story: gap -> method -> applied result.
points: The specific gap and why it mattered.
Your method (docs, sample app, migrating a screen).
Where you applied it in production.
pitfalls: 'I just read the docs' with no application.
No acknowledgment of what was confusing.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you improved app performance or stability.
points: The metric (launch time, crash rate, scroll FPS) and how you measured it.
The change and why that bottleneck.
The quantified result.
pitfalls: 'It felt faster' with no numbers.
Optimizing without profiling first.

behavioral.prompt: Describe dealing with an App Store rejection or a critical 1-star review wave.
points: How you triaged (guideline section, repro).
How you communicated with Apple/users.
The guardrail added (checklist, review step).
pitfalls: Complaining about App Review.
No prevention step.

behavioral.prompt: Why iOS — and why this team?
points: What draws you to the platform (craft, constraints, user impact).
Something specific about this team's app or tech.
How the role fits your trajectory.
pitfalls: Generic praise any candidate could give.
Focusing only on compensation or prestige.

cheatsheet: Optionals: `if let` / `guard let` bind; `?.` chains; `??` defaults; `!` is a scheduled crash.
Value vs ref: struct = independent copy (CoW arrays/dicts); class = shared identity + ARC.
Closures: non-escaping by default; `@escaping` outlives the call — capture lists `[weak self]`.
Lifecycle: loadView -> viewDidLoad (once) -> viewWillAppear (every) -> viewDidLayoutSubviews -> viewDidAppear.
SwiftUI layout: parent proposes -> child chooses -> parent places. @State owns, @Binding borrows.
GCD: async never blocks; sync waits (never sync onto current/main queue). QoS: userInteractive > userInitiated > utility > background.
Modern: async/await + Task; actors isolate state; @MainActor = UI. Cancel tasks; check Task.isCancelled.
Persistence ladder: UserDefaults (settings) < Codable files (docs) < Core Data/SwiftData (queryable) < Keychain (secrets).
Core Data rule: contexts are queue-confined; pass objectIDs across queues, never objects.
Architecture: VC binds views; view model holds state; coordinator owns flow; inject dependencies for tests.
glossary: ARC
Automatic Reference Counting: deterministic deallocation at zero strong references; cycles leak.
Copy-on-write
Value-type optimization: Array/String/Dictionary share storage until mutated.
Existential
`any Protocol`: a boxed protocol value; unavailable for protocols with associated types.
PAT
Protocol with Associated Type: cannot be used directly as a property type.
MainActor
Global actor isolating code to the main thread; the modern main-thread guarantee.
QoS
Quality of Service: priority hint for GCD queues (userInteractive down to background).
Retain cycle
Ownership loop keeping reference counts above zero; broken with weak/unowned.
Coordinator
Object owning navigation flow so view controllers stay reusable.
Merge policy
Core Data rule deciding which change wins on save conflicts.
Debounce
Delay action until input pauses; implemented by cancelling the previous scheduled work.
checklist: Can you narrate the SwiftUI layout algorithm and the UIViewController lifecycle from memory?
Can you draw a retain cycle and fix it with a capture list without hesitating?
Can you explain GCD vs async/await and when you would still reach for GCD?
Do you have two STAR stories (hardest bug, disagreement) rehearsed under 3 minutes?
Have you done one timed mock of each loop type (coding, architecture, debugging, behavioral)?
Is your take-home portfolio piece reviewed against the self-review checklist?
